# N06 — What a two-hour training health test establishes

Research date: 2026-10-11. All claims below carry a source URL.

Claims are marked **[observed]**, **[calculated]**, or **[inference]**.

## 1. Decision answer: useful screening, not a 54-day warranty

A two-hour, fault-free, workload-faithful distributed training run can measure present-step performance, variability, rank stragglers, collective/pipeline behavior, short-term numerical/loss behavior, and—if the test explicitly exercises it—checkpoint creation/publication and restart correctness. It cannot establish rare-fault rates, persistent-media durability across real failures, long-horizon thermal/aging behavior, training convergence over billions of tokens, or probability that this particular rack completes 54 days. [inference] MegaScale reports operationally useful anomalies at scale but its production validation lasted weeks and involved >10,000 GPUs, unlike a rack-local two-hour exposure. [observed] [MegaScale, NSDI’24](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-jiang-ziheng.pdf)

### 1.1 What “training health” means here

Health has separable dimensions: (a) progress and quality trajectory, (b) throughput and its stability, (c) distributed synchronization/stragglers, (d) resilience and state correctness after interruption, and (e) hardware/software events. A single scalar “training passed” obscures these distinctions. [inference] MegaScale instruments logs, heartbeats, RDMA traffic, CUDA events, distributed traces, and automated diagnostics precisely because faults may appear as performance degradation or hangs rather than an explicit error. [observed] [MegaScale](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-jiang-ziheng.pdf)

## 2. Academic methods and what they actually do

### 2.1 MegaScale: observability, diagnosis, and recovery

MegaScale’s production workflow sends heartbeats with executor/process status, logs and RDMA metrics; detects missed heartbeats/anomalous traffic; stops the job, runs diagnostics, evicts faulty nodes and restarts from a checkpoint. Its two-stage checkpoint copies GPU state into host memory (training resumes), then asynchronously persists it to HDFS; on restart, one worker reads shared partitions and broadcasts them. This is staged asynchronous persistence—not proof that a just-copied host-memory checkpoint has already become durable. [observed] [MegaScale §4](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-jiang-ziheng.pdf)

MegaScale’s health analysis also includes CUDA-event timing by rank, heatmaps and distributed timeline traces. It reports ~0.5% slower machines materially constraining training and finding unstable MFU from critical-path skew / late collective launch; removing stragglers improved MFU. Pipeline visualization reveals bubbles and dependencies across ranks. These motivate a benchmark reporting per-rank step-time distributions and collective/pipeline wait, not just rack-average tokens/s. [observed] [MegaScale §5](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-jiang-ziheng.pdf)

MegaScale’s model convergence evidence is not a two-hour stability claim: its controlled convergence microbenchmarks used a smaller 13B model, while the reported production run lasted several weeks and restarted over 100 times. The paper thus demonstrates the value of these mechanisms, not that two hours predicts another rack’s long-run fate. [observed] [MegaScale §§6.2–6.3](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-jiang-ziheng.pdf)

### 2.2 CheckFreq: iteration-granular checkpointing and data position

CheckFreq (FAST ’21) profiles training to choose checkpoint frequency, dynamically tunes it to bound overhead, checkpoints the data-loader state using a resumable iterator, and pipelines a two-phase snapshot/persist path. Snapshot copies learnable state to a user-space CPU buffer; persistence writes durable storage. The resumable iterator is important: resuming weights but replaying/skipping data changes the training trajectory. [observed] [CheckFreq paper](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/fast21-mohan.pdf) · [Microsoft Research summary](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/checkfreq-frequent-fine-grained-dnn-checkpointing/)

A test must distinguish “snapshot finished” from “checkpoint published durably.” A passing write call or file presence is insufficient: require a completed manifest/commit marker, verify all rank shards and checksums, then terminate the writer/process at controlled points and reload only a fully published generation. This is a proposed validation derived from the papers’ staged pipeline, not a claim that CheckFreq’s paper certifies a rack’s power-loss behavior. [inference] [CheckFreq](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/fast21-mohan.pdf)

### 2.3 Oobleck: replica-based recovery, not async checkpointing

Oobleck designs pipeline templates with redundancy; after failure it reinstantiates pipeline(s) from those templates and copies missing model state from pipeline replicas, avoiding a full checkpoint restart. It is therefore replica/state-reconstruction recovery, not “asynchronous checkpointing.” Its paper compares this approach with checkpoint-centered systems including Varuna and CheckFreq. [observed] [Oobleck](https://arxiv.org/html/2309.08125v2)

### 2.4 Varuna: elastic job morphing plus checkpoint-based recovery

Varuna combines pipeline and data parallelism, dynamically morphs pipeline depth/data replicas as spot resources change, and periodically checkpoints at mini-batch boundaries. It checkpoints each layer independently, shards writes across data-parallel replicas, writes first to local SSD and copies to cloud storage in the background. It restores from checkpoint under a new configuration and saves GPU RNG state for recomputation correctness. Heartbeats report per-microbatch forward/backward compute time so the manager can exclude slow fail-stutter workers. This is checkpoint-based elasticity with background remote copying—not Oobleck-style state reconstruction from replicas. [observed] [Varuna EuroSys’22 full paper §§4.5–4.6, 6](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/varuna-eurosys22.pdf) · [Oobleck comparison](https://arxiv.org/html/2309.08125v2)

### 2.5 Gradient-noise scale and stability are workload properties

Gradient noise scale literature estimates a scale-dependent useful batch size from gradient signal/noise; it informs optimization and parallelization, not hardware reliability. A two-hour sample of loss/gradient norms can expose gross divergence, overflow, repeated skipped updates, or anomalies on the exact recipe, but stochastic batches, seed, learning-rate phase, precision, and model/data choice confound extrapolation. It cannot certify eventual convergence or rule out late loss spikes. [observed/inference] [McCandlish et al., “An empirical model of large-batch training”](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.06162) · [OpenAI explainer](https://openai.com/index/how-ai-training-scales/)

Loss spikes are not synonymous with hardware faults. Optimization dynamics, data outliers, numerical precision, and infrastructure can all contribute; triage needs loss plus gradient norm, scaler/overflow and skipped-step counters, sample/data position, per-rank consistency, GPU/NVLink/network telemetry and logs. Compare deterministic replay where feasible, while recognizing nondeterministic kernels and distributed reductions can prevent bitwise equivalence. A spike that appears on all ranks and repeats for the same batch points differently from a rank-local divergence coincident with an XID/link error. [inference] [“Loss Spike in Training Neural Networks” (arXiv:2305.12133), a loss-landscape/feature-condensation study, not infrastructure fault diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.12133v2) · [MegaScale observability](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-jiang-ziheng.pdf)

## 3. MLPerf Training: exact scope and non-scope

For Closed division, MLPerf Training measures wall-clock time for a complete benchmark run to its defined quality target under benchmark-specific rules. Open division permits arbitrary stopping criteria (including fixed time), but requires reporting final quality using the Closed quality measure. Closed division constrains model/data/training semantics; convergence is checked against reference convergence points, and multiple runs characterize score variation. [observed] [MLPerf Training Rules §§1, 4, 9, 12–13](https://github.com/mlcommons/training_policies/blob/master/training_rules.adoc)

This is not an interruption-tolerance certification. General §9.4 says checkpoints are at submitter discretion and are not required to be produced or retained. Exception: v6.1 Qwen3.5-397B-A17B post-training §14 requires a checkpoint after every step in its validation window and evaluates checkpoints offline; scoring uses the passing checkpoint’s weight-update timestamp, excluding checkpoint-writing time. This benchmark-specific scoring protocol does not certify crash recovery, checkpoint atomicity/durability, data-position/RNG restoration, restart correctness, or interruption tolerance. [observed] [MLPerf Training Rules §§9.4, 14](https://github.com/mlcommons/training_policies/blob/master/training_rules.adoc)

MLPerf’s utilization appendix defines model FLOPs utilization as model-definition tensor FLOPs divided by peak system tensor FLOPs/s × runtime; recomputation FLOPs are excluded, and utilization is explicitly not an official MLPerf metric. Thus rack-bench should declare its own MFU numerator, peak denominator (hardware and precision), counted time, and treatment of communication/evaluation/recomputation; a throughput percentage without that denominator is not auditable. [observed] [MLPerf Training Rules §23](https://github.com/mlcommons/training_policies/blob/master/training_rules.adoc)

Current rules also illustrate why benchmark success is workload-specific: v6.1 includes distinct small-LLM, MoE pretraining, fine-tuning and post-training workloads; quality target, evaluation cadence, allowed formats and reference convergence constraints differ. Passing one benchmark does not certify arbitrary Llama-class pretraining recipes or 54-day uptime. [observed/inference] [MLPerf Training Rules](https://github.com/mlcommons/training_policies/blob/master/training_rules.adoc)

## 4. Two-hour candidate health test: measurements and honest interpretations

### 4.1 Run a real distributed workload with meaningful exposure

Use the intended software stack and a representative model/configuration, sequence length, precision, parallelism layout, optimizer, data path and checkpoint target. Warm up, then collect steady-state windows across the full rack; record warm-up separately. Ensure all 18 trays participate. Two hours can establish measured behavior under this configuration, not under different tenant recipes or later software changes. [inference] MegaScale’s findings were tied to full-stack, per-rank observability at large scale. [observed] [MegaScale](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-jiang-ziheng.pdf)

### 4.2 Metrics to collect

1. **Progress/performance:** tokens/s and samples/s; step-time median/p95/p99 and time series; warm-up vs steady-state; GPU clocks/power/temperature/throttle, memory/ECC, XID, NVLink/NIC counters. Record all rank values, not only average. [inference] [MegaScale](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-jiang-ziheng.pdf)
2. **MFU:** state exact FLOPs/token or per-step model FLOPs, peak tensor throughput at the actual precision and deployed GPUs, and counted interval. Report useful-model-FLOPs MFU separately from hardware FLOPs including recomputation. Do not use an undocumented nominal peak as denominator. [observed/inference] [MLPerf utilization rules](https://github.com/mlcommons/training_policies/blob/master/training_rules.adoc#23-utilization)
3. **Stragglers / pipeline:** rank-wise forward/backward/optimizer time; all-reduce/all-gather/reduce-scatter duration and wait; pipeline bubble/idle fraction; data-loader stalls; rank spread and outlier persistence. A rack-average rate hides the slowest rank that gates synchronous progress. [inference] [MegaScale](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-jiang-ziheng.pdf)
4. **Optimization/numerics:** loss and validation trend on a fixed evaluation set; gradient norm, overflow/underflow, skipped optimizer steps, NaN/Inf, LR and optimizer state; sample/token position and seed/RNG state. Treat any loss spike as a triage event, not automatic hardware failure nor harmlessness. [inference] [gradient-noise scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.06162) · [loss-spike landscape study](https://arxiv.org/html/2305.12133v2)
5. **Checkpoint transaction:** record snapshot start/end, durable persistence completion, generation/manifest publication, shard checksums and bytes, then load the published checkpoint in a fresh process. Simulate process kill at snapshot, in-flight persistence, and after publication; verify incomplete generations are rejected and previous committed generation remains loadable. [inference] [CheckFreq](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/fast21-mohan.pdf) · [MegaScale](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-jiang-ziheng.pdf)
6. **Restart semantic correctness:** force a controlled interruption after committed step k; restore model, optimizer, scheduler, scaler, data cursor/shard position, and RNG states; verify next-step inputs and state continuity. Compare resumed trajectory with uninterrupted control using tolerances appropriate to nondeterministic distributed math; check loss/gradients and step counters, not merely that the job restarted. [inference] [CheckFreq](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/fast21-mohan.pdf)
7. **Fault response:** inject at least one process failure and, where safe, a node/link fault; measure detection, restart/replacement time, lost work since durable checkpoint, and successful return to useful throughput. One successful injected event proves only that event/path works once. [inference] [MegaScale](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-jiang-ziheng.pdf) · [Oobleck](https://arxiv.org/html/2309.08125v2)

### 4.3 Distinguish checkpoint staging, publication, and persistence

A GPU-to-host-memory snapshot is staging; async file/object writes are persistence; atomic publication is a separate protocol step. A valid generation must represent a consistent optimizer step across shards and metadata. A checkpoint that exists but lacks a committed manifest, has missing shards, or is still volatile in host memory is not a recoverable durable checkpoint. Rack-bench can test its configured storage path and restart semantics, but cannot infer survival of facility-wide power loss, storage-site loss, or correlated control-plane failure from a two-hour run. [inference] [MegaScale §4.4](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-jiang-ziheng.pdf) · [CheckFreq](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/fast21-mohan.pdf)

## 5. Statistically honest limits of two hours

For a fault-free observation of T hours, under a homogeneous Poisson failure process with independent events, constant rate λ, and complete detection, zero observed failures gives a one-sided 95% upper rate bound of −ln(0.05)/T. At T=2 h, that is 1.498 failures/hour for the *tested unit and event definition*; equivalently, the 95% upper bound on probability of at least one such event in the next 54 days is 1−exp(−1.498×1296), effectively 100%. [calculated] This is not a useful assurance of long-run survival. Under the Poisson model, P(0 events)=exp(−λT); setting this to 0.05 gives λ=−ln(0.05)/T. [NIST Poisson reference](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda366j.htm)

The classic “rule of three” approximation gives 3/T = 1.5 events/hour, same result. [calculated] [Hanley & Lippman-Hand, “If Nothing Goes Wrong, Is Everything All Right?”](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6827763/)

If every GPU/tray were an independent identical component with a constant rate, pooling exposure across components could tighten a *component-event rate* bound, but cannot estimate rack-level common-cause events, correlated failures, changing workload/temperature, repair behavior, or job failure probability without a validated model. Do not apply fleet failure rates to predict this rack’s 54-day completion probability. [inference] [Meta cluster reliability study](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)

Zero-failure exposure is only informative when the monitored event definition, exposure denominator, independence/stationarity assumptions, and censoring are stated. A smoke burn-in that stops at two hours does not show a failure rate; it shows no detected event during those particular observed hours. [inference] [NIST Poisson reference](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda366j.htm)

## 6. Evidence distinctions, examples, and conflicts

- **Checkpoint approach is not one category:** CheckFreq pipelines snapshot and durable persistence and preserves iterator position; MegaScale stages GPU state in host memory then asynchronously writes HDFS; Oobleck reconstructs missing state via pipeline replicas; Varuna combines elastic morphing with periodic layer-wise checkpointing to local SSD and background cloud copy. Their mechanisms and failure assumptions differ. [observed] Sources: [CheckFreq](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/fast21-mohan.pdf), [MegaScale](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-jiang-ziheng.pdf), [Oobleck](https://arxiv.org/html/2309.08125v2), [Varuna full paper](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/varuna-eurosys22.pdf).
- **“Loss decreasing” is weak evidence:** short monotonic loss is consistent with healthy execution but does not prove convergence, absence of a later numerical instability, or data correctness. Gradient noise and stochasticity make small-window comparisons non-deterministic. [inference] [McCandlish et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.06162)
- **MFU can mislead:** formula/peak precision, model FLOP convention, time window and recompute accounting change the result; MLPerf itself calls utilization non-official. Compare fixed recipe and publish denominator, not an unqualified pass threshold. [observed/inference] [MLPerf](https://github.com/mlcommons/training_policies/blob/master/training_rules.adoc#23-utilization)
- **Failure rates do not transfer:** Meta’s two-cluster trace study found job failure exposure varies by job scale and failure causes; its fleet-scale observations are useful evidence that long runs are exposed to diverse events, but not a rate to assign to this Chennai rack. [observed/inference] [Meta study](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)

## 7. Independent node conclusion

A two-hour training health result should state: “This exact 18-tray rack, software image, training recipe and checkpoint path sustained the reported measured throughput and loss behavior during the observed interval; listed restart/fault injections passed or failed.” It should not say “safe for 54 days,” “converges,” or “MLPerf-certified for interruption recovery.” [inference] [MLPerf Training Rules](https://github.com/mlcommons/training_policies/blob/master/training_rules.adoc) · [Meta reliability study](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)

Candidate PASS evidence: complete rack participation; stable per-rank step-time and communication/pipeline metrics against declared thresholds; no uncorrected hardware errors/throttling; numerics within declared tolerances; durable checkpoint publication verified; a controlled restart restores coherent step/data/RNG/optimizer state; injected recovery returns to useful training. Thresholds must be measured thresholds set in the rack-bench profile, not vendor claims. [inference]

The strongest bridge to a 30–90-day commitment is layered evidence: two-hour measured acceptance + explicit restart test + continued production telemetry, checkpoint-retention/restore drills, alerting and operational SLA. These reduce uncertainty but still cannot guarantee no rare or correlated event. [inference] [Meta reliability study](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)

## 8. Sources and confidence

- **High confidence, primary:** MegaScale NSDI’24 full paper; MLPerf current training rules; CheckFreq FAST’21 full paper; Oobleck paper. These directly describe mechanisms and benchmark scope.
- **High confidence, primary:** Varuna EuroSys’22 full paper inspected; it specifies continuous layer-wise checkpointing, local SSD plus background cloud copy, RNG state, and fail-stutter heartbeat screening.
- **Moderate:** gradient-noise-scale primary study supports the limited interpretation of the statistic; application to arbitrary Llama-class recipes remains workload-dependent.
- **Moderate:** Meta failure-trace paper is primary fleet evidence; its datasets and scale differ materially from one rack and cannot yield a rack-specific forecast.
- **Low as a predictor:** two-hour zero-failure observation for a 54-day horizon. The Poisson upper bound is mathematically valid only under stated assumptions and illustrates how little the interval establishes.

## Gaps

- No exact tenant model, token budget, optimizer, data pipeline, checkpoint destination, or acceptance thresholds were specified; these must be fixed for workload-faithful tests.
- Two hours cannot validate all recovery paths. Multiple fault injections and repeated restore drills improve mechanism coverage, not rare-event probability estimation.
- No public study provides a defensible conversion from this particular 18-tray GB300-class, Chennai rack’s two-hour exposure to a 54-day run-success probability.

# Public AI-lab training runs: health, accounting, interruptions, and recovery correctness

Research date: 2026-10-11. All claims below carry a source URL.

Claims are marked **[observed]** (reported directly by a source), **[calculated]** (arithmetic from reported data), or **[inference]** (interpretation or proposed rack-bench implication).

## 1. Executive answer: two hours certify a snapshot, not a 54-day run

### 1.1 Scope of this node

This research asks what public AI-lab training records establish about operational health and scientifically valid recovery. It does not treat vendor specifications as PASS evidence. For rack-bench’s measured category checks (~2h/category) on an 18-tray GB300-class NVL72 rack, a training microbenchmark can establish that a specified workload runs reproducibly at measured throughput, MFU, loss behavior, and checkpoint/resume correctness in the tested software/configuration. It cannot establish multi-week failure rate, day/night stability, the tail of recovery times, or correctness across all interruption causes. **[inference]** That separation follows directly from the scale and duration of the Llama 3, OPT, and BLOOM records, which describe many weeks and real interruptions, rather than a short acceptance run ([Llama 3 paper §3.3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783); [OPT logbook](https://github.com/facebookresearch/metaseq/tree/main/projects/OPT/chronicles); [BLOOM chronicles](https://github.com/bigscience-workshop/bigscience/blob/master/train/tr11-176B-ml/chronicles.md)).

### 1.2 Top findings

1. **Llama is the useful interruption anchor, but its denominator must remain 419 unexpected events.** The 54-day snapshot records 466 total interruptions: 47 planned and 419 unexpected. The report says ~78% of the 419 unexpected interruptions were attributed to confirmed or suspected hardware issues; GPU issues were 58.7% of unexpected issues, not 58.7% of all 466 interruptions. The table’s GPU subtypes and rounded percentages need careful reading (§2). [observed] [Meta primary report](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783).
2. **Failure count is not failure rate or rack lifetime.** Llama ran up to 16,384 H100s on a production cluster; a rack-scale two-hour test samples neither that population nor 54 days of aging/exposure. It can surface existing defects and characterize this sample’s throughput and recovery, but cannot establish a low future event rate. [inference] [Meta report](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783).
3. **MFU is an accounting convention, not a self-validating scalar.** Its numerator depends on model FLOPs/token and useful token throughput; denominator depends on accelerator count, precision-specific theoretical peak, and time window. Dense-vs-MoE, recomputation, padded/dropped tokens, warmup, evaluation/checkpoint pauses, and whether “peak” is a precision-appropriate Tensor Core peak can materially change interpretation. [inference] [Meta report](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783); [DeepSeek-V3 report](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.19437v1); [MFU metric study](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.03880v1).
4. **Recovery correctness requires more than loading weights.** Public BLOOM evidence shows a concrete optimizer/TP synchronization defect that could leave ranks inconsistent, and RNG state also needed synchronization. Validate model, optimizer, scheduler, scaler, RNG, data position, gradient accumulation and step counters—not merely that a process restarts. [observed] [BLOOM chronicle](https://github.com/bigscience-workshop/bigscience/blob/master/train/tr11-176B-ml/chronicles.md).
5. **Two hours can test the mechanism; it cannot predict MTTR distribution.** Inject controlled process/GPU/network/storage failures and record detection-to-useful-step latency, lost useful tokens, rollback point, and exact replay equivalence. Published “automatic recovery” is not evidence of zero downtime or full state equivalence. [inference] [Meta report](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783); [Gemini SOSP’23](https://zhuangwang93.github.io/docs/Gemini_SOSP23.pdf).

## 2. Llama 3.1 405B: verified interruption denominator and reliability claims

### 2.1 Exact scope and counts **[observed]**

Meta’s paper identifies a **54-day snapshot period of Llama 3 405B pre-training**, on a production cluster using up to **16K H100 GPUs**. It reports **466 job interruptions total**, of which **47 were planned** (automated firmware upgrades or operator-initiated configuration/dataset updates), leaving **419 unexpected**. It reports **higher than 90% effective training time**, defined in the paper as time spent doing useful training divided by elapsed time. These are snapshot/run-report values, not a device-level MTTF or guaranteed utilization SLA. ([Meta, “The Llama 3 Herd of Models,” §3.3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783))

### 2.2 What 78% and 58.7% actually mean **[observed]**

- The paper says approximately **78% of the 419 unexpected interruptions** were attributed to confirmed hardware issues or suspected hardware-related issues (examples include silent data corruption and unplanned individual-host maintenance). Denominator: unexpected interruptions, not 466 total interruptions. ([Meta §3.3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783))
- It then says GPU issues are the largest category, “accounting for **58.7% of all unexpected issues**.” The intended denominator is again the 419 unexpected events, not the hardware-only subset and not 466 total interruptions. The paper’s table labels its percentage column “% of Interruptions” and lists subtype percentages that do not all reconcile with the stated unexpected-event denominator: e.g. faulty GPU 148 / 466 = 31.8%, while listed 30.1%; 148 / 419 = 35.3%; the reported 30.1% does not reconcile directly with either. Similarly HBM3 72 / 466 = 15.5%, 72 / 419 = 17.2%, matching the latter. **Do not quote the subtype table percentages as though they shared a consistently auditable denominator.** The paper’s prose-level 58.7% is the anchor to cite, while counts by subtype remain safer than copied percentages. [calculated] ([Meta Table 5 and §3.3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783))
- The reported GPU-related subtype counts include 148 faulty-GPU events, 72 GPU HBM3 memory events, 19 GPU SRAM memory events, 17 GPU system-processor events, 6 silent-data-corruption events, and 6 thermal-interface/sensor events. The paper also lists 35 switch/cable network events, 54 software-bug events, and other host/dependency categories. Counts should not be summed blindly into mutually exclusive root causes absent the source’s taxonomy details. [observed] ([Meta Table 5](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783))
- “Only three” events required significant manual intervention; the rest were handled by automation. This is a statement about intervention burden, not automatic repair correctness, and the paper does not publish a full per-event MTTR distribution in the table. [observed] ([Meta §3.3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783))

### 2.3 What Meta actually did for health, diagnosis, and resilience **[observed]**

Synchronous training means one GPU failure can force a whole distributed job restart. Meta describes production-grade automated maintenance, reduced startup/checkpoint time, rapid diagnosis tooling, PyTorch NCCL flight-recorder metadata and stack traces, automatic trace dumps on watchdog/heartbeat timeout, and online activation of extra tracing without job restart. NVLink failures can manifest as stalled GPU load/store operations without clean error codes; monitoring and timeout detection therefore matter. Slow, still-functioning stragglers can impede thousands of GPUs, so Meta prioritized suspicious process-group communications to find them. ([Meta §3.3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783))

The report also notes 1–2% diurnal throughput variation, attributed to mid-day temperature and GPU DVFS. This is direct evidence that a short test at one time of day may miss a small but real drift; it is not evidence that rack-bench should expect the same magnitude or cause on GB300. [observed] ([Meta §3.3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783))

### 2.4 Calculated event-rate illustrations—not lifetime predictions

- 419 unexpected interruptions / 54 days = **7.76 unexpected job interruptions/day** across the full reported cluster; 54 days × 24 hours / 419 = **3.09 hours per event on average**. This averages the entire cluster-job record; it does **not** mean each GPU fails every 3.09 hours, nor that events are independent or uniformly distributed. [calculated] ([Meta §3.3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783))
- 47 planned + 419 unexpected = 466 total. Planned interruptions are 10.1% of that total; unexpected are 89.9%. These percentages are descriptive of the 54-day snapshot only. [calculated] ([Meta §3.3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783))

## 3. Cross-run evidence: failures, loss behavior, and incompatible claims

### 3.1 OPT-175B logbook: operational granularity, imperfect comparability **[observed]**

OPT’s first-party 10%-through update documents exact incidents: experiment 11.xx had ECC-related restarts, repeated gradient-norm/loss explosions and NaNs after restarts, and instability mitigations (clipping/LR/optimizer changes); experiment 12.xx later had hardware-related restarts including missing GPUs, hangs after adding a node, ECC/CUDA/NCCL errors, and partial checkpoint upload after hardware error. It also reports a dataset formatting problem causing implausibly low perplexity (JSON escaping/whitespace/corpus formatting), a warning that loss metrics need data-pipeline sanity checks. These are dated author reports, not a normalized event-rate dataset. Separately, Gemini summarizes OPT as 992 A100 GPUs and ~110 failures over two months with ~178,000 GPU-hours wasted; do not compare that secondary summary directly to Llama’s 419 job interruptions without harmonized exposure and event definitions. ([OPT 10%-through update, Nov. 17, 2021](https://github.com/facebookresearch/metaseq/blob/main/projects/OPT/chronicles/10_percent_update.md); [Gemini SOSP’23](https://zhuangwang93.github.io/docs/Gemini_SOSP23.pdf))

The logbook’s lasting certification lesson is operational: failures can be frequent enough that restarting manually is untenable; monitoring training behavior and health-checking/replacing suspect nodes matter. Susan Zhang’s public talk describes recurring 2–3 restarts/day at one point and cluster health checks, but that is recollection/talk, not an independently normalized failure-rate dataset. ([Susan Zhang, OPT lifecycle talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=R8cHHKp1Fvg))

### 3.2 BLOOM: checkpoint intervals and recovery correctness **[observed]**

BLOOM chronicles give unusually detailed dated logs. At the beginning of the 176B run, the team reported 105-second iterations, checkpoints taking ~40 seconds, and evaluations every 1,000 iterations costing about seven iterations (~0.7% of training). After losing 7.3 hours when a GPU crashed two iterations before a checkpoint, the team changed checkpoint interval to 200 iterations, then to 100 iterations to bound rollback to roughly three hours. That establishes a **run-specific** checkpoint trade-off, not a universal ideal frequency. ([BLOOM chronicle, Mar 18–22, 2022](https://github.com/bigscience-workshop/bigscience/blob/master/train/tr11-176B-ml/chronicles.md))

A checkpoint interval also incurs save time and can be a correctness boundary. BLOOM uncovered a BF16 optimizer bug that failed to clip gradients on tensor-parallel ranks >1, leaving layer-norm weights/biases out of sync. It could appear to train but damage correctness when merging TP ranks at completion. They wrote a reproducer, fixed optimizer/checkpoint-load synchronization, and later synchronized RNG state. This is concrete evidence that “resumed and loss keeps decreasing” is not a sufficient correctness criterion. ([BLOOM chronicle, Mar 24–Apr 6](https://github.com/bigscience-workshop/bigscience/blob/master/train/tr11-176B-ml/chronicles.md))

BLOOM also logs an LM-loss spike that rose sharply for a few steps and returned near baseline in ~30 iterations, with a concurrent gradient-norm spike. It was not automatically declared a fatal divergence. Elsewhere the chronicle documents evaluation deadlocks, a 5% throughput drop traced to a slow GPU/node, and lost hours due to hangs. Therefore loss, gradient norm, throughput, collectives, data-loader state, and evaluation behavior need joint triage. ([BLOOM chronicle](https://github.com/bigscience-workshop/bigscience/blob/master/train/tr11-176B-ml/chronicles.md))

### 3.3 DeepSeek-V3: stable loss is an outcome, not a general guarantee **[observed]**

DeepSeek-V3 reports 14.8T pretraining tokens on 2,048 H800 GPUs and says it experienced no irrecoverable loss spikes and did not roll back during the full training process. It also states its training efficiency depended on extensive system/model co-design: FP8 mixed precision, high-precision accumulation in selected paths, dynamic expert-load bias adjustment, no token dropping, and communication/computation overlap. These are author-reported results; the report does not provide an interruption-event table or independent audit log comparable to Meta’s. ([DeepSeek-V3 report §§1, 3, 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.19437v1))

DeepSeek’s FP8-vs-BF16 ablations report relative loss error below 0.25% on two smaller baseline MoE models, not a general full-scale rack reliability bound. Its appendix also documents that changing activation-gradient quantization granularity caused divergence at ~300B tokens in a ~16B-parameter MoE experiment. That is an important distinction: stable headline run and ablation evidence are scoped to their recipes/configurations. ([DeepSeek-V3 report §3.3 and Appendix B](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.19437v1))

### 3.4 Reconciling stability claims

Meta reports few loss spikes and no interventions for divergence under its dense Llama 3 recipe, but hundreds of *infrastructure/job* interruptions. DeepSeek reports no irrecoverable loss spikes or rollbacks under a distinct MoE/FP8 recipe. BLOOM records both recoverable training loss spikes and substantial infrastructure/software interruptions. These statements are compatible: numerical stability, hardware uptime, job recovery, and end-to-end useful progress are separate dimensions. [inference] ([Meta](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783); [DeepSeek](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.19437v1); [BLOOM](https://github.com/bigscience-workshop/bigscience/blob/master/train/tr11-176B-ml/chronicles.md))

## 4. Throughput, MFU, useful-token accounting, and eval cadence

### 4.1 MFU requires declared numerator and denominator **[observed + inference]**

A useful standard form is:

`MFU = (useful model FLOPs per token × useful tokens processed per second) / (GPU count × peak FLOP/s per GPU for the chosen precision)`

This is an analytical ratio. It is not the same as `nvidia-smi` utilization, Tensor Core active time, or executed hardware FLOPs. A dense-transformer approximation commonly starts near 6×parameter-count FLOPs/token for forward+backward, with attention terms adding sequence-length-dependent work; exact accounting is architecture-, context-, objective-, and convention-dependent. [observed] ([PaLM, Chowdhery et al., §4.1 and Appendix B](https://arxiv.org/html/2204.02311); [Meta Llama report](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783); [MFU metric study](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.03880v1))

Meta gives an unusually interpretable example: BF16 MFU 43% on 8,192 GPUs, 41% on 16,384 GPUs at 8K context, and 38% on 16,384 GPUs at 128K context. The paper attributes the 43→41% drop to smaller batch per data-parallel group while keeping global tokens/batch constant; the 128K configuration has different context-parallel setup. Thus MFU requires configuration labels and should be measured across the actual job shape, not presented as a rack-invariant property. ([Meta Table 4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783))

**Accounting checks to require:** [inference; grounded in PaLM §4.1 and Appendix B](https://arxiv.org/html/2204.02311)
- State precision and peak table (e.g., BF16 vs FP8 peak; whether Tensor Core peak rather than IEEE FP32 scalar peak is used). [inference]
- State model FLOPs/token formula and whether attention, embeddings/output head, auxiliary losses/MTP, and any sparsity/routing are counted. For MoE distinguish total parameters from activated parameters: DeepSeek V3 is 671B total, 37B activated/token, so dense 6×total-parameter arithmetic is plainly the wrong denominator/numerator proxy for routed layers. [observed/inference] ([DeepSeek report](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.19437v1))
- State whether MFU counts only analytically necessary model FLOPs or all executed work. Activation recomputation increases executed operations; model-FLOPs MFU conventionally treats recomputation overhead differently from hardware FLOPs utilization (HFU). Both can be useful, but they answer different questions. [inference] ([PaLM §4.1 and Appendix B](https://arxiv.org/html/2204.02311); [MFU metric discussion](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.03880v1))
- State “tokens” as input tokens actually consumed, not padded slots, generated/evaluation tokens, or samples×nominal sequence length. Report raw useful tokens/s alongside MFU, and say whether data-loader starvation, skipped steps, gradient accumulation, warmup and eval/checkpoint windows are included. [inference]

A benchmark with warmup excluded from steady-state MFU but including its wall time in end-to-end goodput can look efficient by MFU and still deliver fewer useful tokens per wall-clock hour. Report both steady-state throughput/MFU and wall-clock goodput: useful training tokens / elapsed benchmark time, with setup, warmup, eval, checkpoint and recovery overhead included. [inference]

### 4.2 Evaluations and scientific health monitoring

BLOOM scheduled a multi-dataset evaluation once every 1,000 iterations, with an observed cost of ~7 training iterations (~0.7%). Llama 3 assessed adaptation after context-length changes using short-context eval recovery and needle-in-a-haystack tests. DeepSeek’s public report says no irrecoverable spikes/rollbacks but does not publish a universal evaluation cadence. These show that eval is both a measurable throughput cost and an essential model-quality signal. [observed] ([BLOOM chronicle](https://github.com/bigscience-workshop/bigscience/blob/master/train/tr11-176B-ml/chronicles.md); [Meta §3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783); [DeepSeek](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.19437v1))

### 4.3 Loss-spike triage: operationally useful policy **[inference]**

A short rack-bench run cannot certify that a customer’s full data/model recipe will never diverge. It can certify the diagnostic loop and check for immediate numerical pathologies. Record per-step/short-window loss, gradient norm (global and if possible per-layer), skipped/NaN/Inf updates, learning rate, token count, throughput, GPU error counters, collective timeout/trace evidence, temperatures/power, and per-rank agreement. A single spike should trigger synchronized evidence capture; repeated spikes, non-finite state, persistent loss offset, or a rank mismatch should fail or require explicit investigation. Do not automatically reset loss history or silently skip updates. [inference] ([BLOOM incident evidence](https://github.com/bigscience-workshop/bigscience/blob/master/train/tr11-176B-ml/chronicles.md); [Meta diagnostic methods](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783); [DeepSeek numeric-stability ablations](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.19437v1))

For any spike, compare before/after checkpoints on the *same fixed validation token set* and recipe. Replay the affected batch sequence, compare loss/gradients/update tensors and optimizer state, inspect data corruption/duplicate or cursor changes, precision/scaler state, collective/rank consistency, and hardware logs. This separates a transient outlier from persistent numerical divergence or a recovery-state mismatch. This is a proposed triage protocol, not a claim that a single public lab uses exactly this rubric. PaLM reports roughly 20 irregular loss spikes, mitigated by resuming about 100 steps before a spike and skipping 200–500 batches; BLOOM also logs transient loss/gradient spikes and instability. These source examples motivate evidence capture and triage, not a universal pass/fail rule. [inference] ([PaLM §5.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2204.02311))

## 5. Checkpoint and restart correctness: what state must survive

### 5.1 Full-resume state inventory **[inference]**

For ordinary synchronous optimizer training, a valid restart generally needs, as applicable:

1. Model parameters (including all shards/ranks and master weights).
2. Optimizer state (e.g. Adam first/second moments, step counters, FP32 master weights, gradient-scaler state).
3. Learning-rate scheduler state and global optimizer/update step.
4. RNG states for Python, NumPy, framework CPU and each GPU/rank; RNG synchronization matters when topology/parallel ranks are involved.
5. Data sampler/shuffle state, dataset shard/epoch and exact cursor/consumed-sample/token position; worker/prefetch state where it changes order.
6. Gradient accumulation/microbatch position and any in-flight gradient state—or checkpoint only at a well-defined optimizer-step boundary and replay from there.
7. Training configuration/code/data identity, parallelism mapping, tokenizer, precision mode, and checkpoint manifest/version.

This inventory is a correctness requirement inferred from optimizer dynamics and directly motivated by public logs of optimizer-state, TP-rank and RNG synchronization problems; it is not a blanket claim that every cited lab publicly lists every field. ([BLOOM chronicle](https://github.com/bigscience-workshop/bigscience/blob/master/train/tr11-176B-ml/chronicles.md); [PyTorch distributed checkpoint docs](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.checkpoint.html))

### 5.2 A convincing resume-equivalence test **[inference]**

Run a deterministic baseline from state S for K updates and save final model/optimizer/scheduler/RNG/data-cursor state. Separately restart from a checkpoint at step k and execute the same remaining data, with the same world-size/parallel layout. Compare: step and consumed-token counters; next-batch/sample IDs; LR; loss and gradient norms; model/optimizer tensor checksums or bounded numerical differences; final checkpoint manifest; and a fixed validation loss. For hardware failures that require topology change, exact bitwise equality may not be achievable; predeclare numerical tolerances and compare against a clean run under that same changed topology. Verify that the restart neither repeats nor skips data silently, and that a partially written checkpoint is not treated as complete. A mere process reaching “step K” does not prove equivalence. This proposed test is anchored in PaLM’s bitwise-reproducibility claim from checkpoints and BLOOM’s optimizer/TP synchronization and RNG-state defects; PyTorch distributed-checkpoint documentation describes save/load support, but does not validate application-level replay. [inference] ([PaLM §5](https://arxiv.org/html/2204.02311); [BLOOM chronicle](https://github.com/bigscience-workshop/bigscience/blob/master/train/tr11-176B-ml/chronicles.md); [PyTorch distributed checkpoint docs](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.checkpoint.html))

### 5.3 Checkpoint interval, save cost, and MTTR are separate quantities

Checkpoint frequency governs potential lost work; save time governs pause/overlap cost; retrieval/reload/warmup and machine replacement govern recovery time. Gemini’s SOSP paper explicitly models average wasted time from checkpoint time, half the checkpoint interval (assuming uniformly distributed failures), and retrieval time; it measured >13× faster recovery than baselines in its tested setup and describes high-frequency in-memory checkpointing. Those are its evaluated configurations, not a guaranteed NVL72 outcome. ([Gemini SOSP’23](https://zhuangwang93.github.io/docs/Gemini_SOSP23.pdf))

Meta says startup/checkpoint time reduction helped achieve >90% effective training time, but does not publish event-level MTTR distribution in the cited section. The Llama report’s three significant manual-intervention events do not imply 416 zero-duration recoveries. Report median and tail recovery latency separately, plus useful progress lost, automatic/manual classifications, and denominator. ([Meta §3.3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783))

## 6. What two hours can measure on rack-bench—and what it misses

### 6.1 Practical measured checks (PASS means observed evidence) **[inference]**

Within a two-hour training-category slot, pin the model recipe, software, precision, GPU topology, data sample and clock/thermal conditions; then collect:

- **Repeatable training throughput:** useful tokens/s, step-time median/p95, rank skew, and wall-clock goodput including warmup/eval/checkpoint. Run enough steady-state steps to identify outliers and compare repeated windows.
- **Declared MFU:** calculate from measured useful tokens/s × declared model FLOPs/token divided by installed GPU count × precision-appropriate published peak. Publish the full formula and configuration. Keep MFU and useful tokens/s side by side; neither alone certifies training quality.
- **Loss/numerical health:** baseline and interval loss, gradient norm, NaN/Inf/skipped steps, rank equality, fixed validation sample. Use an actual training step with backward/optimizer work, not just GPU burn.
- **Checkpoint mechanism:** save/restore at a clean optimizer boundary; verify the full state manifest and next data batch/cursor. Inject a process kill and, if safely supported, a single-GPU/node/network interruption; record detection-to-first-useful-step and lost useful tokens.
- **Repeated interruption drill:** test checkpoint interruption during/around save (atomicity), restart from newest complete checkpoint, and recovery after stale/corrupt/incomplete checkpoint rejection. A single successful retry demonstrates one path, not a reliability probability.
- **Telemetry correlation:** correlate XID/ECC/HBM/PCIe/NVLink/network/storage errors, thermal/power/throttle indicators and training pauses with step-level timeline. Compare per-GPU performance to identify a straggler.

These are proposed actionable two-hour checks based on public mechanisms and incidents, not claims that these exact tests are published as universal industry protocol. ([Meta report](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783); [BLOOM chronicle](https://github.com/bigscience-workshop/bigscience/blob/master/train/tr11-176B-ml/chronicles.md); [Gemini](https://zhuangwang93.github.io/docs/Gemini_SOSP23.pdf))

### 6.2 Honest misses

Two hours cannot empirically establish:

- a 30–90-day hazard rate, failure-free probability, or aging/thermal-cycle behavior; one run’s event rate cannot be projected without assumptions and a much longer observation window;
- day/night, seasonal, utility-power, facility cooling, sustained storage pressure, network drift, or fleet-wide correlated failure behavior;
- a statistically meaningful MTTR tail or rare multi-node correlated interruption rate;
- production recipe’s convergence and model quality over trillions of tokens, rare data pathologies, delayed numerical instability, or long-horizon checkpoint corruption;
- that benchmarked throughput equals 54-day useful-token throughput after all eval, checkpoint, maintenance, data and recovery overhead;
- equivalence to a customer’s exact model, data, precision, training framework or distributed parallelism if those differ from the rack-bench workload.

A measured 2h PASS should therefore be phrased: “this rack/configuration completed the specified workload and recovery drills with these observed values,” not “will survive a 54-day Llama-class run.” The 54-day commitment still needs operational monitoring, periodic fault drills, checkpoint/restore rehearsal, and an agreed service/recovery objective. [inference] ([Meta](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783); [DeepSeek](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.19437v1); [Gemini](https://zhuangwang93.github.io/docs/Gemini_SOSP23.pdf))

## 7. Source confidence and limits

- **High confidence:** primary Meta paper for interruption totals, scope, definitions, tooling and MFU table; DeepSeek’s own technical report for its reported stability/recipe; first-party BLOOM operational chronicles for timestamps, checkpoint policy and concrete state bugs. Each is attributable to the team, but reports remain self-reported and the BLOOM logbook is a dated public operational diary rather than a controlled reliability study.
- **High confidence, narrower scope:** Gemini is a peer-reviewed SOSP’23 systems paper with explicit failure/checkpoint model, test setup and results. Its hardware/workloads are AWS A100/V100-era and should not be treated as measured NVL72 or GB300 performance.
- **Medium confidence:** arithmetic derived from those records is transparent but inherits source taxonomy and denominator limitations. Llama Table 5 percentage denominator inconsistencies mean prose claims and raw counts are safer than subtype percentages.
- **Not established:** independent reproduction of Llama/DeepSeek production telemetry, all event-level root-cause records, event-by-event MTTR, or a public 30–90-day trial of the target rack class.

## 8. Sources

- Kept: [The Llama 3 Herd of Models, Meta (arXiv HTML)](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783) — primary source for 54-day snapshot, 466/47/419 denominator, 78%/58.7% prose, effective training time, diagnostic tooling, MFU, and temperature variation.
- Kept: [DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report (arXiv HTML)](https://arxiv.org/html/2412.19437v1) — primary author report for stable-loss claim, architecture/precision context, compute accounting and ablation boundaries.
- Kept: [BLOOM 176B training chronicles](https://github.com/bigscience-workshop/bigscience/blob/master/train/tr11-176B-ml/chronicles.md) — first-party dated logbook with checkpoint cadence, eval costs, spikes, interruptions, synchronization defects and restart changes.
- Kept: [OPT chronicles source tree](https://github.com/facebookresearch/metaseq/tree/main/projects/OPT/chronicles) — primary dated author update fetched for specific numerical-instability, data-formatting and restart incidents; not a full logbook/event census. Gemini supplies a separately labeled secondary summary of failure counts and wasted GPU-hours.
- Kept: [Gemini: Fast Failure Recovery in Distributed Training with In-Memory Checkpoints, SOSP 2023](https://zhuangwang93.github.io/docs/Gemini_SOSP23.pdf) — primary peer-reviewed systems work for checkpoint frequency/recovery mechanisms and experimental qualifications.
- Kept: [Evaluating MFU as a Proxy for GPU Power, arXiv 2608.03880](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.03880v1) — recent technical treatment of MFU’s analytical definition and limits; it is not the original definition paper.
- Kept: [PyTorch Distributed Checkpoint documentation](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.checkpoint.html) — implementation reference for distributed state checkpointing; not evidence of a particular rack’s recovery correctness.
- Dropped: [Tom’s Hardware Llama failure article](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/artificial-intelligence/faulty-nvidia-h100-gpus-and-hbm3-memory-caused-half-of-the-failures-during-llama-3-training-one-failure-every-three-hours-for-metas-16384-gpu-training-cluster) — secondary summary; primary Meta report used instead, particularly because its paraphrasing risks mixing denominators.
- Dropped: general commercial training/recovery blogs and non-primary MFU explainers — excluded where primary reports or systems paper supported the claim.

## Gaps

- Llama Table 5’s printed subtype percentages do not consistently reconcile with raw counts under one denominator. The prose denominator for 78% and 58.7% is clear (419 unexpected events); no attempt is made here to invent a reconciliation for every table percentage.
- Meta does not publish per-event interruption timestamps, MTTR distribution, lost-token totals, or machine-level exposure needed to derive a defensible failure rate per GPU-hour from this section.
- OPT primary evidence was retrieved from one dated 10%-through update only; it supports the specific dataset-formatting, numerical-instability, and restart examples in §3.1, but is not a comprehensive extraction of the full OPT chronicles or a source for a normalized failure rate.
- No cited public run is a GB300/NVL72 Chennai rack or a 30–90-day controlled reliability trial. Short-test-to-long-run prediction remains unquantified.
- Resume correctness tolerances depend on deterministic kernels, software version, topology changes and precision; customer training stack must define acceptable equivalence for an actual acceptance plan.

# N07 — Books and canonical guides for rack training validation

Research date: 2026-10-11. All claims below carry a source URL.

Claims are marked [observed] (explicitly present in source), [calculated] (arithmetic), or [inference] (application to rack certification). This is an independent research node. Scope: a GB300-class NVL72-class rack (18 trays) in Chennai; measured category checks, about two hours per category, plus smoke burn-in. PASS means measured, not vendor-claimed. The tenant wants to know whether a 54-day Llama-3-class run can survive before committing for 30–90 days.

## 1. Executive answer

[Inference] Books are useful for systems framing, but current operational guides and reliability papers are stronger for distributed pretraining failure engineering: NVIDIA documents restart, checkpointing and straggler features ([Megatron Bridge resiliency](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/training/resiliency.html)); PyTorch documents distributed checkpoint and torchrun restart semantics ([DCP](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.checkpoint.html), [torchrun tutorial](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/ddp_series_fault_tolerance.html)); recent SDC papers detail failure modes ([AEGIS](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi26/presentation/lei), [controlled SDC study](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.00726v1)). Among books, DMLS and *Reliable Machine Learning* are treated as an equal-priority tier: DMLS is a broad foundation ([author TOC](https://github.com/chiphuyen/dmls-book)); *Reliable Machine Learning* complements it with reliability/monitoring ([O’Reilly TOC](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/reliable-machine-learning/9781098106218)); *AI Engineering* is lower priority for pretraining because the official TOC emphasizes finetuning, dataset engineering and inference ([O’Reilly catalog](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/ai-engineering/9781098166298)).

[Inference] Two hours can measure present-state throughput/MFU for a specified workload, rank-to-rank variation, observed data stalls, checkpoint write/read/resume correctness and latency, short-run loss behavior, and immediate flaky-node indicators under the exact test load. It cannot establish 54-day uptime, rare intermittent fault rate, long-term thermal/aging behavior, dataset correctness at full scale, or final model convergence. Smoke burn-in increases exercised exposure; it does not turn an hours-long sample into a 54-day reliability guarantee ([AEGIS deployment scale](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi26/presentation/lei); [SDC study](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.00726v1)).

## 2. Ranked canon

### 2.1 Rank 1 — NVIDIA Megatron Bridge: resiliency, checkpointing, performance guide

[Observed] NVIDIA’s current Bridge resiliency guide explicitly covers fault tolerance (hang detection/restart), NVRx straggler detection, preemption, async checkpoint saves, local checkpointing, experimental rerun attribution for NaN/spiky loss, and in-process restart. It explicitly warns that one feature does not cover all failure modes, recipes may not enable features by default, and users should layer features. It says straggler detection identifies slow-performing nodes; it does not stop training by default. [NVIDIA Megatron Bridge Resiliency](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/training/resiliency.html)

[Observed] The page gives meaningful operational caveats: fault tolerance requires Slurm and `ft_launcher`, an accessible checkpoint directory, and is not compatible with Nsight Systems profiling; async save requires `torch_dist`; rerun state machine is alpha/experimental; in-process restart is not suitable for hardware-level switch failures or network partitions. [same guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/training/resiliency.html)

[Inference] This is the best single practical entry point for recovery/checkpoint correctness, flaky-node screening, and loss-spike investigation on NVIDIA distributed training. Read its linked checkpointing and performance guides alongside it; a rack certificate should not represent an API feature as enabled merely because the software package supports it.

Mapping: MFU/throughput — performance guide (specific recipe/config matters); recovery/checkpoint correctness — resiliency + checkpointing; loss spikes — rerun state machine, but experimental; flaky-node screening — straggler detector; data stalls — partial (step timing/profiling required); tenant acceptance — high value as a checklist, not certification evidence.

### 2.2 Rank 2 — PyTorch distributed checkpointing and torchrun docs

[Observed] PyTorch Distributed Checkpoint (DCP) documentation describes multi-rank parallel save/load and load-time resharding across cluster topologies. It records that DCP creates multiple files, operates in place, and currently provides no backwards-compatibility guarantees for saved state dictionaries. The current stable page identifies PyTorch 2.14.0 and last update July 8, 2026. [PyTorch DCP](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.checkpoint.html)

[Observed] The PyTorch fault-tolerant DDP tutorial says torchrun restarts all processes from the last saved snapshot; snapshots need continuity-relevant state, not only model weights. It also says failures lose progress since last checkpoint. The tutorial was last verified November 5, 2024, so treat examples as conceptual and verify against installed versions. [PyTorch fault-tolerant training tutorial](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/ddp_series_fault_tolerance.html)

[Inference] These sources are authoritative for building a real restore drill: save model, optimizer, step/consumed-data position and relevant RNG/sampler state; kill/restart the job; verify restart at expected step with equivalent training state; verify checkpoint completeness and integrity; time save, load and lost-work window. DCP supports the mechanics, but a two-hour test cannot prove a production tenant’s custom trainer’s exact state contract unless it runs that trainer or a faithful harness.

Mapping: MFU/throughput — low; recovery/checkpoint correctness — very high; loss spikes — none; flaky-node screening — none directly; data stalls — checkpoint I/O stalls and loader throughput only if instrumented; tenant acceptance — very high for explicit restart test and measured RPO/RTO.

### 2.3 Rank 3 — current reliability papers, not books

[Observed] OSDI ’26’s AEGIS paper reports deployment over 35 million GPU-hours, identifying 18 real-world SDC incidents and 13 faulty GPUs with 0.86% performance overhead. It presents an online sensor/verifier approach to SDC. This is large-scale production evidence, not a rack-sized test recipe. [USENIX OSDI 2026 paper](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi26/presentation/lei)

[Observed] The paper *Exploring Silent Data Corruption as a Reliability Challenge in LLM Training* reports injected GPU matrix-multiply faults can produce NaNs, transient loss/gradient/attention-logit spikes, and persistent parameter divergence. It also notes loss spikes can arise from normal dynamics, limiting loss-only diagnosis. [arXiv paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.00726v1)

[Inference] For contemporary distributed-training reliability, papers beat books on what can silently go wrong and the evidence behind detection. They do not replace executable vendor/framework docs for a rack acceptance workflow. Do not claim this rack’s two-hour loss trace has ruled out SDC: rare corruption may be invisible, and a normal loss curve is not a correctness proof.

Mapping: MFU/throughput — paper-dependent secondary evidence; recovery/checkpoint correctness — not primary focus; loss spikes — very high; flaky-node screening — very high at scale; data stalls — low; tenant acceptance — strong rationale for monitoring and honest limits, weak as a simple short test.

### 2.4 Rank 4 (tie) — Chip Huyen, *Designing Machine Learning Systems* (O’Reilly, 2022)

[Observed] The author’s book resource repository identifies DMLS as an O’Reilly 2022 work and provides the table of contents and chapter materials. The relevant named sections include Chapter 6 “Model Development and Offline Evaluation” (including “Distributed Training” and “Debugging ML Models”), Chapter 8 “Data Distribution Shifts and Monitoring,” and Chapter 10 “Infrastructure and Tooling for MLOps” (storage/compute, resource management, ML platform). [Author’s book repository](https://github.com/chiphuyen/dmls-book); [O’Reilly official catalog and contents](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/designing-machine-learning/9781098107956)


[Inference] DMLS is valuable for translating an acceptance test into whole-system requirements, instrumentation, data and compute dependencies, and monitoring. Its “Distributed Training” section is not a substitute for current Megatron/NeMo failure engineering, checkpoint semantics, GPU screening or long-horizon reliability evidence.

Mapping: MFU/throughput — useful framing, not current benchmark protocol; recovery/checkpoint correctness — weak; loss spikes — debugging concepts, not robust SDC methods; flaky-node screening — weak; data stalls — useful system-level framing; tenant acceptance — strong requirements/observability framing.

### 2.5 Rank 4 (tie) — Cathy Chen et al., *Reliable Machine Learning* (O’Reilly, 2022)

[Observed] O’Reilly’s official catalog identifies the book, its authors, and its focus on running ML reliably, production troubleshooting, monitoring, and organizational practice. Its official contents list “Evaluating Model Validity and Quality,” “Fairness, Privacy, and Ethical ML Systems,” “Monitoring and Observability for Models,” “Integrating ML into Your Organization,” and “Case Studies: MLOps in Practice.” Official chapter pages expose Chapter 4 “Feature and Training Data” and Chapter 9 “Monitoring and Observability for Models”; Chapter 9 includes “What Is Production Monitoring and Why Do It?” [O’Reilly title page](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/reliable-machine-learning/9781098106218) [Official Chapter 4](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/reliable-machine-learning/9781098106218/ch04.html) [Official Chapter 9](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/reliable-machine-learning/9781098106218/ch09.html)

[Observed] Direct access to the publisher’s full catalog page returned access denied during research. Search indexing of O’Reilly’s official domain exposed the contents and chapter headings; claims are limited to visible headings, not inaccessible full text. [Official catalog URL](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/reliable-machine-learning/9781098106218)

[Observed] The catalog supplement adds a Google Research abstract for the book's data-management chapter.
The abstract names SLOs, SLIs, monitoring, and data handling.
An author states that the book contains no code examples.
Sources: [Google Research abstract](https://research.google/pubs/chapter-1b-data-management-principles-_reliable-machine-learning-applying-sre-principles-to-ml-in-production),
[author Q&A](https://datatalks.club/books/20221121-reliable-machine-learning.html).
[Inference] These records strengthen general reliability context, not operational distributed-training validation.
Keep the book beside DMLS; do not promote it above current recovery guides.
The [source note](oreilly/reliable-ml.md) retains metadata conflicts and full-text limits.

[Inference] Treat it as tied with DMLS overall, with stronger relevance specifically to monitoring and ML reliability framing; both rank below operational distributed-training docs/papers. The verified contents do not establish Megatron-scale checkpoint restart, GPU stragglers, MFU or pretraining SDC defenses.

Mapping: MFU/throughput — not established by visible TOC; recovery/checkpoint correctness — not established; loss spikes — not established; flaky-node screening — not established; data stalls — Chapter 4 is relevant conceptually, not device-level stalls; tenant acceptance — monitoring/validity framing is useful, no rack test procedure.

### 2.6 Rank 5 — *Machine Learning Platform Engineering* (Manning, 2026)

[Observed] Manning names Benjamin Tan Wei Hao, Varun Mallya, and Shanoop Padmanabhan.
The catalog lists February 2026 and 504 pages.
Public samples verify Chapters 8–9 training and validation, and Chapter 11 monitoring.
Chapter 9 covers PersistentVolumes, TensorBoard, MLflow, and lineage.
Sources: [publisher](https://www.manning.com/books/machine-learning-platform-engineering),
[catalog](https://learning.oreilly.com/library/view/-/9781633437333/?orm_source=mcp),
[Chapter 8](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-platform-engineering/chapter-8),
[Chapter 9](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-platform-engineering/chapter-9),
[Chapter 11](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-platform-engineering/chapter-11).

[Inference] Read these selected chapters before older cloud-specific pipeline material.
They add direct platform context for training metrics, data management, and artifact records.
They do not establish MFU accounting, complete resume state, or GPU screening methods.
This reading change does not establish full-book supersession of *MLOps Engineering at Scale*.
See the [source note](oreilly/ml-platform.md) for samples, pagination limits, and proposed checks.

Mapping: metrics and lineage — verified topics; recovery and screening — unverified; tenant acceptance — platform context only.

### 2.7 Rank 6 — Carl Osipov, *MLOps Engineering at Scale* (Manning)

[Observed] Manning’s official catalog describes an AWS/serverless-oriented PyTorch pipeline, dataset ETL/SQL, deployment of training pipelines as service endpoints, monitoring/managing pipeline lifecycle and measuring performance improvements. It mentions PyTorch Lightning, Optuna and MLflow. It frames reducing infrastructure management through cloud vendors’ prebuilt services, not validation of physical GPU racks. [Manning official title page](https://www.manning.com/books/mlops-engineering-at-scale)

[Observed] The public Manning page confirms these topics but the retrieved catalog did not expose a complete chapter-by-chapter contents list. Do not infer chapter numbers or recovery coverage. [Manning official title page](https://www.manning.com/books/mlops-engineering-at-scale)

[Inference] This is useful for pipeline operations and lifecycle monitoring, but poorly matched to 54-day distributed pretraining resilience. It is more relevant than *AI Engineering* for pipeline operations, yet its serverless/cloud abstraction is not evidence about NVL72 fabrics, checkpoint reliability or flaky-node detection.

Mapping: MFU/throughput — performance measurement generally, no MFU; recovery/checkpoint correctness — not established; loss spikes — not established; flaky-node screening — not established; data stalls — ETL/pipeline concepts, not device-level stalls; tenant acceptance — lifecycle monitoring useful at general process level.

### 2.8 Rank 7 — Chip Huyen, *AI Engineering* (O’Reilly, 2025)

[Observed] The O’Reilly catalog and author companion repository list chapters: 7 Finetuning, 8 Dataset Engineering, 9 Inference Optimization and 10 AI Engineering Architecture and User Feedback; [O’Reilly official catalog](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/ai-engineering/9781098166298); [author companion repository](https://github.com/chiphuyen/aie-book)

[Inference] Chapter 8 can help reason about dataset construction and provenance; chapter 9 is inference optimization, not pretraining infrastructure. Chapters 7–10 do not establish long-run pretraining failure handling. Do not recommend this as the main rack-training validation book, nor imply that inference-focused content teaches fault tolerance for a 54-day pretraining run.

Mapping: MFU/throughput — low for pretraining; recovery/checkpoint correctness — very low; loss spikes — low; flaky-node screening — none; data stalls — dataset engineering concepts, not loader diagnostics; tenant acceptance — low/indirect.

### 2.9 Optional catalog candidates

[Inference] These candidates add selected topics, not operational rack-validation authority.
The [catalog supplement](oreilly.md) records ten source entries and their access limits.

| Candidate | Verified public scope | Reading decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Machine Learning System Design](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-system-design/chapter-10) | Pipeline testing; Chapter 14 monitoring and reliability. | Optional pipeline-testing and reporting context. |
| [Designing Deep Learning Systems](https://livebook.manning.com/book/designing-deep-learning-systems/chapter-4) | Training service, parallelism, and hyperparameter optimization. | Optional training-service context. |
| [Parallelism Deep Dive](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781806110896/?orm_source=mcp) | Catalog lists parallelism and Chapter 14 checkpoint strategies. | Optional introduction; videos and recovery results remain uninspected. |
| [DMLS in the Cloud](https://www.oreilly.com/videos/designing-machine-learning/0636920953234) | Catalog lists training data, experiment tracking, automation, and observability. | Lower priority; year, runtime, and playback remain unverified. |
| [Deep Learning for Vision Systems](https://www.manning.com/books/deep-learning-for-vision-systems) | Vision systems; contents name project structure and hyperparameter tuning. | Low priority for distributed pretraining validation. |

The [System Design sample](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-system-design/chapter-14)
separates software health, data quality, and model quality.
This separation does not establish checkpoint-resume correctness.
The [Deep Learning Systems publisher](https://www.manning.com/books/designing-deep-learning-systems)
names Chi Wang and Donald Szeto; the supplied catalog names Kit Pang Szeto.
Keep this naming difference explicit; do not infer an alias.

### 2.10 Alternate formats

## 4. What two hours can and cannot establish

### 4.1 Useful measured evidence in a two-hour category window

[Inference] With a representative multi-node training harness and collection at per-step/per-rank granularity, measure (using workload-specific profiling and the stated framework instrumentation) ([PyTorch profiler recipe](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/recipes/recipes/profiler_recipe.html); [Megatron Bridge resiliency](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/training/resiliency.html)): steady-state tokens/s and step-time distribution after warm-up; MFU with declared FLOP convention; per-rank throughput/straggler spread; GPU clocks, power, temperature and error telemetry; NCCL collective behavior under that workload; dataloader wait time, CPU utilization and storage-read stalls; checkpoint write and restore wall time; and a forced process/job restart that resumes from a validated checkpoint without silent duplicate/skipped steps. Report expected rollback and replay separately. Document any test interruptions and all measured intervals.

[Observed] DCGM diagnostics are intended to assess GPU deployment/readiness, active hardware/integration/stress tests, and health telemetry, but are invasive and can consume GPU, memory, PCIe, NVLink, CPU, power and cooling resources. Coordinate with the scheduler and isolate tested resources. [NVIDIA DCGM diagnostics overview](https://docs.nvidia.com/datacenter/dcgm/latest/learn/modules/dcgm-diagnostics.html)

[Inference] Existing rack smoke burn-in plus a reproducible training-loop test provides complementary evidence: stress can uncover immediate faults and a training workload exposes application-path performance. Neither is a statistical demonstration of low multi-week failure probability.

### 4.2 Remains unknown after two hours

[Inference] Unknowns include: probability and clustering of rare failures over 54 days; intermittent SDC below available detection; failures induced by long-term thermal/power/environment drift; complete checkpoint recovery under every failure mode; production data quality/coverage and full-run convergence; multi-day storage/network contention; scheduler/preemption and human-response behavior; and interactions with tenant-specific framework, data loader, model, optimizer and checkpoint format.

[Calculated] 54 days is 1,296 hours, 648 times a two-hour observation. [Inference] This exposure ratio is not a reliability estimate; the distinction is illustrated by large-scale fleet evidence in [AEGIS](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi26/presentation/lei). Even assuming a simplified stationary Poisson failure process (an assumption, not established for hardware faults), zero events in a two-hour sample gives a very weak upper bound on rare-event rate; it cannot certify zero failures in the future run. No numerical reliability claim should be inferred without an explicit statistical model, confidence level and representative exposure.

[Inference] Acceptance wording should be “measured healthy under named workload for stated interval,” plus restore-test results and untested risks—not “will survive 54 days.”

# ClusterMAX and training-run health: what a short acceptance test can establish

Research date: 2026-10-11. All claims below carry a source URL.

## 1. Executive answer

ClusterMAX 3.0 is not merely a configuration audit: its current published methodology describes two short, real training workloads (Llama 3.1 8B pretraining and GPT-OSS MoE) alongside detailed compute/network/storage benchmarks, an eight-hour combined GPU/network burn-in, and explicit health-check fault injection. The published procedures are designed to expose gross performance/configuration defects, collective-path problems, thermal degradation, detectable GPU errors, and some scheduler/remediation failures; this research did not reproduce the runs. [observed methodology] [ClusterMAX 3.0 methodology](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)

The public evidence does not establish that a two-hour test validates a 54-day run, model convergence, or even restart correctness end to end. [observed] [ClusterMAX 3.0 methodology](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)

For this rack-bench project—GB300-class NVL72, 18 trays, Chennai—treat these as separate evidence types: audit/configuration, component and workload benchmarks, burn-in, injected-fault response, and actual training convergence.
