## 4. What a two-hour rack-bench can honestly say

A two-hour category check cannot recreate ClusterMAX's eight-hour burn-in or its longer provider evaluation. It can still produce useful, measured evidence if it is explicitly a short-window screen. [inference] [basis: ClusterMAX describes an eight-hour combined burn-in and up to five days of test access per scheduler](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard) [PROPOSAL] For this rack, run a representative Llama-3-class training workload using the intended software/configuration and record exact recipe, parallelism, batch/sequence lengths, precision, data source, seed, and checkpoint policy.

[PROPOSAL; motivated by ClusterMAX’s named Llama 3.1 training run and listed telemetry/metrics, but not a ClusterMAX procedure](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard) Suggested training-health observations within two hours: (a) successful distributed initialization and stable steps; (b) step-time distribution and throughput after warm-up; (c) measured MFU with formula and hardware peak assumptions disclosed; (d) loss/gradient/parameter finite-value checks and trend review against the run's expected short-horizon behavior; (e) GPU clocks/temperature/power/ECC/XID and NCCL errors correlated to steps; (f) one checkpoint save and restore, followed by deterministic or tolerance-bounded state/output comparison under an explicitly controlled recipe. These are proposed rack-bench checks, not procedures attributed to ClusterMAX.

[PROPOSAL; ClusterMAX publicly describes separate node reboot/XID fault tests and DCP save/load benchmarking, but not training interruption/resume](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard) If time allows, perform one operator-approved, non-destructive interruption (for example preemption/worker process restart, not physical PCIe fault injection) after checkpoint creation, then report detection, pause, restart, lost steps, checkpoint age, resumed throughput, and state-equivalence result. Do not count this as evidence that provider hardware fault remediation preserves training state unless the fault is actually exercised in the training path.

[PROPOSAL; the CLI uses discrete pass/warning/fail/skipped states and ClusterMAX separates audit, performance, and reliability phases](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/clustermax) Report PASS only for the measured interval and defined assertions. Report separately: config/audit PASS; component benchmark PASS; short burn-in PASS; actual training smoke PASS; checkpoint round-trip PASS; injected-fault response PASS. Avoid a single umbrella “54-day safe” verdict.

## 5. Decision for the tenant considering 30–90 days

ClusterMAX evidence is useful for screening the infrastructure and management stack, and its short Llama/MoE runs establish more than synthetic GEMM alone. It does not answer “will my 54-day run survive?” on public evidence. A two-hour rack-bench can reduce uncertainty about immediate performance, numerical sanity, basic checkpoint handling, and observed faults; it cannot infer the probability of multi-week outages or guarantee convergence. [inference] [basis: published reliability testing is time-bounded and SemiAnalysis identifies reliability over time as outside direct hands-on measurement](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard) [3.0 methodology](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)

[PROPOSAL; ClusterMAX identifies SLA definitions, downtime, monthly review, and acceptance testing as contract topics](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard) Before committing, require an operational plan: checkpoint cadence and externally durable copies; tested resume procedure and ownership; telemetry/log retention; maintenance and interruption notice; escalation SLA; rack/NVL72 downtime definition; and a customer-visible interruption/goodput report over time. These are buyer safeguards proposed here, not claims that ClusterMAX publicly validates them. [Reliability criteria](https://www.clustermax.ai/criteria/reliability) [3.0 methodology](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)

## 6. Source confidence and limits

- **High confidence** that ClusterMAX 3.0 publicly describes Llama 3.1 8B and GPT-OSS MoE training, simultaneous eight-hour GEMM/all-to-all burn-in, and specified node health-check/fault injection: these are direct statements in the primary methodology article. [observed] [3.0 methodology](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)
- **High confidence** about public CLI limits: README explicitly calls it an audit, says it omits performance/reliability tests and provider results/benchmark implementations. [observed] [public repo](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/clustermax)
- **High confidence** about listed Reliability criteria, but criteria are expectations/checklist entries and should not be mistaken for verified test execution in every provider. [observed] [Reliability criteria](https://www.clustermax.ai/criteria/reliability)
- **Moderate confidence** in claims of absence: limited to the named public corpus. Internal proprietary methodology, dashboards, paid material, and unpublished run artifacts were not available for inspection. [observed] [methodology](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard) [repo](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/clustermax)
- Provider results and full benchmark scripts were not audited independently; this brief reports what the published methodology says is done, not a reproduction of ClusterMAX runs. [observed] [methodology](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)

## Gaps

- SemiAnalysis’ internal training scripts, run lengths, exact pass thresholds, loss records, and per-provider results are not public in the inspected corpus; request these directly if the decision depends on them.
- No public evidence establishes numerical checkpoint-resume equivalence during a real training interruption, nor interruption-to-goodput accounting for the named Llama run.
- No published multi-day or 54-day stability dataset was found; a two-hour measurement cannot supply that guarantee.
- The task references sibling checkpoint/datagen work, but its implementation artifacts were not present in this worktree. The sibling storage brief is linked; its storage claims were not re-derived.
- The public methodology gives no per-provider MFU/convergence data for the named Llama pretraining job. Its MFU references belong to the future PostTrainingX description.

# Training bench research: failure modes and bench design

Research date: 2026-10-11.

Seven category briefs support this document:
[neoclouds](../neoclouds.md), [hyperscalers](../hyperscalers.md),
[ai-labs](../ai-labs.md), [large-companies](../large-companies.md),
[clustermax](../clustermax.md), [academia](../academia.md), and [books](../books.md).
The briefs contain source URLs and evidence limits.
Section references below refer to those briefs.
This document proposes checks; it contains no rack measurements.

Target: one GB300-class NVL72-class rack, 18 trays, Chennai, India.
Window: approximately two hours for `bench training`.
PASS requires measured assertions for the named workload.
Vendor specifications do not constitute PASS evidence.

## Why training is next

The tenant question is concrete: can this rack support a 54-day training run?
A 30–90-day commitment requires more than a fast GPU benchmark.
The run also needs correct updates, usable data, checkpoints, and recovery.

Meta reports 466 interruptions during a 54-day Llama 405B snapshot.
This total includes 47 planned interruptions and 419 unexpected interruptions.
Approximately 78% of unexpected interruptions involve confirmed or suspected hardware issues.
The paper attributes 58.7% of unexpected issues to GPUs.
Some printed table percentages do not match their counts.
Keep the prose denominators; do not silently repair the table.
Meta reports more than 90% effective training time despite these interruptions.
These fleet observations do not predict this rack's future failure rate.
See ai-labs §2 and [Meta §3.3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783v3#S3.SS3.SSS4).

Public provider evidence covers availability terms and recovery mechanisms.
It does not provide comparable multi-week job interruption distributions for the reviewed neoclouds.
Health checks can also cause interruptions.
ClusterMAX reports Together checks that incorrectly drain active nodes after diagnostic timeouts.
It reports one Nebius GB300 recovery that takes 8h40m.
These events are not provider-wide MTTR estimates.
See neoclouds §§8–9 and [ClusterMAX 3.0](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard).

ClusterMAX 3.0 already describes real dense and MoE training workloads.
It also describes an eight-hour combined compute/network burn-in.
Its public `cmax` tool remains a configuration audit.
The inspected public methodology does not establish numerical resume equivalence or multi-week survival.
Do not describe ClusterMAX as a checkpoint-only or synthetic-only suite.
The proposed difference is explicit training-state correctness and progress accounting.
This is a bounded public-method gap, not a claim about private procedures.
See clustermax §§2–3 and [public cmax](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/clustermax).

## Part 1 — Failure-mode catalog

“2h” means feasible within the proposed window, subject to workload and checkpoint size.
“Yes” means the check can expose the fault, not that it finds every occurrence.

| Failure mode | Evidence and mechanism | 2h | Catching check |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Missing ranks or wrong topology | Hyperscalers §§2, 9: transport and topology require platform-specific setup. | Yes | Capture unique ranks, device identities, tray mapping, and selected transport. |
| High MFU with weak accounting | AI-labs §4; academia §3: FLOP convention, precision peak, and time change MFU. | Yes | Publish formula, useful tokens, precision peak, and measured interval. |
| Fast steps but poor progress | AI-labs §§2, 4; large-companies §§4, 6: recovery and pauses reduce useful progress. | Yes, short window | Report steady-state throughput and full-window goodput separately. |
| Slow GPU or tray | Large-companies §3: synchronous training waits for slow ranks. | Partial | Compare repeated per-rank compute and communication spans. |
| Timeout with wrong diagnosis | Large-companies §3.2: a rank can stall before it enters a collective. | Yes | Align collective sequence, rank logs, loader wait, and fabric counters. |
| Data-loader starvation | Large-companies §3.3; academia §4: data waits can resemble fabric faults. | Partial | Compare cache states and log input wait per step. |
| Load-dependent hardware error | Large-companies §2: static checks can miss transient faults. | Partial | Run actual training; compare pre/post error counters and load telemetry. |
| Thermal throughput decline | AI-labs §2.3: Meta reports 1–2% diurnal variation. | Partial | Log clocks, power, temperature, throttling, and throughput over time. |
| Loss spike or non-finite update | AI-labs §3; books §2: numerical and hardware causes differ. | Partial | Capture loss, gradient norm, batch IDs, rank state, and hardware logs. |
| Silent in-range corruption | Large-companies §5: valid-looking gradients can still contain errors. | Partial | Repeat known-answer steps and compare reference state. |
| Weights-only recovery | AI-labs §§3.2, 5: optimizer, TP, and RNG defects can invalidate recovery. | Yes | Compare full resume state against an uninterrupted control. |
| Partial checkpoint selection | Academia §§2.2, 4.3: staging and persistence are different operations. | Yes | Kill an in-flight save; reject incomplete generations. |
| Async save mistaken for durable save | Academia §2.1; large-companies §4.3: host staging precedes persistence. | Yes | Record snapshot, persistence, and publication completion separately. |
| Automatic node repair without job resume | Hyperscalers §2.1; neoclouds §8: repair and resume differ. | Partial | Kill a worker; measure launcher action and restored progress. |
| Health check drains active work | Neoclouds §8.4: intrusive diagnostics and timeouts can cause false failure. | Partial | Audit active/passive policy; test only isolated allocations. |
| Restart loop on a suspect node | Large-companies §4.1: repeated retries can spread interruption costs. | Partial | Verify exclusion, bounded retries, and visible resource identity. |
| Lease expiry or missing replacement | Hyperscalers §3: capacity terms can terminate or change allocations. | No future proof | Record terms, notice handling, replacement ownership, and untested risks. |

### What two hours honestly cannot establish

- A 30–90-day failure rate or a 54-day completion probability.
- Rare silent-error absence, component aging, or all data-dependent faults.
- Day/night or seasonal Chennai cooling and power behavior.
- A recovery-time tail distribution from one or two drills.
- Full tenant-model convergence or quality after trillions of tokens.
- Checkpoint retention through long periods or correlated storage/site failures.
- Multi-rack contention or replacement capacity outside the tested allocation.
- Correctness for different frameworks, precision, topology, data, or model recipes.

A 54-day interval contains 1,296 hours: 648 times the test window.
This ratio measures duration, not reliability.
Academia §5 explains why zero events do not establish a useful long-run rate bound.
Do not pool GPU-hours to hide common rack failure modes.

## Part 2 — The suite: `bench training`, evidence-aligned

All check names below are proposals.
Existing category tests remain separate.
`bench training` uses their artifacts but tests actual forward, backward, and optimizer work.
It does not replace GPU, fabric, storage, internet, inference, or lifecycle tests.

### A. Test profile and evidence contract

Pin the profile before the run.
Record model architecture, initialization, sequence length, global batch, microbatch, optimizer, and learning-rate schedule.
Record precision, accumulation precision, parallelism, activation recomputation, seeds, and kernel determinism settings.
Record container digest, code revision, driver, CUDA, NCCL, framework, firmware, launcher, and environment.
Record dataset identity, sample IDs, packing/padding policy, cache state, loader configuration, and checkpoint target.
Measure actual GPU count and tray participation; do not assume the advertised count.

Use a small deterministic reference for state correctness.
Use a representative rack-scale dense workload for performance and stalls.
Use an MoE workload when expert collectives represent the tenant's workload.
Replace part of the dense window with MoE; do not silently extend the two-hour budget.
A small workload is not proof of 405B convergence or checkpoint-scale recovery.
See ai-labs §§4–6, hyperscalers §9, and clustermax §2.3.

### B. Check families

| Proposed check | Procedure | Required evidence | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `training.profile` | Freeze recipe; enumerate ranks and transport. | Configuration hashes, actual rank map, versions, logs. | Hyperscalers §9; books §3. |
| `training.numerics` | Run seeded reference updates; compare expected state. | Loss, gradients, finite checks, tensor differences, tolerance. | AI-labs §§3, 5; large-companies §5. |
| `training.throughput` | Measure repeated post-warmup windows at full rack scale. | Useful tokens/s, step-time p50/p95, sample count, time series. | AI-labs §4; academia §4. |
| `training.mfu` | Calculate declared model FLOPs over measured time. | FLOPs/token formula, precision peak, GPU count, interval. | AI-labs §4; academia §3. |
| `training.rank_skew` | Compare per-rank compute, communication, and wait spans. | Rank/tray identity, timing distributions, persistent outliers. | Large-companies §3; academia §2.1. |
| `training.input` | Use actual loader and storage path in declared cache states. | Batch IDs, input wait, storage/CPU counters, GPU idle. | Large-companies §3.3; books §4. |
| `training.checkpoint_commit` | Save complete state; verify publication and reload. | Shard inventory, hashes, commit marker, bytes, stage timings. | Academia §§2.2, 4.3; ai-labs §5. |
| `training.resume_equivalence` | Restart at step boundary; compare the remaining updates. | Counters, next batches, state tensors, validation loss. | AI-labs §5; books §2.2. |
| `training.recovery` | Kill an approved worker; restart through the actual launcher. | Detection, relaunch, load, first valid step, rollback. | Hyperscalers §2; large-companies §4. |
| `training.checkpoint_reject` | Interrupt a save; try the newest generation. | Explicit rejection; successful load of the prior complete generation. | Academia §4.3; ai-labs §6. |
| `training.loss_triage` | Inject a software anomaly in an isolated reference run. | Synchronized evidence capture and correct event classification. | Books §2.1; large-companies §5. |
| `training.goodput` | Count accepted unique progress over the complete window. | Progress counters, pauses, replay, skipped updates, billing basis. | AI-labs §4; neoclouds §5. |

NVIDIA's rerun state machine repeats work on the same and different GPUs.
It helps distinguish numerical behavior from hardware effects, but NVIDIA labels it experimental.
NVRx straggler detection does not stop training by default.
Verify enabled features and constraints in the pinned release.
See [Megatron Bridge resiliency](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/training/resiliency.html).

### C. Accounting rules

Define useful tokens as non-padding training tokens in valid optimizer updates.
State how packing, masking, auxiliary objectives, and MoE routing affect that count.
Do not use total MoE parameters as dense activated FLOPs.
Keep HFU and MFU separate; executed recomputation is not necessary model FLOPs.

`MFU = useful_model_FLOPs_per_token * useful_tokens_per_second / (GPU_count * precision_peak_FLOPs_per_GPU)`

This formula requires a declared architecture-specific FLOP convention.
State whether the precision peak includes sparsity.
Use a peak appropriate to the operations; mixed precision requires explicit assumptions.
Publish the peak source, not only the percentage.
Report warmup exclusion and interval boundaries.
Keep useful tokens/s beside MFU.
See ai-labs §4 and academia §3.

`wall_clock_goodput = unique_accepted_training_tokens / complete_elapsed_seconds`

The denominator includes setup, warmup, validation, checkpoints, stalls, and recovery.
Do not double-count rolled-back or replayed progress.
Record executed tokens separately when useful.
Report paid GPU-hour goodput only when actual allocation and billing records support it.
Do not equate service uptime, device utilization, MFU, or useful progress.
See neoclouds §5 and large-companies §4.2.

For recovery, record checkpoint age and progress lost before restart.
Separate event detection, diagnosis, replacement, relaunch, state load, and warmup.
Record time to the first valid update and time to previous progress.
Expected rollback can repeat batches; report those repeats.
Fail silent data skipping or unexplained order changes.
One observed drill is not an MTTR distribution.
See ai-labs §5 and large-companies §4.

### D. Checkpoint state and equivalence

Save model shards, optimizer state, master weights, scheduler state, and applicable precision/scaler state.
Save global step, consumed tokens, RNG state, sampler state, and data position.
Save framework-specific FP8 history or other numerical state when the trainer requires it.
Record configuration, tokenizer, dataset, and parallelism identities.
Checkpoint at a complete optimizer-step boundary unless the format preserves partial accumulation.
Verify every shard and the published generation manifest.
A host-memory snapshot is not durable persistence.
A completed async submission is not necessarily a completed write.

Compare an uninterrupted control with a resumed branch using the same remaining batch sequence.
Compare next sample IDs, step counters, learning rate, loss, gradients, and model/optimizer tensors.
Declare absolute/relative tolerances before the test.
Use bitwise equality only where deterministic execution supports it.
Test changed topology separately; a same-topology PASS does not establish resharding correctness.
Reject incomplete, stale, or corrupt generations according to the defined recovery policy.
See ai-labs §5, academia §4.3, and books §2.2.

### E. Proposed 120-minute schedule

| Minutes | Activity | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0–10 | Freeze profile; capture health and rank map. | Complete provenance and pre-run counters. |
| 10–25 | Run known-answer steps and reference/control branches. | Numerical baseline and state checks. |
| 25–80 | Run full-rack training with representative input. | Throughput, MFU, rank timing, loss, and thermal series. |
| 80–105 | Save, kill, restart, and compare state. | Checkpoint commit, recovery timing, resume result. |
| 105–115 | Interrupt a save or test checkpoint rejection. | Prior-generation recovery and explicit rejection. |
| 115–120 | Capture final counters; write evidence summary. | Counter deltas, coverage, verdicts, and misses. |

Collect telemetry throughout the complete window.
Reserve checkpoint time from measured state size and backend performance.
If a representative restore exceeds the budget, report incomplete coverage.
Do not substitute a tiny checkpoint without stating the size difference.
Stage the agreed input and container before the timed window; record staging separately.
Require operator approval for process interruption.
Do not reset PCIe, inject hardware errors, or remove power in the default suite.

### F. Result and PASS rules

Use `PASS`, `FAIL`, `NOT_TESTED`, and `INCONCLUSIVE` per assertion.
Use numeric gates only when the profile defines thresholds before the run.
Without a threshold, report the measurement; do not invent a performance PASS.
Unexplained rank loss, wrong collective output, invalid updates, or state mismatch fail correctness assertions.
A retry does not erase the first failure.
Report every attempt, intervention, excluded component, and final configuration.
Keep short-run workload success separate from injected-recovery success.
Never label this certificate “54-day reliable” or “SDC-free.”

Suggested result text:
“This configuration completes the named workload during the stated interval.
The report contains measured throughput, numerical checks, and the tested recovery result.
The result does not establish multi-week reliability or full-run convergence.”

MLPerf Closed measures time to a defined quality target under benchmark rules.
Open permits different stopping behavior with reported quality.
General rules make checkpoint retention optional, with workload-specific exceptions.
Neither result constitutes interruption-recovery certification.
See academia §3 and [MLPerf rules](https://github.com/mlcommons/training_policies/blob/master/training_rules.adoc).

## Part 3 — Implementation tickets

These tickets propose work; they do not claim an existing `bench training` implementation.

1. **Profile schema.** Add pinned workload, topology, precision, data, checkpoint, thresholds, and tolerance fields.
2. **Training runner.** Use the selected framework's existing trainer and launcher; avoid a new training framework.
3. **Reference branch.** Add seeded control/resume runs with full-state comparison and explicit determinism limits.
4. **Step telemetry.** Save per-step loss, gradients, sample IDs, tokens, skipped updates, and phase timings.
5. **Rack telemetry join.** Join GPU, fabric, storage, and host events by timestamp and rank/tray identity.
6. **Accounting module.** Calculate MFU and goodput from declared conventions and measured progress.
7. **Checkpoint verifier.** Check generation publication, shard integrity, restore state, and next data position.
8. **Recovery drill.** Add operator-approved worker termination, bounded retries, and phase-specific timing.
9. **Incomplete-save drill.** Reject the interrupted generation and restore the previous complete generation.
10. **Verdict report.** Add per-assertion states, raw evidence paths, every attempt, and untested limits.
11. **Long-run runbook.** Define alerts, quarantine ownership, checkpoint cadence, retention, and periodic restore drills.
12. **Tenant handoff.** Record maintenance notice, lease end, replacement capacity, response objectives, and billing treatment.

Use the existing report and artifact conventions when maintainers select the implementation plan.
Keep the default suite safe and rack-local.
Treat scale-out topology and destructive fault drills as separate approved profiles.

## Reading list

Start with [Megatron Bridge resiliency](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/training/resiliency.html)
and [PyTorch Distributed Checkpoint](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.checkpoint.html).
These guides explain usable mechanisms and constraints, not rack reliability outcomes.

Read [Llama 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783v3),
[BLOOM chronicles](https://github.com/bigscience-workshop/bigscience/blob/master/train/tr11-176B-ml/chronicles.md),
and [MegaScale](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-jiang-ziheng.pdf) for actual operational failures.
Read [CheckFreq](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/fast21-mohan.pdf) for checkpoint staging and data-position recovery.
Read [MLPerf rules](https://github.com/mlcommons/training_policies/blob/master/training_rules.adoc) for benchmark boundaries.

Use *Designing Machine Learning Systems* Chapters 6, 8, and 10 for systems context.
Use *Reliable Machine Learning* Chapters 4 and 9 for data and monitoring context.
These books keep the same general reading priority.
Their verified contents do not establish executable rack-scale recovery procedures.

Add *Machine Learning Platform Engineering* Chapters 8, 9, and 11 for training metrics, artifacts, and lineage.
Its [public Chapter 9](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-platform-engineering/chapter-9) names TensorBoard, MLflow, and dataset management.
Read these selected chapters before older cloud-specific pipeline material.
Keep *MLOps Engineering at Scale* for its cloud-specific pipeline context, not NVL72 fault certification.
The new title does not replace framework recovery guides or establish full-book supersession.

Use *Machine Learning System Design* Chapters 10 and 14 as optional pipeline-testing and monitoring reading.
Its [public Chapter 10](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-system-design/chapter-10) names property-based testing.
The [parallelism course](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781806110896/?orm_source=mcp) optionally introduces parallel layouts and checkpoint strategies.
Its catalog does not establish measured rack recovery results.
Keep *Designing Deep Learning Systems* optional for training-service design.
Keep the cloud video and vision book at lower priority for distributed pretraining validation.
Do not count alternate audio/video formats as independent technical evidence.

*AI Engineering* has lower priority for distributed pretraining reliability.
Books §2 and the [catalog supplement](../oreilly.md) record verified coverage and access limits.
No book or guide supplies a universal GB300 two-hour PASS threshold.

# Hyperscaler guidance for long training runs: preflight, recovery, and the two-hour limit

Research date: 2026-10-11. All claims below carry a source URL.

Claims are marked **[observed]** (explicitly stated in cited source), **[calculated]** (arithmetic from cited values), or **[inference]** (bounded interpretation). This is an independent category brief for a GB300-class NVL72-class rack (18 trays) in Chennai. Cloud recipes demonstrate operational questions and mechanisms; they do not certify this rack or establish that its hardware, topology, drivers, software, or failure behavior match any hyperscaler system.

## 1. Executive answer: what two hours can and cannot establish

### 1.1 The useful claim

[Inference] A two-hour training bench can establish that a specified software stack, at a specified scale and rank layout, completed a reproducible training workload with correct loss/state behavior, sustained useful throughput, and observable telemetry during that test window. It can exercise checkpoint creation, read-back/restore, a controlled process restart, and measure the resulting recovery time. It cannot establish 54-day survival, future power/network/storage stability, provider replacement capacity, a usable termination notice, or that a 30–90 day lease covers the actual run. [Source basis for measurable checkpoint/restart scope: AWS auto-resume](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html); [Google checkpoint guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events).

[Observed] AWS guidance separates node health/replacement from job restart at the last saved checkpoint; Google’s TPU guidance says checkpoint recovery is essential and notes automatic recovery has edge cases; Google GPU maintenance documentation gives GPU-family-specific notice windows and says attached-GPU VMs stop rather than live-migrate. Sources: [AWS HyperPod recovery](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html), [Google TPU maintenance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events), [Google GPU maintenance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/live-migration-process).

### 1.2 Relevant arithmetic, not reliability extrapolation

[Calculated] Using the tenant scenario’s 54-day run and 30–90 day lease, two hours is 120 minutes: 1/648 of 54 days, 1/360 of 30 days, and 1/1080 of 90 days. These are exposure fractions only, not reliability estimates. Even observing zero faults in two hours cannot support a meaningful claim about rare faults across weeks without a justified statistical model and representative independent exposure. [Scenario basis: task context; AWS capacity-period caveat](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-capacity-blocks.html).

[Inference] The certifiable output should therefore say “measured X for Y minutes on workload/configuration Z,” not “will complete a 54-day run.” A tenant still needs a recovery design and capacity/lease terms. [Source basis: AWS checkpoint restart](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html); [Google checkpoint guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [Azure health/monitoring](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#node-health-checks).

## 2. What hyperscaler guidance tells tenants to check

### 2.1 AWS: health checks are not the same as resumable training

[Observed] SageMaker HyperPod’s Slurm recovery guidance describes two distinct mechanisms: automatic node recovery (reboot/replace faulty infrastructure) and auto-resume (restart training from the last saved checkpoint after failures). Recovery triggers can include health-monitoring agent findings, basic checks, and deep health checks. [AWS HyperPod resiliency](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm.html); [automatic node recovery and auto-resume](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html).

[Observed] AWS’s documented checks include NVIDIA SMI for GPU health and EFA connectivity tests using all available EFA cards. The specific recovery path is conditional: Slurm GRES allocations can prevent in-place allocation changes, so HyperPod may requeue the faulty job and restart it from the beginning unless the job is arranged for supported auto-resume. AWS instructs users to use an exclusive allocation, a single `srun` entrypoint, rebuild environment on replaced nodes, and avoid relying on potentially stale `SLURM_JOB_NODELIST` after resumption. [AWS auto-resume guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html).

[Inference] Tenant check: verify the exact scheduler, GRES, launcher, retry mode, node replacement action, and checkpoint restore path in the intended deployment. “Automatic recovery enabled” is not proof that this tenant job resumes at the latest valid checkpoint. A bench can test the job’s restart behavior with a controlled worker/process interruption, but cannot prove AWS-specific service automation on an independently operated rack. [Source basis: AWS checkpoint restart](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html); [Google checkpoint guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [Azure health/monitoring](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#node-health-checks).

### 2.2 Azure: health agents, scheduler state, and topology are operational configuration

[Observed] Azure’s public CycleCloud Slurm project documents a Healthagent daemon and Slurm `HealthCheckProgram` that can drain nodes when health errors are found. Its configuration describes checks on a 60-second interval, with checks applying across node states by default in that project documentation. Monitoring can expose Node Exporter, NVIDIA DCGM exporter, and AzSlurm scheduler metrics; the described AzSlurm exporter includes job terminal states/reasons, node states, provisioning/quota availability, and scheduler-cycle metrics. [Azure CycleCloud Slurm project](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm).

[Observed] The Azure Slurm project documents topology generation, including VMSS, Fabric Manager/SHARP, and NVLink-domain options; it cautions that autoscaling does not account for or update topology. Its GB200/GB300-specific `scale_m1` procedure requires rack-aligned scaling, generation and installation of block topology, then enabling the Slurm block topology plugin in the correct order. This is directly relevant as a concrete software/topology example, not proof that a Chennai NVL72 rack has the same topology semantics. [Azure project: topology and GB200/GB300 scale_m1](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#scaling-with-scale_m1-gb200gb300).

[Observed] Microsoft’s CycleCloud Slurm reference documents `slurm.resume_timeout` defaulting to 1800 seconds and `slurm.hpc` placement behavior for tightly coupled MPI nodes, illustrating that node startup and placement are configured operational parameters, not instantaneous guarantees. [CycleCloud Slurm integration](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cyclecloud/slurm?view=cyclecloud-8).

[Inference] Tenant check: pin exact Azure Slurm/CycleCloud project version and configuration; ask which checks drain nodes, whether they are intrusive, how often they run, whether health events are surfaced to a tenant, and what topology is static versus autoscale-generated. The current GitHub project README reflects a moving project and is not a contractual SLA; the Microsoft Learn page includes legacy examples and defaults that may not apply to current project versions. Check version/date before adopting settings. [Source basis: AWS checkpoint restart](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html); [Google checkpoint guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [Azure health/monitoring](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#node-health-checks).

### 2.3 Google: checkpoint frequently, but know the restart boundary

[Observed] Google’s Cloud TPU maintenance guide recommends checkpoints approximately hourly as a rule of thumb; save time can range from seconds to minutes. TPU jobs can recover automatically from most maintenance events, but edge cases may require deleting/recreating TPU resources and restarting from a saved checkpoint. The guide recommends retrying training scripts only in conjunction with checkpoints and recording maintenance events. [Google Cloud TPU maintenance events](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events) (page updated 2026-10-09).

[Observed] Google Cloud’s Multi-slice description says training jobs can restart from a previous checkpoint after slice failures and GKE can retry jobs after errors; it describes coordination across intra-slice ICI and inter-slice data-center networking. That is a product/example description, not a measured guarantee for arbitrary GPU racks. [Google TPU Multislice overview](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/compute/using-cloud-tpu-multislice-to-scale-ai-workloads).

[Observed] For Compute Engine VMs with GPUs, Google documents that they do not live-migrate during maintenance: they must stop and optionally restart. Notice is 60 minutes for most GPUs but 10 minutes for A4X, A4, and A3 Ultra. Do not generalize these exact figures to unrelated SKUs or assume that a notice is a hardware failure warning. [Google live migration and GPU limits](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/live-migration-process) (updated 2026-10-09).

[Inference] Tenant check: prove checkpoint completeness and restore on the actual intended storage path, not merely that a save call returned. Validate signal handling, termination notice consumption, graceful-stop deadline, retry behavior, and how long provisioning/restart takes. Hourly checkpoints are a vendor rule of thumb, not a universal optimum; select interval from checkpoint duration, expected interruption exposure, storage cost, and acceptable lost work. [Source basis: AWS checkpoint restart](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html); [Google checkpoint guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [Azure health/monitoring](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#node-health-checks).

## 3. Lease duration, interruption notice, and capacity are separate questions

### 3.1 Capacity reservation can end the job on schedule

[Observed] AWS says Capacity Blocks reserve GPU capacity for a defined future period and support P5/P5e and other listed instance families in only selected regions; availability is constrained by region/SKU and reservation conditions. A Capacity Block ends at 11:30 UTC, and instance termination begins at 11:00 UTC on its final day. AWS calls this predictable capacity assurance for the reserved period, not perpetual capacity. [AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-capacity-blocks.html).

[Observed] AWS PCS documentation says when a Capacity Block expires, instances terminate and active jobs might fail depending on Slurm settings; the compute node group remains but cannot launch new instances from the expired block. [AWS PCS Capacity Block expiration](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/pcs/latest/userguide/capacity-blocks.html).

[Inference] Lease check: compare the complete run plan (including setup, validation, checkpointing, pauses, and recovery reserve) to the exact lease end and termination policy. A 30-day lease cannot be treated as sufficient for a 54-day continuous run absent documented extension/replacement capacity and tested restart semantics. Even a 90-day lease leaves less than 36 days of slack before overhead if the nominal run is 54 days; that arithmetic says nothing about capacity or performance. [Scenario basis: task context; AWS documents reservation end/termination semantics](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-capacity-blocks.html).

### 3.2 Replacement capacity and topology may change

[Observed] Google’s AI Hypercomputer capacity documentation describes reservation-bound options, future-reservation limits for supported types, and managed recovery modes that automatically replace faulty machines; it warns topology can change after replacement. [Google AI Hypercomputer consumption models](https://docs.cloud.google.com/ai-hypercomputer/docs/consumption-models); [reserve capacity](https://docs.cloud.google.com/ai-hypercomputer/docs/reserve-capacity).

[Inference] A provider must answer in writing whether replacement hardware is guaranteed for the entire tenant term, whether replacement preserves rack/switch/NVLink/fabric topology, whether replacement capacity has the same SKU and software baseline, and whether repair/replacement consumes paid lease time. Two-hour rack tests can measure current rank mapping and detect gross topology/configuration issues; they cannot guarantee future replacement availability or stable placement. [Source basis: AWS checkpoint restart](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html); [Google checkpoint guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [Azure health/monitoring](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#node-health-checks).

### 3.3 Notice is useful only if the workload handles it

[Observed] Google’s GPU maintenance notice examples distinguish 60-minute and 10-minute windows by family, and GPU instances stop rather than live-migrate. Google TPU guidance separately advises monitoring maintenance notifications and using autocheckpointing/checkpoint restore. [Google GPU maintenance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/live-migration-process); [Google TPU maintenance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events).

[Inference] Ask for event semantics (planned maintenance vs emergency fault), notice channel and minimum notice, what actions are allowed, whether notice reaches the job, and whether the tenant can finish a checkpoint within that window. A short test can inject a software-level termination signal and measure checkpoint-and-exit time; it cannot validate a provider’s real notice delivery or minimum notice unless that mechanism is available in the tested environment. [Source basis: AWS checkpoint restart](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html); [Google checkpoint guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [Azure health/monitoring](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#node-health-checks).

## 4. Failure mechanisms and concrete tenant checks

### 4.1 Health screening: detect bad parts before allocating ranks

[Observed] AWS documents GPU and EFA checkers, while Azure’s project documents health agents that can label/drain nodes. This operational pattern is to detect errors and exclude unhealthy nodes before or during scheduling, not to promise that no new faults occur. [AWS recovery](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html); [Azure CycleCloud Slurm project](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm).

[Inference] Bench candidate: after the existing burn-in, collect per-GPU error/health telemetry, ECC/XID counters, link state, fabric errors, PCIe/NVLink status, temperatures/power/throttling, kernel logs, and scheduler-visible health state; verify a suspect node is excluded from allocation. Use safe, non-destructive signals and agreed operational procedures. A 2-hour PASS is a snapshot plus short trend, not latent-defect screening over weeks. [Source basis: AWS checkpoint restart](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html); [Google checkpoint guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [Azure health/monitoring](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#node-health-checks).

### 4.2 Distributed correctness: a running step counter is not correctness

[Inference] Run a representative distributed training script at full rack scale and record rank/world-size, global batch, data-parallel/tensor/pipeline layout, collective completion, loss, tokens/second, and per-rank progress. Check that loss is finite and behaves within expected tolerance; compare against a known-good reference/configuration where feasible. Test an all-reduce/checksum or deterministic small validation batch before/after checkpoint restore. Success means the workload made valid progress and all ranks participated, not that a 54-day optimization converges to a target model quality. [Source basis: AWS checkpoint restart](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html); [Google checkpoint guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [Azure health/monitoring](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#node-health-checks).

[Observed] Google describes different communication paths for Multislice: intra-slice ICI and inter-slice DCN, with collectives and hierarchical communication. AWS describes EFA connectivity checks. These sources underscore that network path/topology and the workload’s communication pattern matter; neither makes a small-scale pass proof of different scale/topology performance. [Google Multislice](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/compute/using-cloud-tpu-multislice-to-scale-ai-workloads); [AWS auto-resume](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html).

### 4.3 Checkpoint integrity, durability, and restart time

[Inference] Bench candidate: write a realistic checkpoint containing model, optimizer, scheduler, RNG, dataloader/sampler position, global step, and any framework-specific state; verify manifest/size/checksum and atomic commit semantics; read it back in a fresh process; resume and verify expected step/loss/data position. Exercise an interrupted or partial-write scenario safely if supported; ensure incomplete checkpoints are not selected. Measure checkpoint wall time, restore wall time, data-loss window (steps since last committed checkpoint), and end-to-end time to useful training throughput after restart. [Source basis: AWS checkpoint restart](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html); [Google checkpoint guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [Azure health/monitoring](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#node-health-checks).

[Observed] Google describes checkpoint times spanning seconds to minutes and notes recovery from the saved checkpoint; AWS auto-resume likewise restarts from last saved checkpoint, while its GRES caveat can lead to restart from the beginning. [Google TPU maintenance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [AWS auto-resume](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html).

[Inference] Durability is separate from successful local write: test the actual persistent/shared/object storage target, permissions, capacity, concurrent access, and retention/replication contract. A two-hour test can read back a just-written checkpoint; it cannot demonstrate months-long retention, protection against correlated site/storage loss, or contractual durability. [Source basis: AWS checkpoint restart](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html); [Google checkpoint guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [Azure health/monitoring](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#node-health-checks).

### 4.4 Rank mapping, data pipeline, and monitoring

[Inference] Bench candidate: capture rank-to-tray/GPU/NIC mapping; verify expected rank count, unique ranks, GPU visibility, affinity, local/remote link paths, and collective traffic. Measure step-time distributions and per-rank skew, GPU utilization, network utilization/retries, storage throughput/latency, CPU utilization, dataloader wait time, queue depth, and input-cache behavior. Include representative dataset reads and enough warm/cold data to expose obvious stalls; log metrics at a cadence useful for correlating stalls with step-time spikes. [Source basis: AWS checkpoint restart](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html); [Google checkpoint guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [Azure health/monitoring](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#node-health-checks).

[Observed] Azure’s project exposes node/GPU/scheduler metrics and topology tooling, but also explicitly describes limitations: topology may not be updated under autoscaling. [Azure CycleCloud Slurm project](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm). Google’s Multislice system depends on known ICI/DCN hierarchy for communication. [Google Multislice](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/compute/using-cloud-tpu-multislice-to-scale-ai-workloads).

[Inference] The bench can find a current mapping error, an obvious slow rank, repeated input stalls, low GPU busy time, and missing/uncorrelated monitoring. It cannot infer behavior for a different dataset, cache state, checkpoint frequency, model parallelism, training framework version, or tenant-side preprocessing code. [Source basis: AWS checkpoint restart](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html); [Google checkpoint guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [Azure health/monitoring](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#node-health-checks).

## 5. Recommended two-hour training category protocol

### 5.1 A bounded test plan

[Inference] Reserve the training category’s ~120 minutes for a defined, versioned tenant-like workload rather than claiming a generic vendor “training ready” status: [Source basis: AWS checkpoint restart](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html); [Google checkpoint guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [Azure health/monitoring](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#node-health-checks).

1. Record image/container digest, driver/runtime/framework versions, firmware/config, model/test configuration, exact tray/GPU/rank layout, scheduler settings, and dataset/storage path.
2. Run a brief distributed preflight: every expected rank visible; collective correctness and connectivity; representative data batch; finite loss; no unexplained health/error counters.
3. Run a sustained workload long enough to obtain step-time and utilization distributions across warm-up and steady state. Report medians and tails, not a single peak; correlate outlier steps with GPU, network, storage, CPU, and dataloader signals.
4. Save a realistic checkpoint; verify it is complete and readable; stop/relaunch a controlled worker/process; restore and continue. Measure checkpoint duration, restore time, lost steps, and time back to steady useful progress.
5. Report every intervention, anomaly, retry, and excluded component. Do not hide a repaired/retried run behind a PASS; report per-run outcomes and final state.

[Inference] The exact time split depends on workload/checkpoint size. If the realistic checkpoint itself takes a substantial part of two hours, reduce other test scope rather than using a tiny checkpoint and implying equivalence. Report the test as a screened configuration, not a lease-level reliability verdict. [Source basis: AWS checkpoint restart](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html); [Google checkpoint guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [Azure health/monitoring](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#node-health-checks).

### 5.2 Suggested PASS language

[Inference] “Measured on [date] for [duration] using [configuration/workload]. All N ranks completed [steps/tokens]; loss was finite and within [declared bounds]; observed throughput/step-time distribution was [metrics]; [checkpoint] was written, verified, restored, and training resumed in [time], with [steps] of progress lost; observed health/error counters were [results]. This does not establish multi-week availability, replacement capacity, checkpoint durability beyond the tested target/period, or 54-day completion.” [Source basis: AWS checkpoint restart](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html); [Google checkpoint guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [Azure health/monitoring](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#node-health-checks).

## 6. Policy, empirical evidence, and extrapolation are different

### 6.1 Policy and feature documentation

[Observed] Capacity reservation windows, configured health agents, termination notice rules, and auto-resume functionality are documented service policies/features. They answer what mechanisms are offered under specified conditions, not the rack’s measured reliability. Examples: [AWS Capacity Blocks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-capacity-blocks.html), [AWS HyperPod recovery](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html), [Google GPU notice behavior](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/live-migration-process).

### 6.2 Empirical evidence

[Inference] Rack-bench evidence should be its own measured record: observed errors, rank/step progress, throughput distribution, monitored stalls, checkpoint/restore behavior, restart time, test workload and exact tested configuration. A vendor recipe or health-agent status is not that measurement. [Source basis: AWS checkpoint restart](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html); [Google checkpoint guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [Azure health/monitoring](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#node-health-checks).

### 6.3 No unsupported GB300 extrapolation

[Observed] Azure’s public CycleCloud Slurm project includes GB200/GB300-specific topology and `scale_m1` instructions, but those instructions concern Azure’s software/project workflow. [Azure GB200/GB300 Slurm scaling](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#scaling-with-scale_m1-gb200gb300).

[Inference] This source is evidence that rack-aware rank mapping and topology setup are operational concerns for this class of hardware, not evidence that the Chennai 18-tray rack matches Azure’s implementation or passes it. AWS P5/P5e, AWS EFA, Azure ND, Google A3, and Google TPU recipes are not interchangeable specifications for GB300 NVL72. A finding transfers only where the specific tested hardware, firmware, fabric, scheduler, driver, framework and workload are shown to match. [Source basis: AWS checkpoint restart](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html); [Google checkpoint guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [Azure health/monitoring](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#node-health-checks).

## 7. Tenant due-diligence questions before signing 30–90 days

1. **Duration and interruption:** What is the guaranteed start/end time, what terminates at lease expiry, and can the lease be extended? What happens to a running job at the boundary? AWS Capacity Blocks show why exact end-of-block semantics matter. [AWS Capacity Blocks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-capacity-blocks.html).
2. **Notice and action:** What event types generate notice, through what channel, with what minimum notice, and can tenant code checkpoint/exit before termination? Google documents GPU notices by family, not a universal GPU rule. [Google maintenance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/live-migration-process).
3. **Replacement:** Is capacity reserved for replacement nodes for the full term? Can a replacement change tray/rack/fabric topology, GPU count, software baseline, or rank mapping? Is replacement downtime billable? [Google AI Hypercomputer capacity/recovery](https://docs.cloud.google.com/ai-hypercomputer/docs/reserve-capacity).
4. **Recovery semantics:** Does recovery reboot/replace node, restart job, or merely requeue it? Does the job resume from latest committed checkpoint or beginning? Which scheduler/GRES/launcher configurations are supported? [AWS auto-resume limitations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html).
5. **Checkpoint:** Which state is included, how often is it committed, where is it stored, what durability/retention is contractually provided, and what restore time is demonstrated? Google recommends roughly hourly checkpoints as a starting point, not a service-level promise. [Google TPU checkpoint guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events).
6. **Observability and escalation:** Can the tenant access job, GPU, fabric, storage, dataloader, health-agent and maintenance events with timestamps? Who drains/repairs nodes and what response-time commitment applies? Azure’s published monitoring examples show useful metrics but do not create an SLA for this rack. [Azure project](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm).

## 8. Findings in brief

1. [Inference] Two hours can provide a measured workload/configuration screen, distributed correctness check, short performance/stall profile, and checkpoint/restore/restart measurement. It cannot establish 54-day survival.
2. [Observed] AWS explicitly distinguishes node recovery from job auto-resume and documents configurations that can cause restart from the beginning rather than latest-checkpoint continuation. [AWS guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html).
3. [Observed] Google recommends frequent checkpoints and documents GPU maintenance notice and stop behavior that varies by GPU family; TPU recovery can still require resource recreation and restart. [TPU guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [GPU guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/live-migration-process).
4. [Observed] Lease/capacity end semantics can terminate active jobs; exact reservation duration and replacement capacity must be checked independently of rack health. [AWS Capacity Blocks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-capacity-blocks.html); [AWS PCS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/pcs/latest/userguide/capacity-blocks.html).
5. [Inference] PASS must be scoped to measured rack/workload/configuration and disclose the specific tested checkpoint/restart result; never translate hyperscaler documentation or a two-hour PASS into an unsupported GB300 reliability claim.

## Sources and confidence

- **High confidence, primary vendor documentation:** AWS HyperPod recovery and EC2 Capacity Blocks; Google Cloud TPU and Compute Engine maintenance docs; Microsoft Learn CycleCloud Slurm reference. These directly document mechanisms and stated limits.
- **Moderate confidence, primary but version-sensitive project documentation:** Azure `cyclecloud-slurm` GitHub README. It provides unusually concrete topology, health, and monitoring details, including GB200/GB300 workflow; repository content can change, so pin release/commit before using operationally.
- **Lower confidence for empirical reliability:** None of these materials provide an independently measured reliability rate for the tenant’s 54-day scenario or this Chennai rack; the 54-day duration is supplied by the task scenario, not established by these vendor sources. Product feature descriptions and vendor examples are not empirical outcomes for the subject system.

## 9. Seeded primary preflight recipes: concrete checks to borrow, not hardware equivalence claims

The following are provider-authored procedures for the named platforms. **[Proposal]** means a candidate rack-bench check derived from those recipes; it is not a vendor requirement, a certified GB300 procedure, or an inferred performance threshold. Pin the tested image/container and software versions in every result. The sources are live documentation; version-specific values below are snapshots of the pages checked on the research date.

### 9.1 AWS P5/P5e: EFA/NCCL setup, tests, and important version caveats

[Observed] EC2’s primary “Get started with EFA and NCCL” guide walks through an EFA-enabled security group, supported OS/instance setup, GPU/CUDA/cuDNN, GDRCopy, EFA software, NCCL, `nccl-tests`, and a multi-GPU MPI-launched `all_reduce_perf` test. EFA needs self-referencing inbound/outbound security-group rules; the example’s broad SSH rule is explicitly testing-only. The sample validates EFA provider selection from NCCL logs (`NET/OFI Selected Provider is efa*`) and suggests cluster placement groups for low latency in a single AZ, while stating placement groups are recommended rather than mandatory. [AWS EC2 EFA+NCCL recipe](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html).

[Observed] The AWS recipe’s page currently names EFA installer `1.50.0`, NCCL `2.30.4-1`, and CUDA path `/usr/local/cuda-13` in its generic installation example; the recipe requires EFA-compatible NCCL (2.4.2+), and its sample `mpirun` exports `FI_EFA_USE_DEVICE_RDMA=1`, enables NCCL debug logging, and runs `all_reduce_perf` across eight GPUs (adjust `-n`/`-N` for the instance). Those generic current values are not a P5/P5e-specific supported matrix; validate against the actual AMI, instance type, PyTorch-bundled NCCL, and EFA installer release. [AWS EC2 EFA+NCCL recipe](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html); [AWS EFA-supported libraries](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa.html).

[Observed] AWS’s current GPU quickstart matrix lists distinct driver/CUDA/EFA/NCCL combinations by SKU. Its page search extract lists P5 at driver 530/CUDA 12.1/EFA 1.24.1/NCCL 2.18.3; P5e at driver 550/CUDA 12.1/EFA 1.24.1/NCCL 2.18.3; P5en similarly at driver 550/CUDA 12.1/EFA 1.24.1/NCCL 2.18.3. The page separately notes a P5.4xlarge EFA/NCCL GPU-to-GPU compatibility issue, mitigated by EFA 1.43.1+ and `FI_HMEM_DISABLE_P2P=1`. Do not apply that P5.4xlarge-specific workaround automatically to P5.48xlarge, P5e, or another platform. Read the live SKU table and release notes before freeze. [AWS GPU setup/version matrix](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/gpu-instances-started.html).

[Observed] AWS’s SageMaker EFA container guidance says the container must include EFA/Libfabric/Open MPI and its own MPI/NCCL stack; with PyTorch, the container NCCL version should match the NCCL version used by PyTorch (`torch.cuda.nccl.version()`). It shows checking EFA recognition with `fi_info -p efa`, and explains TCP control/peer traffic can use ENI while kernel-bypass OFI traffic uses EFA. [AWS SageMaker EFA container guidance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/your-algorithms-training-efa.html).

[Proposal] On the tested rack, record `nvidia-smi`, driver/CUDA/runtime/framework/NCCL versions (including `torch.cuda.nccl.version()`), `fi_info -p efa` or the actual fabric’s equivalent inventory, loaded NIC/RDMA libraries, and container-visible device mappings; save NCCL debug logs showing the selected transport/provider rather than assuming the intended path was used. Run a collective correctness test at rack scale with the actual launcher and rank count, and a short representative distributed training step. AWS’s EFA commands are examples only: this rack may not use EFA, Libfabric, AWS’s plugin, security groups, or placement groups. Source basis: [AWS EC2 recipe](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html), [AWS container guidance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/your-algorithms-training-efa.html).

### 9.2 Azure ND: InfiniBand, NCCL and node health

[Observed] Microsoft’s current ND H100 v5 SKU page states each VM has eight H100 GPUs, NVLink 4.0 inside the VM, and eight dedicated topology-agnostic 400 Gbps NVIDIA Quantum-2 CX7 InfiniBand connections, with GPU Direct RDMA; it describes cross-VM connections as automatically configured for VMs in the same VM scale set. It marks InfiniBand supported and Live Migration not supported. These are ND H100 v5 product facts, not NVL72 facts. [Azure ND-H100-v5 specifications](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/nd-h100-v5-series).

[Observed] Azure’s current `cyclecloud-slurm` project README documents Healthagent on nodes and Slurm health check/drain behavior. In that project, the configured Slurm check invokes Healthagent and defaults to 60-second cadence; the README also describes NVIDIA DCGM, Node Exporter, and AzSlurm exporters, with job terminal reasons, node state, available partition capacity, and scheduler metrics. Configuration is version-sensitive: README’s project version is 4.x and `slurm.enable_healthchecks` is a toggle; consult the exact project release and deployed Slurm config rather than importing values from old CycleCloud examples. [Azure CycleCloud Slurm project, health and monitoring](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#node-health-checks); [Microsoft CycleCloud Slurm integration](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cyclecloud/slurm?view=cyclecloud-8).

[Observed] Azure’s public CycleCloud Slurm project includes topology generation and warns autoscaling does not account for topology or update it. It also documents a GB200/GB300 `scale_m1` workflow with rack/block topology and `TopologyParam=BlockAsNodeRank`, but that describes this Azure project’s deployment mechanics—not the topology of this Chennai rack. [Azure topology and scale_m1](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#scaling-with-scale_m1-gb200gb300).

[Proposal] For an ND-inspired preflight, report actual node/SKU and GPU count, driver/CUDA/NCCL/MPI/PMIx versions, `nvidia-smi topo -m`, GPU↔NIC/RDMA device association, link state/rate, Slurm node/GRES and rank mapping, topology file/plugin and placement boundaries. Run the same NCCL collective across one node and all allocated nodes; record whether the expected InfiniBand/GPU-direct path is selected, correctness/error count, bus bandwidth, and per-rank skew. Capture Healthagent/Slurm drain and DCGM/host metrics with timestamps. Anchors: [ND H100 v5](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/nd-h100-v5-series), [Azure health/monitoring](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#node-health-checks), [Azure topology](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#topology).

### 9.3 Google Cloud A3 Mega: Cluster Toolkit deployment and NCCL preflight

[Observed] Google’s A3 Mega Slurm deployment guide requires Cluster Toolkit `v1.62.0` or later, capacity/consumption planning, and a minimum 10 TiB HIGH_SCALE_SSD Filestore quota for that blueprint. It recommends validating provisioned clusters with NCCL tests and provides a Slurm deployment blueprint; the guide notes A3 Mega’s availability and machine-type limitations. These requirements are for its A3 Mega blueprint, not a rack certification checklist. [Google A3 Mega Slurm deployment](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cluster-toolkit/docs/deploy/slurm/deploy-a3-mega-cluster).

[Observed] Google’s A3 Mega GPUDirect-TCPXO guide requires Cluster Toolkit v1.51.1+ for the documented cluster, describes topology-aware scheduling for clusters created with v1.39.0+, and details Slurm prolog/epilog behavior: check `import-helper`, install the NCCL net plugin, start/stop RxDM. RxDM startup can take 10–20 seconds. For single-node jobs, enabling the GPUDirect-TCPXO plugin without RxDM can time out; Google recommends `NCCL_NET_PLUGIN=none` for that case or configuring RxDM for all jobs. The guide builds/runs `nccl-tests` under Slurm, eight GPUs per node, and examines collective output including `#wrong` and out-of-bounds counts. [Google A3 Mega GPUDirect-TCPXO/NCCL guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cluster-toolkit/docs/machine-learning/a3-mega-enable-gpudirect-tcpxo).

[Proposal] For an A3-inspired but hardware-neutral preflight, first enumerate the precise device and topology: per-rank GPU, NIC, and tray mapping; effective Slurm `NodeList`, `SLURM_PROCID`/local rank, world size, GPUs per node, topology/rank order, and all relevant environment variables. Then run NCCL tests at intra-node and full-rack scope with the production launcher/container; confirm collective correctness (`#wrong`/out-of-bounds zero), expected network plugin/path, no timeout, and stable per-rank participation. Run a short training step with the same image and environment and preserve logs. On this rack, use its actual fabric/plugin names; do not set Google-specific `NCCL_NET_PLUGIN` or expect RxDM unless those components are actually used. Sources: [Google deployment guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cluster-toolkit/docs/deploy/slurm/deploy-a3-mega-cluster), [Google NCCL/TCPXO guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cluster-toolkit/docs/machine-learning/a3-mega-enable-gpudirect-tcpxo).

### 9.4 Cross-provider preflight record for this rack [Proposal]

[Proposal] Add the following evidence fields to the two-hour training result. These are practical proposed observations based on the cited AWS EFA, Azure ND/CycleCloud, and Google A3 recipes—not claimed vendor requirements or thresholds: [Source basis: AWS checkpoint restart](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html); [Google checkpoint guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [Azure health/monitoring](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#node-health-checks).

- **Identity and versions:** rack/tray inventory; GPU model/count; OS/kernel; BIOS/BMC/firmware; driver; CUDA; NCCL; framework and PyTorch-bundled NCCL; MPI/PMIx; scheduler; container digest; fabric plugin/driver. Record exact output and timestamp. [AWS version compatibility guidance](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/your-algorithms-training-efa.html); [AWS GPU matrix](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/gpu-instances-started.html).
- **Topology and ranks:** GPU/NIC/RDMA visibility; `nvidia-smi topo -m` or platform equivalent; rank-to-tray/GPU/NIC mapping; expected/actual world size; local rank and global rank uniqueness; Slurm node list/GRES; topology file/plugin; launcher command and environment. [Azure topology tooling](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#topology); [Google A3 blueprint/NCCL test](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cluster-toolkit/docs/machine-learning/a3-mega-enable-gpudirect-tcpxo).
- **Transport and collective correctness:** show actual selected NCCL network plugin/provider in debug logs; run representative collective sizes intra-node and all 18 trays; save throughput/latency and correctness counters; fail on hangs, mismatched ranks, or reported wrong elements. A measured result must not be replaced by advertised link rate. [AWS EFA test](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html); [Google NCCL test](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cluster-toolkit/docs/machine-learning/a3-mega-enable-gpudirect-tcpxo).
- **Health and monitoring:** snapshot pre/post health signals; GPU error/temperature/power/throttle counters, link/fabric errors, kernel logs, node drain state; confirm alerts and timestamps align with a deliberately observed (non-destructive) event. [Azure CycleCloud health/metrics](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#node-health-checks); [AWS HyperPod health checks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html).
- **Workload and data path:** record model/config, global and per-rank batch, sequence length, dataset path/cache state, dataloader workers, step-time distribution, useful tokens/s, loss and data-wait time; establish a checkpoint/restore cycle on the tenant’s intended storage. These are proposed measurements, not claims that any cited vendor prescribes this exact schema. [Checkpoint motivation and intervals](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [Google A3 training deployment](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cluster-toolkit/docs/deploy/slurm/deploy-a3-mega-cluster).

[Inference] These checks address configuration mistakes and short-run path/correctness failures. A zero-error collective test is evidence only for the tested topology, versions, sizes, duration, and routes. A matching hyperscaler recipe does not show that the rack shares its topology, throughput, replacement policy, or long-term reliability. [Source basis: AWS checkpoint restart](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html); [Google checkpoint guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [Azure health/monitoring](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#node-health-checks).

### Source/version caveats

[Observed] The AWS EFA/NCCL primary guide now contains very recent generic toolchain values (including EFA 1.50.0 and NCCL 2.30.4-1), while AWS’s SKU matrix lists older distinct P5/P5e combinations. This is not necessarily a contradiction: the recipe is generic and the SKU matrix describes documented bundled/setup combinations. Resolve it against the exact tested AMI and compatibility matrix; do not combine numbers from different recipes without validation. [AWS EFA+NCCL guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html); [AWS GPU matrix](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/gpu-instances-started.html).

[Observed] Google’s A3 documentation has explicit version gates: its current deployment guide requires Cluster Toolkit v1.62.0+, whereas the GPUDirect-TCPXO procedure states v1.51.1+ for that feature. Use the current deployment guide’s gate for a new deployment and preserve the exact toolkit/blueprint revision. The feature guide’s RXDM and environment behavior is A3 Mega-specific. [A3 deployment](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cluster-toolkit/docs/deploy/slurm/deploy-a3-mega-cluster); [A3 TCPXO guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cluster-toolkit/docs/machine-learning/a3-mega-enable-gpudirect-tcpxo).

[Inference] All preceding policy caveats remain: documented auto-recovery, notices, reservations, and retry features are policy/mechanism statements, not independent uptime measurements; capacity may be SKU/region/time limited; and a two-hour test cannot validate multi-week durability or a future replacement pool. The exact Google GPU notice windows and AWS Capacity Block expiry behavior in §§3 and 7 remain platform-specific and must not be generalized to this rack. [Source basis: AWS checkpoint restart](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html); [Google checkpoint guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [Azure health/monitoring](https://github.com/Azure/cyclecloud-slurm#node-health-checks).


## Gaps

- **No independent multi-week reliability comparison:** The primary documents reviewed describe mechanisms and product policies, not apples-to-apples observed failure rates for AWS P5/P5e, Azure ND, Google A3, or the Chennai rack. The 54-day duration is the tenant scenario, not a vendor-validated guarantee. [AWS recovery](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html); [Google A3](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cluster-toolkit/docs/deploy/slurm/deploy-a3-mega-cluster).
- **Azure ND recovery-notice limits remain unresolved:** The ND-H100-v5 SKU page establishes InfiniBand and lack of live migration, but the sources reviewed do not establish an ND-specific tenant checkpoint/restart limit or guaranteed maintenance notice window. Do not borrow Google or AWS notice values. [Azure ND H100 v5](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/nd-h100-v5-series).
- **AWS version matrix needs SKU/image pinning:** The current generic EFA recipe and AWS SKU setup table show different version contexts. The exact compatible versions for a chosen P5/P5e AMI, container, framework and NCCL plugin must be verified against that image before use; this brief intentionally does not claim a single universal AWS stack. [AWS EFA recipe](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html); [AWS GPU matrix](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/gpu-instances-started.html).
- **Rack-specific workload details are unspecified:** Model size/configuration, optimizer state, dataset, checkpoint format/size, parallelism strategy, storage target, and target-quality criterion are unknown. They affect whether a realistic checkpoint/restore fits the two-hour test and what correctness evidence is meaningful. The proposed record is a template, not a calibrated acceptance threshold. [Google checkpoint guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/maintenance-events); [Google A3 training guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cluster-toolkit/docs/deploy/slurm/deploy-a3-mega-cluster).
- **No unsupported hardware equivalence:** AWS EFA/P5, Azure ND-H100 InfiniBand, and Google A3 TCPXO examples are platform-specific. Their exact commands, environment variables, software versions, topologies, or failure behavior cannot be presumed to apply to a GB300 NVL72-class rack. [AWS EFA](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html); [Azure ND](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machines/nd-h100-v5-series); [Google A3](https://docs.cloud.google.com/cluster-toolkit/docs/machine-learning/a3-mega-enable-gpudirect-tcpxo).
large-companies.md:
# Large-company training reliability: what a two-hour rack test can and cannot establish

Research date: 2026-10-11. All claims below carry a source URL.

Claims are marked **[observed]** when directly reported by a source, **[calculated]** for arithmetic from reported values, and **[inference]** for transfer to rack-bench. The scope is one GB300-class NVL72-class rack (18 trays) in Chennai. A measured two-hour category check and smoke burn-in can establish short-window health and behavior; it cannot establish survivability of a 30–90-day or 54-day Llama-3-class run. Large-company practices are useful as causal design patterns, not as GB300 guarantees.

## 1. Executive answer: reliability is a chain, not a pass/fail component test

### 1.1 What hyperscalers actually do

- **[observed]** The common operating chain is: preflight/screen hardware → continuously collect correlated device, network, runtime and training signals → detect anomaly/timeout/performance regression → diagnose by differential evidence and targeted tests → quarantine or replace suspect nodes/components → restore a validated checkpoint and verify progress/loss. Meta describes categorization, triage, node selection, cluster validation and restore; ByteDance implements heartbeat-triggered diagnostics, eviction/replacement and checkpoint resume; Google TPUv4 couples preflight, health telemetry, scheduler exclusion and rescheduling. [Meta, “How Meta keeps its AI hardware reliable,” opening and “Infrastructure strategies”](https://engineering.fb.com/2025/07/22/data-infrastructure/how-meta-keeps-its-ai-hardware-reliable); [MegaScale, §§4.1–4.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.15627v1); [Google TPUv4, §§3.1, 3.6](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-zu.pdf)
