- **[inference]** A rack certification can test pieces of this chain and capture evidence, but cannot certify a future model’s application-level correctness, long-horizon fault rate, checkpoint cadence/recovery time under real state size, or provider’s operational response unless those are explicitly exercised and measured. [Meta FAIR §II-D](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1); [NVIDIA resiliency guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/training/resiliency.html)

### 1.2 Direct answer for two hours

- **[inference]** Two hours can measure: current inventory/health; gross hardware and fabric defects exposed by load; repeatable GPU/NVLink/NIC/storage performance; short-duration rank skew and stalls; temperature/power behavior under the tested workload; checkpoint write/read/restore correctness for a representative checkpoint; a forced restart/recovery path; and immediate numerical sanity checks against deterministic/reference results. [Meta SDC strategies](https://engineering.fb.com/2025/07/22/data-infrastructure/how-meta-keeps-its-ai-hardware-reliable); [NVIDIA rerun state machine](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/training/resiliency.html)
- **[inference]** Two hours cannot establish: rare/intermittent faults whose manifestation takes days or depends on aging, environment or data; fleet-scale recurrence/MTTF; 54-day ETTR/goodput; all possible silent data corruption (SDC); actual end-to-end model convergence; workload-specific loader behavior at full dataset scale; long-run thermal/clock or shared-fabric contention; checkpoint integrity after many cycles, outage or storage corruption; real-world restart frequency and MTTR across operator escalation. [MegaScale §§6.2–6.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.15627v1); [Llama 3 Herd §3.3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783)
- **[calculated]** A 54-day run is 648 times longer than a two-hour observation. [Llama 3 Herd §3.3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783) Even assuming an unrealistically stationary independent failure process, a short sample with zero failures does not establish a useful low failure rate without many more node-hours and confidence bounds; correlated rack/system failures further invalidate simple extrapolation.

## 2. Detecting failures before a run: screen, then keep the evidence

### 2.1 Health checks are repeated, layered, and exclusion-capable

- **[observed]** Meta’s two research clusters ran node health checks every five minutes, with pass/fail/warning codes spanning GPU XIDs, filesystem mounts and services. Checks overlap: PCIe failure can reveal an inaccessible GPU even without its own XID. Severe cases (GPU inaccessible, NVLink, uncorrectable ECC, row-remap, PCI/IB link, block device, missing mount) trigger immediate removal/rescheduling; lower-severity findings can defer remediation until the job ends. A failed node stays unschedulable until fixed and checks pass. [Meta FAIR, “Revisiting Reliability…,” §II-C, exact text “every five minutes” and “transitioned to a remediation state”](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)
- **[observed]** The same study reports health-check false positives on fewer than 1% of successfully completed jobs (authors explicitly caution that observed correlation is not causation). Its operating principle is to avoid a second job failure from the same bad node. [Meta FAIR, §II-C](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)
- **[observed]** Google’s TPUv4 runs preflight before each job: an end-to-end mini workload covers hardware/software interactions; a separate intent-driven checker compares physical metrics against golden thresholds. Failure results in rescheduling to different cubes. Continuous healthd telemetry monitors TPU ASICs, PCIe and ICI links, using modeled expected values and thresholds. [Google TPUv4, §§3.1, 3.6.1–3.6.2, pp. 764, 767–768](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-zu.pdf)
- **[observed]** Azure’s published operational guidance recommends Node Health Checks before training and NCCL tests for distributed all-reduce; it also calls out checkpoint intervals, data volume and storage capacity/performance as decisions to make, rather than assuming a checkpoint exists. This is provider guidance, not evidence of an Azure customer SLO. [Microsoft Learn, “Well-architected considerations…,” “Megatron-LM test use,” “Implement checkpoint storage”](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cloud-adoption-framework/ai/infrastructure/well-architected)
- **[inference] rack-bench check:** record per-device identity/firmware, ECC/XID/row-remap counters, PCIe/NVLink link state/errors, NIC/fabric counters and link flaps, disk/media errors, mount and filesystem status *before and after* load. Run a reproducible mini training and in-rack collectives, then repeat the same checks. Preserve counters and timestamps, not merely PASS. Mark exclusions and rerun only after repair; an audit snapshot is not a health screen. [Google TPUv4 §3.6](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-zu.pdf); [Meta FAIR §II-C](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)

### 2.2 Flaky nodes can pass simple static checks

- **[observed]** Meta separates static failures (does not power/enumerate), transient/load-dependent failures (thermal runaway, intermittent uncorrectable errors, condition-dependent faults), and silent errors. It says artificial workloads can make transient faults reproducible and “sticky” status telemetry can retain evidence after a transient event. [Meta engineering, “Types of hardware faults encountered at Meta”](https://engineering.fb.com/2025/07/22/data-infrastructure/how-meta-keeps-its-ai-hardware-reliable)
- **[observed]** Meta’s Fleetscanner uses directed microbenchmarks and telemetry signatures, with scheduled fleet coverage every 45–60 days; Ripple runs short co-located tests (milliseconds to seconds) for faster fleet coverage. Meta explicitly notes the periodic dedicated test can be too slow for some SDCs. These are fleet systems, not a claim that two-hour testing provides equivalent coverage. [Meta engineering, “Novel SDC detection mechanisms”](https://engineering.fb.com/2025/07/22/data-infrastructure/how-meta-keeps-its-ai-hardware-reliable)
- **[observed]** Meta FAIR found “lemon” nodes that health checks and normal repair workflows missed. Seven candidate signals included distinct jobs excluding node, XID count, repair tickets, scheduler removals, and single-/multi-node failure counts/rates. Historical 28-day signals identified 40 faulty nodes; >85% failed one of subsequent tests; reported detection accuracy exceeded 85%, and large-job failures (512+ GPUs) fell from 14% to 4%. This depends on history; it is not a two-hour diagnostic yield. [Meta FAIR, §IV-A](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)
- **[inference] rack-bench check:** do repeated warm/cold and sustained-load cycles, with thermal soak and transition conditions; compare each GPU/tray/rank to peers, not only aggregate averages. Keep per-component error deltas. A candidate that is a repeatable outlier is a quarantine/investigation signal even if it passes a vendor threshold. Two hours can find gross/intermittent faults, not establish 28-day history. [Meta FAIR §IV-A](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)

## 3. Telemetry to diagnosis: attribute causes rather than blame the loudest symptom

### 3.1 Measure step-level behavior and rank tails

- **[observed]** MegaScale’s driver receives periodic executor heartbeats carrying process/hardware status, stdout/stderr and RDMA traffic metrics. It parses warning/error keywords. Because steps should have recurring traffic patterns, a decline or fluctuation in RDMA traffic is an anomaly; zero traffic triggers automatic recovery. It reports second-level monitoring for host/network health and millisecond-level monitoring for congestion and whether data-/pipeline-parallel transfers reach physical limits. [MegaScale, §4.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.15627v1)
- **[observed]** MegaScale records CUDA-event durations per rank and critical segment, then displays heatmaps and cross-rank timelines. About 0.5% of machines were substantially slower in training; after removing outliers, peak MFU became consistent. Some hosts took ~10% longer on forward computation; removing them improved MFU by ~0.7%. This exposes stragglers that single-GPU GEMM microbenchmarks did not. [MegaScale, §§5.1, 6.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.15627v1)
- **[observed]** ByteDance reports a long-run performance decline where compute and optimizer times stayed stable but step time rose. Their differential analysis isolated delayed reduce-scatter initiation (rank skew), traced it upstream to forward-stage variation including irregular garbage collection and PyTorch operations, then removed/modified code and stabilized MFU. This is a concrete example of a network-looking symptom arising from software timing rather than link bandwidth. [MegaScale, §6.3, “MFU decreasing”](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.15627v1)
- **[inference] rack-bench check:** collect step-time distributions and per-rank/per-tray compute, communication, input-wait, checkpoint and synchronization spans. Report p50/p95/p99, max/min spread, rank identity, missed/late heartbeats, NIC traffic, retransmit/error counters and clocks/temperature against time. An average throughput number conceals stragglers and stalls. [MegaScale §§5.1–5.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.15627v1)

### 3.2 NCCL timeout is a symptom, not a diagnosis

- **[observed]** Meta FAIR warns a collective timeout may mean network trouble, but may instead mean a rank never entered the collective because it stalled loading the next batch, deadlocked in application code, or failed elsewhere. Root-cause requires comparing rank logs and collective sequence: find the first collective some ranks entered and others did not; if all entered but did not complete, inspect traffic and expected messages. [Meta FAIR, §§II-E, V “Debugging Tools”](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)
- **[observed]** MegaScale logs each worker’s in-progress event at communication timeout and maps rank dependencies over tensor/pipeline/data parallel groups. Waiting ranks log their operation; a defective GPU may hang and fail to log, helping localize the origin rather than treating all timeout cascades as faults. [MegaScale, §5.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.15627v1)
- **[inference] rack-bench check:** include one deliberately induced/controlled rank or link interruption if safe, and verify system reports root node/rank and timestamps rather than only a generic NCCL error. Compare fabric tests with loader-paused and loader-active conditions. Do not infer a faulty fabric from a timeout alone. [Meta FAIR §II-E](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)

### 3.3 Data-loader and storage stalls are first-class failure hypotheses

- **[observed]** MegaScale says data preprocessing/loading creates GPU idle time; per-GPU loaders can contend for disk bandwidth. It overlaps preprocessing with communication and uses a shared-memory tree loader to eliminate redundant reads. [MegaScale, §3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.15627v1)
- **[observed]** Meta FAIR specifically gives “stuck trying to load data for the next iteration” as a cause of a rank missing a collective and misleading peers into timing out. [Meta FAIR, §II-E](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)
- **[inference] rack-bench check:** run the training/inference smoke with representative data source, shard count, preprocessing and cache state; measure loader wait, storage latency/throughput, queue depth, read errors and GPU idle intervals. Exercise cold-cache and warm-cache behavior. A synthetic fio pass or preloaded batch does not certify a production loader. [MegaScale §3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.15627v1); [Meta FAIR §II-E](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)

## 4. Containment and recovery: quarantine, reconfigure, restore, verify

### 4.1 Exclude and replenish rather than retry on the same suspect hardware

- **[observed]** MegaScale recovery: missing heartbeat or abnormal process → suspend all executors → run lightweight self-check diagnostics → submit faulty node identities for Kubernetes eviction → replenish with healthy nodes passing diagnostics → resume from latest checkpoint. More than 90% of software/hardware faults in its reported production run were automatically identified/fixed; detection plus diagnostic tests averaged <10 minutes. [MegaScale, §§4.1, 6.2–6.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.15627v1)
- **[observed]** Google TPUv4’s health monitor excludes faulty cubes; Borg reschedules, with preflight of replacement resources. OCS reconfiguration and fault-tolerant routing let TPUv4 route around some link/switch faults, but routing has workload-dependent performance penalties. It reports 99.98% system availability and hardware outages affecting ~1% of training jobs; these are TPUv4 pod/system results, not a per-job promise transferable to a single GPU rack. [Google TPUv4, abstract, §§3.1, 4, 5.2–5.3](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-zu.pdf)
- **[observed]** Meta FAIR’s periodic checks prevent repeated allocation to known bad nodes; historical lemon detection tackles recurrent nodes not caught by checks. Unfiltered retries can create restart loops: one 1024-GPU job requeued 35 times and caused 548 preemptions affecting >7,000 GPUs in their example. [Meta FAIR, §§II-C, III “Preemptions and Failure Cascades,” IV-A](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)
- **[inference] rack-bench check:** verify failed-node containment at rack scope: alert carries tray/GPU/NIC identity; scheduler/admin can mark the unit unavailable; replacement or reduced allocation is explicit; subsequent run does not silently reuse the same suspect unit. A single rack has limited spare/reconfiguration capacity, unlike hyperscale clusters; document whether failure halts the job or permits degraded continuation. [Google TPUv4 §§3–4](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-zu.pdf); [MegaScale §4.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.15627v1)

### 4.2 Restart statistics and MTTR matter as much as raw fault count

- **[observed]** MegaScale’s several-week production run on >10,000 GPUs restarted >100 times, while loss continued to converge. It reports >90% effective training time, average detection/diagnosis <10 min, and catch-up to pre-crash training progress within 15 min from latest checkpoint. These figures describe their proprietary stack, HDFS, model and cluster; they are not hardware-only metrics. [MegaScale, §§6.2–6.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.15627v1)
- **[observed]** Meta’s Llama 3 public summary says training used 16K GPUs, automated error detection/handling/maintenance, improved SDC detection and scalable checkpoint/rollback storage; combined improvements yielded >95% effective training time. It does not disclose a per-rack failure rate, checkpoint interval, or per-event MTTR in that summary. [Meta, “Introducing Meta Llama 3,” “Scaling up pretraining”](https://ai.meta.com/blog/meta-llama-3)
- **[observed]** Meta FAIR defines ETTR as productive runtime / available wall-clock time, including both re-training lost since checkpoint and restart initialization overhead as unproductive time. It distinguishes ETTR from MFU: ETTR captures interruptions/restarts/queueing, MFU captures compute efficiency. This source says the exact productive-runtime definition is workload-dependent. [Meta FAIR, §II-D](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)
- **[calculated]** The Llama 3.1 405B paper reports 466 interruptions in a 54-day snapshot. Dividing by 54×24 = 1,296 elapsed hours gives 0.360 interruptions/hour, or one interruption per 2.78 hours on average (466/54 = 8.63 interruptions/day). This is the observed *job interruption frequency* for that specific 16K-H100 production run—not downtime fraction, component failure rate, nor a GB300 estimate. It does not reveal duration of each interruption. The paper separately reports >90% effective training time, defined as useful training time / elapsed time. [Llama 3 Herd, §3.3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783)
- **[inference]** Report measured throughput and run health separately: steady-state tokens/s or steps/s; rank-tail and trend; loader wait; checkpoint overhead; restarts and recovery; and effective useful progress / elapsed time. A 2-hour performance PASS means only measured performance under defined load and contention, not 54-day goodput. [Meta FAIR §II-D](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)

### 4.3 Checkpoint correctness is more than “file exists”

- **[observed]** MegaScale separates checkpointing into a short GPU→host-memory stage, then asynchronously persists the state to HDFS. Restore reads shared state once per data-parallel group and broadcasts it, reducing storage load. The point is to limit training pause and restore time; it does not make a checkpoint valid merely because a write completed. [MegaScale §4.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.15627v1)
- **[observed]** Meta says scalable storage reduced checkpointing/rollback overhead for Llama 3, but does not publish checkpoint interval, sizes or restore-time distribution in the product post. [Meta Llama 3, “Scaling up pretraining”](https://ai.meta.com/blog/meta-llama-3)
- **[observed]** Google’s MaxText recovery demonstration shows a concrete configuration failure: a 135-GiB checkpoint could not fit through a proxy configured for 100 GB. After correction, the run restarted from committed step 3300 after reaching 3388, losing 88 steps. This is a specific TPU/GKE example, not a GB300 claim. [Google Developers Blog, recovery walkthrough](https://developers.googleblog.com/we-terminated-a-tpu-mid-training-and-it-recovered-in-seconds-introduction-to-elastic-training-with-maxtext)
- **[inference]** Check the checkpoint manifest and expected shard count; verify checksums or equivalent integrity; ensure optimizer, scheduler, RNG and data-position state are included; restore in a fresh process; and compare resumed step, loss and deterministic reference outputs. Simulate an interrupted write and confirm recovery selects the last committed checkpoint rather than a partial newer one. A storage throughput pass is not a correctness test. [MegaScale §4.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.15627v1); [NVIDIA checkpointing guidance](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/training/resiliency.html)

## 5. Silent numerical corruption and loss-spike attribution

### 5.1 Device errors are not equivalent to numerical correctness

- **[observed]** Meta defines silent data corruption (SDC) as hardware miscomputation without detectable traces. SDC may depend on input, voltage, frequency, temperature or lifecycle; the input space is impractical to exhaust, and some faults may emerge only after months. Fleetscanner, Ripple and application-exception analysis improve coverage but have limits. [Meta Engineering, “Silent errors” and “Key challenges presented by SDCs”](https://engineering.fb.com/2025/07/22/data-infrastructure/how-meta-keeps-its-ai-hardware-reliable)
- **[observed]** Meta distinguishes NaN propagation, which can spread from a few accelerator computations and halt training, from in-range corrupted gradient variance. The latter can appear to make progress while training diverges or reaches a poor local minimum; detection may take weeks or months. [Meta Engineering, “SDCs in training workloads”](https://engineering.fb.com/2025/07/22/data-infrastructure/how-meta-keeps-its-ai-hardware-reliable)
- **[observed]** Meta’s mitigation examples include deterministic known-model iterations, mini-training binary-search triage for NaNs, and more frequent checkpoints to narrow the corruption window. Meta cautions that reproducibility depends on data, electrical and temperature conditions; gradient clipping may help some NaNs but can introduce partial errors. [Meta Engineering, “Detection of SDCs in AI hardware”](https://engineering.fb.com/2025/07/22/data-infrastructure/how-meta-keeps-its-ai-hardware-reliable)
- **[observed]** NVIDIA’s Megatron Bridge rerun state machine is an alpha/experimental approach for comparing same- and different-GPU reruns to attribute NaN or spiky loss; it offers validation and determinism-statistics modes. This is explicitly not exhaustive SDC coverage. [NVIDIA guide, “Re-run State Machine”](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/training/resiliency.html)
- **[inference] rack-bench check:** run known-answer GPU compute tests and repeated seeded small training steps; assert finite loss/gradients and compare rank outputs against references. Retain per-step loss/gradient norm and available RAS telemetry. This may expose gross/deterministic errors, but cannot rule out rare, data-dependent or long-latency SDCs. [Meta SDC strategies](https://engineering.fb.com/2025/07/22/data-infrastructure/how-meta-keeps-its-ai-hardware-reliable); [NVIDIA rerun guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/training/resiliency.html)

### 5.2 Loss spikes need temporal and rank-correlated evidence

- **[inference]** A loss spike alone does not identify cause. Align loss and gradient-norm changes with data sample/step, checkpoint boundaries, rank-specific errors, thermal/power/clock events, fabric retries/flaps, loader stalls and software changes. A shared spike may implicate data/algorithm/shared events; a first divergence on one rank motivates checking that device/path. This is a diagnostic procedure, not a validated universal classifier. [Meta Engineering, “Corrupted gradient variance”](https://engineering.fb.com/2025/07/22/data-infrastructure/how-meta-keeps-its-ai-hardware-reliable); [MegaScale §§4.2, 5.1–5.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.15627v1)
- **[inference]** Two hours can validate the telemetry and test response to an injected, known anomaly; it cannot observe corruption whose latent effects emerge after weeks. Report “none observed in these tests,” not “SDC-free.” [Meta Engineering, SDC discussion](https://engineering.fb.com/2025/07/22/data-infrastructure/how-meta-keeps-its-ai-hardware-reliable)

## 6. Thermal, fabric contention and goodput

### 6.1 Thermal and hardware telemetry

- **[observed]** Meta identifies temperature range and workload sensitivity as contributors to transient hardware faults and describes artificial workloads to make such failures reproducible. [Meta Engineering, “Transient errors”](https://engineering.fb.com/2025/07/22/data-infrastructure/how-meta-keeps-its-ai-hardware-reliable)
- **[inference] rack-bench check:** sustain load long enough to approach thermal equilibrium in the test window. Log GPU clocks, power, temperature, throttling reasons and available inlet/environment sensors against throughput. Repeat under representative site conditions. Two hours cannot establish seasonal HVAC, dust, facility-power or long-term aging resilience. [Meta Engineering, “Transient errors”](https://engineering.fb.com/2025/07/22/data-infrastructure/how-meta-keeps-its-ai-hardware-reliable); [Llama 3 Herd §3.3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783)

### 6.2 Fabric faults and contention

- **[observed]** MegaScale reports network-interface flapping causing stalls or speed drops, with packets lost while a link is down; it traced the problem to link quality involving NIC, cable and switch, and tuned timeouts/retransmission for short flaps. Its monitoring uses second-level host/network health and millisecond-level congestion/transfer measurements. [MegaScale §§4.2, 6.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.15627v1)
- **[observed]** Meta FAIR reports 50–75% bandwidth loss during one fabric bring-up episode with link errors. Its adaptive-routing experiments improved 512-GPU all-reduce bandwidth under injected bit errors and reduced variance under concurrent traffic; benefits depend on workload and topology. [Meta FAIR §IV-B](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)
- **[observed]** Google TPUv4 reports single-OCS-fault all-to-all throughput at 92.2% of healthy for one 4×4×4 slice; other topologies differed. This depends on TPU’s OCS/ICI design and does not predict NVLink/NVSwitch or Ethernet/InfiniBand behavior. [Google TPUv4 §4.3, Table 2](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-zu.pdf)
- **[inference] rack-bench check:** run in-rack collectives and bandwidth/latency tests across representative message sizes, intended rails and GPU pairs; record per-link errors/retries/flaps and congestion signals if exposed. Add safe concurrent traffic when relevant. An isolated peak all-reduce result does not establish shared-fabric goodput; a single rack cannot certify scale-out spine or multi-rack contention. [MegaScale §§4.2, 6.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.15627v1); [Meta FAIR §IV-B](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)

### 6.3 Short-run speed is not long-run useful work

- **[observed]** MegaScale found MFU could decline while forward/backward/optimizer time and apparent bandwidth stayed stable: rank arrival skew delayed reduce-scatter. Its CUDA-event tools also exposed a ~0.5% slow-machine tail that constrained synchronous progress. [MegaScale §§5.1, 6.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.15627v1)
- **[observed]** Meta FAIR separates MFU (model compute efficiency) from ETTR (productive time after interruption, restart and queue effects) and cluster goodput. These metrics answer different questions. [Meta FAIR §II-D](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)
- **[inference]** Publish throughput and run health separately: steady tokens/s or steps/s, rank-tail and time trend, loader wait, checkpoint cost, interruptions/recovery, and useful progress per elapsed time. A short performance PASS is limited to its workload and test window; it is not evidence of 54-day goodput. [Meta FAIR §II-D](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1); [MegaScale §§5–6](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.15627v1)

## 7. Practical two-hour training-health protocol for rack-bench

All items below are **[inference]** recommendations for measurable checks, informed by [Meta FAIR §§II-C–D](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1), [MegaScale §§4–6](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.15627v1), [Google TPUv4 §3.6](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-zu.pdf), and [NVIDIA resiliency guidance](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/training/resiliency.html); acceptance thresholds must be locally specified and are not claimed by the sources.

### 7.1 Suggested evidence sequence (fit to the category’s two-hour allocation)

1. **Baseline snapshot (10 min):** enumerate all 18 trays and accelerators; capture firmware/software, GPU RAS/XID/ECC, PCIe/NVLink, NIC/fabric and storage health counters; temperature/power/clock; verify mounts and data access. Timestamp and retain raw outputs.
2. **Correctness/preflight (15–20 min):** repeat deterministic GPU compute validation; run representative multi-GPU and inter-tray collectives; verify every expected rank and data path; run a small known-model training with seeded data, finite loss/gradients and reference comparison. Record per-device results, not only overall exit status.
3. **Sustained smoke (45–60 min):** run a representative distributed training loop using real loader/storage path. Capture step-time percentiles, per-rank CUDA event spans, loader wait, collective times, data rate, GPU idle, thermal/power/clocks, fabric counters, errors and loss/gradient norms continuously. Include concurrent traffic if safely representative.
4. **Checkpoint/recovery (15–20 min):** save a real representative state, validate manifest/checksums, terminate/restart a worker or job, restore, and show expected resumed step plus valid loss. Measure detection, diagnosis, exclusion, restore, restart and lost work separately. If destructive fault injection is out of scope, state that recovery was not measured.
5. **Final delta check (5–10 min):** compare counters and device status with baseline; disclose errors, outliers, retries, throttling, stale counters, skipped checks, and test limits. PASS applies only to observed checks.

### 7.2 Metrics and causal evidence to publish

- **[inference]** Detection: event-to-alert latency; missed heartbeat; per-rank loss/gradient anomaly; error-counter delta; device/link identity.
- **[inference]** Diagnosis: time to narrow to software, loader/storage, GPU/device, PCIe/NVLink, fabric or facility domain; attach evidence and explicitly mark ambiguous attribution.
- **[inference]** Containment: whether suspect resource was excluded; blast radius; continued-vs-aborted training; successful replacement/reroute if supported.
- **[inference]** Recovery: checkpoint age and integrity, lost steps/tokens, restore/reinitialization duration, time to return to productive progress, and whether loss resumes expected trajectory.
- **[inference]** Efficiency: step/token throughput distribution and trend; p95/max rank skew; loader stall share; checkpoint duty-cycle cost; thermal throttling; useful work per wall time for the test window.
- **[inference]** Avoid “MTBF” or “54-day reliable” from two hours. Provide exposure denominator (GPU-hours/tray-hours), observed event count, test workload and confidence limitation. Any rate estimate from zero failures should state the statistical model and its assumptions.

## 8. Transfer limits to GB300-class NVL72-class, Chennai

### 8.1 What transfers robustly

- **[inference]** Transfer the operational principles: preflight and health telemetry; repeated checks; rank-level timeline; counter deltas; differential diagnosis; node/tray quarantine; checkpoint/restore validation; loss/gradient monitoring; separate performance from goodput. These are architecture-independent requirements demonstrated across Meta, ByteDance, Google and Microsoft practice.
- **[inference]** Validate the specific rack’s physical and software topology rather than import published thresholds: 18 trays, GPU/NVLink/NVSwitch fabric, host CPU/PCIe, NIC/fabric, storage, cooling and power. A vendor’s link-rate or health claim is not a measured PASS. [Microsoft Azure guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cloud-adoption-framework/ai/infrastructure/well-architected)

### 8.2 What does not transfer numerically or structurally

- **[observed]** Sources use different hardware and deployment regimes: Meta Llama 3 used H100-class 16K-GPU-scale clusters; MegaScale’s production cluster was >10,000 NVIDIA Ampere GPUs with custom 200G multi-rail RoCE-era network and HDFS; Google’s paper is TPUv4 with 4096 chips, 3D torus ICI, optical circuit switches and Borg; Meta FAIR analyzed A100 clusters. Their failure rates, diagnostic thresholds, recovery times, availability and routing behavior are not GB300 specifications. [Meta Llama 3](https://ai.meta.com/blog/meta-llama-3); [MegaScale, §§3.6, 6](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.15627v1); [Google TPUv4, §§2–5](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-zu.pdf); [Meta FAIR, §§II–IV](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)
- **[inference]** NVL72’s rack scale may change the failure unit and blast radius, but cited results do not give GB300 NVL72 reliability data. Do not infer 18 trays are equivalent to 72-GPU servers, TPU cubes, or a 10K-GPU cluster. [MegaScale](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.15627v1); [Google TPUv4](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-zu.pdf) Validate NVIDIA-specific RAS, NVLink/NVSwitch counters, rack firmware, NIC/fabric and orchestration available on this exact system.
- **[inference]** Chennai adds local facility/context variables—ambient and inlet temperature, power quality, cooling redundancy, maintenance, and WAN/operator path—that these cited training studies do not quantify for this deployment. Test rack telemetry in its actual site conditions and leave site-level long-term resilience as an explicit gap. [Llama 3 Herd §3.3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783)

## 9. Source confidence, conflicts and evidence limits

### 9.1 Confidence assessment

- **High confidence for mechanisms and measured claims:** ByteDance MegaScale is a peer-reviewed USENIX NSDI’24 systems paper with detailed implementation and multi-week production-run evidence; Google TPUv4 is a peer-reviewed NSDI’24 paper with architecture, preflight, health telemetry and fleet statistics; Meta FAIR is a quantitative 11-month analysis of 150M+ A100 GPU-hours and 4M jobs. These are primary engineering/system sources, but largely self-reported deployments. [MegaScale](https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi24/presentation/jiang-ziheng); [Google paper](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-zu.pdf); [Meta FAIR](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)
- **High confidence for Meta’s disclosed SDC taxonomy and methods; moderate for external generalization:** Meta’s engineering post is first-party operational disclosure and clearly distinguishes static/transient/silent errors, but does not provide enough public denominators to reproduce all SDC rates or show coverage for a two-hour test. [Meta engineering](https://engineering.fb.com/2025/07/22/data-infrastructure/how-meta-keeps-its-ai-hardware-reliable)
- **Moderate confidence for Meta’s distinct Llama metrics:** Meta’s April 2024 product blog reports >95% effective training time as an aggregate outcome, with limited methodological detail. The July 2024 Llama 3 Herd paper gives a separate >90% result for its 405B production pretraining and details a 54-day snapshot with 466 total interruptions (47 planned, 419 unexpected), including >90% automated handling and only three cases requiring significant manual intervention. Do not conflate these values: sources/context differ and no reconciliation is published. [Meta Llama 3 blog](https://ai.meta.com/blog/meta-llama-3); [Llama 3 Herd §3.3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783)
- **Moderate for Microsoft practices:** Azure Learn is authoritative provider guidance on checkpoints, monitoring and Node Health Checks, not an empirical large-run reliability study or contractual performance result. [Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cloud-adoption-framework/ai/infrastructure/well-architected)

### 9.2 Apparent conflicts are metric/scope differences

- **[observed]** Meta Llama 3 says >95% effective training time, while the FAIR paper cites Llama 3 MFU of 38–43% as an example. These do not conflict: ETTR/effective training time counts useful wall-clock time after interruption overhead; MFU measures achieved model FLOPs relative to peak. [Meta Llama 3](https://ai.meta.com/blog/meta-llama-3); [Meta FAIR §II-D](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)
- **[observed]** MegaScale reports >90% effective training time in its >10K-GPU run and >100 restarts; Meta Llama 3 reports >95%. Neither establishes that failures were rare; both show automation/checkpointing can preserve useful progress despite interruptions. The workloads, clusters, metric definitions and reporting differ. [MegaScale §§6.2–6.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.15627v1); [Meta Llama 3](https://ai.meta.com/blog/meta-llama-3)
- **[observed]** Google’s 99.98% system availability is an infrastructure availability result, while ~1% training jobs had outages and were handled by reconfiguration/recovery. System availability must not be read as uninterrupted job success or 99.98% goodput. [Google TPUv4 abstract and §5](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-zu.pdf)
- **[inference]** Failure rates differ materially even within Meta’s two clusters and over time; the FAIR paper notes changing rates, driver bugs, mount issues, and a burst of IB failures on a few nodes. This argues against importing a universal rate or predicting a particular rack from a short observation. [Meta FAIR §§III, IV-A](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)

## 10. NVIDIA Megatron Bridge / NVRx: workload-side recovery controls

### 10.1 Features and constraints

- **[observed]** Megatron Bridge layers resiliency features from NVIDIA Resiliency Extension (NVRx). Fault tolerance monitors setup, training-step and checkpoint sections with distinct timeouts, then restarts; it supports in-job restarts within a Slurm allocation and new job launches, with configurable limits. It requires Slurm plus `ft_launcher` (not `torchrun`), accessible checkpoint storage and RankMonitorClient; it is incompatible with Nsight Systems profiling. [NVIDIA guide, “Fault Tolerance”](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/training/resiliency.html)
- **[observed]** NVRx straggler detection scores relative and individual rank performance, but does **not** stop training by default: `stop_if_detected=True` is required for automatic termination. It requires NVRx; tune `profiling_interval` and do not enable NVRx and legacy MCore detectors together. [NVIDIA guide, “Straggler Detection” and “Practical Caveats”](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/training/resiliency.html)
- **[observed]** The re-run state machine is experimental/alpha with limited integration. It reruns computations on same and different GPUs to attribute NaN/spiky loss to transient error, persistent hardware fault or correct-but-unexpected output; modes are `disabled`, `validate_results`, and `report_determinism_stats`, with exit codes 16/17 controlling job behavior. [NVIDIA guide, “Re-run State Machine”](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/training/resiliency.html)
- **[inference]** Same-input/state anomaly reproducible on one GPU but not another suggests device-specific persistent fault; intermittent same-GPU results suggest transient behavior; reproducibility across devices points toward data/model/software or expected numerical behavior. These are hypotheses, not definitive attribution: nondeterminism, topology and execution-path changes can confound. Keep exact input, checkpoint, seed and comparison outputs. [NVIDIA guide, “Re-run State Machine”](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/training/resiliency.html)
- **[observed]** In-process restart is experimental and requires PyTorch ≥2.5.1 and NCCL ≥2.26.2; it is unsuitable for switch failures/network partitions and should be combined with job-level fault tolerance. Preemption handling observes termination at the end of each training step. Async checkpoint save requires `torch_dist`; local checkpointing requires sufficient local storage and configured replication degree. [NVIDIA guide, “Preemption,” “Async Checkpoint Save,” “Local Checkpointing,” “In-Process Restart”](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/training/resiliency.html)

### 10.2 rack-bench implications

- **[inference]** For the tenant’s actual recipe, record launcher, checkpoint path, timeout configuration, restart limits, NVRx detector status and whether `stop_if_detected` is enabled. Test a chosen same/different-GPU rerun and inspect exit codes; verify that a suspect device is not silently reused. Mark alpha functionality and anything untested. [NVIDIA guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/training/resiliency.html)

## Gaps

- No public source reviewed provides GB300/NVL72 rack failure rates, SDC coverage, validated health thresholds, or 30–90-day rack goodput results. [inference]
- Meta’s Llama-3 >95% effective-training-time headline does not publish its calculation details, checkpoint intervals, restart distribution or MTTR; the later Meta SDC article adds mechanisms, not that run’s raw telemetry. [observed]
- ByteDance’s >90% effective time and recovery timings apply to its proprietary >10K-Ampere cluster, software, storage and workload. Public disclosure does not establish that identical automation is available in a tenant’s rack. [observed]
- A two-hour category check cannot establish meaningful long-horizon MTTF, silent-error absence, full-cycle thermal/facility behavior, recurrent lemon-node history, seasonal Chennai conditions, or storage integrity across dozens of checkpoint generations. [inference]
- Exact acceptance thresholds for the proposed two-hour checks must be defined for the customer’s chosen model, precision, parallelism, dataset, checkpoint size, and intended scale. The cited companies do not provide a universally portable threshold set. [inference]

# Neoclouds: promises and evidence for multi-week training

Research date: 2026-10-11. All claims below carry a source URL.

Claims are marked **[observed]** (directly stated in cited material), **[calculated]** (arithmetic from stated values), or **[inference]** (bounded interpretation). “Availability” means provider/service uptime as contractually defined; “run reliability” means the probability a customer job completes without an interruption; “goodput” means useful completed training progress per paid GPU-hour. They are not interchangeable.

## 1. Executive answer: an SLA is not a 54-day run result

Source basis: [Crusoe screening](https://www.crusoe.ai/resources/blog/how-crusoe-burn-in-tests-every-node-before-it-reaches-you),
[CoreWeave terms](https://docs.coreweave.com/policies/terms-of-service),
[Nebius SLA](https://docs.nebius.com/legal/sla), and
[ClusterMAX observations](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard).
The following conclusions use these sources and the product evidence in §8.

- **[observed]** Public neocloud material makes three kinds of promise: monthly service availability/credits, node qualification and monitoring, and orchestration that detects/replaces failed nodes or resumes work. These claims do not generally publish fleet-level distributions of training-job interruptions, recovery duration, lost work, or successful 30–90-day completion. A 2-hour rack test can produce a measured baseline and expose immediate instability; it cannot validate a 54-day survival probability or prove the provider's job recovery path over weeks.
- **[inference]** A tenant deciding on a 30–90 day lease needs evidence on (a) rack health now, (b) job checkpoint/restart correctness, (c) provider control-plane and replacement behavior, and (d) historical interruption and recovery distributions for the exact SKU/site/topology. Public uptime targets chiefly address (a narrow definition of) service availability, not model progress or economic goodput.
- **[observed]** Publicly available figures that look quantitative are scarce and heterogeneous. Crusoe publishes a 99.5% GPU-VM uptime SLA and node-burn-in description; Nebius publishes service-specific SLAs and describes managed-Kubernetes node autohealing; CoreWeave’s retrieved terms define monthly uptime and exclusions/remedy but the fetched current page extract did not expose its numerical table. None of those is a multi-week run-interruption dataset.

## 2. The three metrics buyers must keep separate

### 2.1 Advertised availability

- **[observed]** Crusoe’s burn-in article says GPU-enabled VMs have a **99.5% uptime SLA**, with details linked to its customer terms ([Crusoe burn-in article](https://www.crusoe.ai/resources/blog/how-crusoe-burn-in-tests-every-node-before-it-reaches-you)). This is a contractual monthly availability statement, not observed completion reliability for a distributed job.
- **[observed]** CoreWeave terms define monthly uptime as total month minutes minus downtime minutes divided by month minutes. They say credits are the sole/exclusive remedy and require customer notice and logs; downtime excludes certain upstream-carrier events and announced maintenance ([CoreWeave TOS](https://docs.coreweave.com/policies/terms-of-service)). The page is marked last modified June 30, 2022; it should not be used to assert a current numeric target without checking the current order form and the applicable regional terms.
- **[observed]** Nebius describes its SLA as applying to specific linked services and paid services; unavailability requires customer reporting and cooperation ([Nebius SLA](https://docs.nebius.com/legal/sla)). Specific service-level pages can differ: its disks page states 99.50% and measures availability in two-minute intervals, with service-specific exclusions and credits ([Nebius disk SLA](https://docs.nebius.com/legal/sla-levels/disks)). Do not generalize a disk commitment to GPU compute.
- **[calculated]** If a service had constant availability p, expected unavailable time over 54 days is 54×24×(1−p): 6.48 hours at 99.5%, 12.96 hours at 99%, and 1.296 hours at 99.9%. These are arithmetic illustrations only—not forecasts, confidence bounds, or job downtime, since events may be correlated, excluded, or scoped differently.
- **[inference]** Monthly aggregation hides event count and duration: one outage and many short interruptions can have equal downtime but very different checkpoint loss and recovery overhead. Credits do not reimburse the GPU-hours consumed by replay, failed optimizer steps, or missed completion dates unless the contract expressly says so.

### 2.2 Observed interruption statistics

- **[observed]** Crusoe cites Pinckney et al. (2024) for cluster-scale event rates: mean time between failures of roughly 47 days at 8 GPUs, 8 hours at 1,024 GPUs, and 1.8 hours at 16,384 GPUs ([Crusoe article](https://www.crusoe.ai/resources/blog/how-crusoe-burn-in-tests-every-node-before-it-reaches-you); [paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)). These are research-cluster-scale figures reported by Crusoe, not Crusoe customer-run interruption statistics and not directly transferable to an 18-tray GB300 rack. Verify paper scope/definitions before using them as a prediction.
- **[observed]** Crusoe explains that a distributed job can stop while a failure is detected, replacement provisioned, and the job rolls back to its last checkpoint; without checkpointing, interruption delays can be substantial ([Crusoe article](https://www.crusoe.ai/resources/blog/how-crusoe-burn-in-tests-every-node-before-it-reaches-you)). It gives no public denominator, per-run interruption histogram, checkpoint interval distribution, MTTR percentiles, or multi-week completion rate.
- **[observed]** Nebius announced node autohealing in its managed Kubernetes service, intended to replace faulty nodes and minimize training interruptions, plus inline health checks to identify/isolate compromised nodes ([Nebius Q1 2025 updates](https://nebius.com/blog/posts/q1-2025-cloud-updates)). Announcement establishes feature availability, not observed interruption reduction or a service guarantee.
- **[inference]** The sources establish selected mechanisms and a few independently tested events, but not comparable provider-specific interruption rates or p50/p95 recovery distributions with job/GPU-hour denominators ([ClusterMAX 3.0](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard); provider docs in §8).

## 3. Mechanisms that can protect training progress

### 3.1 Pre-admission screening and live health

- **[observed]** Crusoe describes per-node qualification across node, GPU and fabric domains, including DCGM diagnostics, ECC, PCIe, sustained power, pulsed power, storage performance/latency, NIC checks, RDMA bandwidth and multi-node NCCL/RCCL tests. It says tests run in customer-like VMs; failed nodes are repaired/replaced and retested, and targeted validation follows upgrades ([Crusoe burn-in article](https://www.crusoe.ai/resources/blog/how-crusoe-burn-in-tests-every-node-before-it-reaches-you)). This is unusually specific public evidence of mechanism, but provider-authored and not independently audited.
- **[observed]** Crusoe describes AutoClusters detecting unhealthy nodes and replacing them from a burn-in-validated spare pool, typically within minutes of detection, for managed Kubernetes workloads ([Crusoe burn-in article](https://www.crusoe.ai/resources/blog/how-crusoe-burn-in-tests-every-node-before-it-reaches-you); [AutoClusters article](https://www.crusoe.ai/resources/blog/autoclusters-minimizing-hardware-failures-in-large-gpu-clusters)). “Typically” is not a measured percentile or guarantee; scope is managed Kubernetes, not necessarily every bare-metal/Slurm offer.
- **[observed]** Nebius reports managed-Kubernetes health checks and node autohealing ([Nebius update](https://nebius.com/blog/posts/q1-2025-cloud-updates)). Public page does not quantify detection delay, replacement availability, or job-state preservation.
- **[inference]** Preflight certification can assess component health, sustained load, fabric collectives, and checkpoint-path write/read behavior. It cannot reproduce fleet-wide spare exhaustion, control-plane outages, rare correlated power/network failures, or provider-side repair operations.

### 3.2 Checkpoint and restart are application/platform responsibilities

- **[observed]** Crusoe explicitly describes rollback to the last checkpoint as the way a distributed training job recovers after an interruption ([Crusoe article](https://www.crusoe.ai/resources/blog/how-crusoe-burn-in-tests-every-node-before-it-reaches-you)). Its public article does not specify checkpoint atomicity, optimizer/RNG/data-loader state, storage durability, or a mandatory checkpoint cadence.
- **[inference]** “Auto-recovery” can mean node replacement, scheduler requeue, container restart, or restoration of a complete training state. Only the last, combined with correct distributed coordination and durable checkpoint storage, resumes useful learning. Ask provider and tenant to identify exactly which layer owns each step and what state is restored.
- **[inference]** Before a lease, a controlled kill/restart exercise is stronger than a promise: save a real multi-rank checkpoint, terminate one worker/job, requeue/restart, validate step number, optimizer and scheduler state, RNG/data position as applicable, checkpoint integrity, and compare resumed loss/progress. Repeat from the actual shared checkpoint filesystem. A two-hour test can exercise this once or a few times; it cannot establish a rare-event recovery distribution.

### 3.3 Spot/preemption and elastic restart

- **[observed]** Nebius preemptible VMs can stop at any time, signal with SIGTERM 60 seconds before SIGKILL, preserve attached volumes but lose local SSD data, and do not support automatic `RECOVER`; they have no guaranteed availability ([Nebius preemptible docs](https://docs.nebius.com/compute/virtual-machines/preemptible)). Comparable policies for CoreWeave, Lambda, and Together were not verified.
- **[inference]** For fixed-size synchronous LLM pretraining, elastic restart is not automatic: a failed rank commonly disrupts the collective job, and changing world size can alter optimizer and training semantics. “Elastic” must be demonstrated for the exact framework, launcher, checkpoint format, and model configuration ([PyTorch DCP recipe](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/recipes/distributed_checkpoint_recipe.html); [CoreWeave Slurm signal guide](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/sunk/run_workloads/handle-slurm-signals)).

## 4. Provider evidence snapshot (public evidence, not provider ranking)

| Provider | What public evidence supports | What it does not establish |
|---|---|---|
| **Crusoe** | **[observed]** 99.5% GPU VM uptime SLA claim; detailed published pre-customer burn-in; managed-Kubernetes AutoClusters node detection/replacement typically within minutes ([burn-in article](https://www.crusoe.ai/resources/blog/how-crusoe-burn-in-tests-every-node-before-it-reaches-you)). | **[observed]** No public customer-run interruption denominator, run completion probability, MTTR percentile, or checkpoint recovery success rate found in cited material. The burn-in description is first-party. |
| **Nebius** | **[observed]** Service-specific SLA framework; e.g. disk SLA 99.50%; managed K8s autohealing and inline health checks announced ([SLA](https://docs.nebius.com/legal/sla), [disk SLA](https://docs.nebius.com/legal/sla-levels/disks), [Q1 2025 update](https://nebius.com/blog/posts/q1-2025-cloud-updates)). | **[observed]** Disk SLA is not GPU/job SLA; feature announcement provides no observed training interruption/recovery statistics. |
| **CoreWeave** | **[observed]** Terms define monthly uptime accounting, downtime and exclusions, support evidence and credits/remedy ([TOS](https://docs.coreweave.com/policies/terms-of-service)). | **[observed]** Retrieved TOS is old (2022) and the extracted page did not expose a reliable current GPU SLA percentage. Confirm current SKU/region/order-specific terms; no run-interruption distribution found. |
| **Lambda** | **[observed]** [1CC docs](https://docs.lambda.ai/public-cloud/1-click-clusters) specify multi-week reservations and attached Lambda filesystems, with ephemeral local NVMe; [ClusterMAX](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard) reports bounded health-check and XID events (§8.3). | **[observed]** No job recovery contract or shared-filesystem durability SLA established by these sources. |
| **Together** | **[observed]** [Storage docs](https://docs.together.ai/docs/gpu-clusters-overview) and [health docs](https://docs.together.ai/docs/health-checks) specify persistent shared volumes and active/passive checks; [ClusterMAX](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard) reports an active-job drain and replacement events (§8.4). | **[observed]** No comparable fleet statistics or complete filesystem durability/backup contract established. |
| **Others** | **[observed]** Provider marketing increasingly describes managed orchestration, health visibility, node replacement and job resumption; these are mechanisms worth testing, not measured outcomes ([Crusoe training](https://www.crusoe.ai/cloud/solutions/model-training)). | **[inference]** Do not pool unlike managed-service and raw-instance claims into one reliability score. |

## 5. Economic GPU-hour goodput: availability is only one factor

Source basis: [Meta productive-time accounting](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.21680v1)
and [Crusoe checkpoint rollback](https://www.crusoe.ai/resources/blog/how-crusoe-burn-in-tests-every-node-before-it-reaches-you).
The calculations below state their assumptions.

- **[inference]** A practical measure is useful completed training progress / paid GPU-hours. A conceptual decomposition is: productive fraction ≈ uptime × (1 − recovery/replay overhead) × useful-work efficiency; this omits queueing, throttling, data stalls, and failed/invalid steps, so report those separately rather than implying one universal formula.
- **[calculated]** With checkpoint interval C and a failure occurring uniformly between checkpoints, expected lost computation per failure is about C/2, before restart time. Shorter intervals reduce replay but consume checkpoint I/O and can stall training. The approximation assumes periodic checkpoints and uniform failure timing.
- **[inference]** For a 54-day run, compare offers using expected usable progress and downside tails, not the SLA credit alone: GPU rental cost during restart, replayed GPU-hours, checkpoint storage and write stalls, replacement wait/queue, and the chance the job misses its deadline. Request actual paid-versus-useful GPU-hour data from comparable runs; do not infer it from claimed uptime or peak benchmark throughput.

## 6. Candidate two-hour checks for rack-bench (no multi-week claim)

Proposal basis: [CoreWeave checkpoint signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/sunk/run_workloads/handle-slurm-signals),
[Crusoe screening](https://www.crusoe.ai/resources/blog/how-crusoe-burn-in-tests-every-node-before-it-reaches-you),
and [ClusterMAX observations](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard).
The statistical limit uses the [Poisson model](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda366j.htm).
The proposals do not establish provider results.

1. **[inference] Establish a continuous baseline:** run representative distributed training/collectives for the full available window; timestamp rank health, GPU XID/ECC/thermal/power clocks, NCCL errors/retries, link counters, filesystem latency, checkpoint duration, step time, loss, and completed tokens/steps. Report measured uptime only for this two-hour interval.
2. **[inference] Test checkpoint path under load:** write a representative checkpoint to the actual shared durable filesystem while training continues; record bytes, duration, throughput, latency, integrity/checksum, and whether all ranks agree on completed step. Read it back and validate.
3. **[inference] Controlled restart/requeue:** with operator approval, terminate a test worker or job (not hardware/power fault injection), trigger the documented scheduler path, and measure detection→reschedule→checkpoint-read→first-valid-step. Verify exact state continuity and no silent loss/corruption. Repeat only if time allows.
4. **[inference] Separate host survival from job survival:** compare process, node, and fabric event timelines. A clean smoke test is not an SLA observation; a recovery demonstration is not a measured provider-wide MTTR.
5. **[inference] Capture provenance:** exact rack/SKU, software stack, scheduler, job shape/world size, checkpoint backend, test start/end, all event logs, and PASS criteria. PASS is the observed result only; absence of failure in 2h is not proof of low multi-week failure probability.

### What two hours cannot certify

- **[inference]** No meaningful direct estimate of rare multi-week failure probability from one short test. Even a zero-failure interval is weak evidence: under a simplistic Poisson model, zero events over two hours gives a 95% upper rate bound of roughly 3/2 = 1.5 events/hour, far too loose for multi-week inference; real failures are not necessarily Poisson or independent.
- **[inference]** No validation of spare capacity under simultaneous regional incidents, control-plane availability, upstream power/cooling/transit resilience, long-run thermal drift, firmware/maintenance changes, provider staffing/repair quality, or a 54-day storage-retention guarantee.
- **[inference]** No inference from a successful small-scale or short synthetic workload to 405B-class convergence, full-run MFU, or model quality. A single restart proves only that tested recovery path worked once under tested conditions.

## 7. Evidence quality and unresolved issues

- **High confidence, narrow scope:** Nebius legal SLA framework and service-specific disk page; CoreWeave legal definitions (but old page/version caution); direct provider description of Crusoe’s test mechanisms. These establish text of promises/mechanisms, not actual operational outcomes.
- **Medium confidence:** Crusoe’s cited cluster-scale MTBF figures, because the provider reproduces a peer-reviewed paper but they are secondary presentation and not the same workload, provider, or rack scale. Consult paper definitions before quantitative reuse.
- **Low/absent public evidence:** comparative provider run reliability, observed interruption statistics, checkpoint/restart success, and economic GPU-hour goodput. Marketing case studies without exposure duration, job count, interruption denominator and censored-run handling cannot establish these quantities.


## 8. Targeted product and policy evidence (verified follow-up)

This section adds direct product documentation and ClusterMAX 3.0 counterevidence. A documented mechanism is a vendor statement; SemiAnalysis observations are independent of those vendors but are still a limited external test sample, not a fleet-wide dataset.

### 8.1 CoreWeave: SUNK, stragglers, checkpoints, Tensorizer

- **[observed — vendor mechanism]** CoreWeave SUNK GPU Straggler Detection uses NCCL telemetry to identify lagging ranks/nodes and surface rank-level dashboards; docs say SUNK v8+ enables the plugin by default, with configuration prerequisites and opt-out ([CoreWeave straggler docs](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/sunk/discover_sunk/straggler-detection); [enable guide](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/sunk/optimize_workloads/enable-gpu-straggler-detection)). The docs describe detection/diagnosis and recommendations, not guaranteed automatic replacement or restoration of a training job.
- **[observed — vendor mechanism]** CoreWeave’s Slurm signal-handling guide demonstrates catching SIGTERM, saving model and optimizer state to a writable shared filesystem or AI Object Storage checkpoint path, then exiting so a job can be requeued/resumed ([CoreWeave Slurm signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/sunk/run_workloads/handle-slurm-signals)). This is a recipe requiring checkpoint-capable user code; it does not claim provider-side transparent checkpointing or test complete optimizer/RNG/dataloader continuity.
- **[observed — vendor product scope]** Tensorizer serializes/deserializes PyTorch modules/tensors, including from HTTP/HTTPS and S3, primarily to accelerate model loading ([CoreWeave Tensorizer project](https://github.com/coreweave/tensorizer); [product article](https://www.coreweave.com/blog/coreweaves-tensorizer-decrease-pytorch-model-load-times)). It is not by itself distributed training checkpoint/restart orchestration. For training checkpoint path evidence, CoreWeave’s SUNK signal recipe and ClusterMAX’s Torch DCP checkpoint benchmark are more directly relevant.
- **[observed — independent ClusterMAX observation]** SemiAnalysis reports CoreWeave added GPU straggler detection that attributes lagging ranks from NCCL telemetry and supports remediation advice; testers described its use in customer calls, alongside active idle-node burn-in and rigorous node bring-up ([ClusterMAX 3.0](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)). This corroborates a real operational mechanism but publishes no false-positive/negative rates, detection latency distribution, or resulting multi-week goodput uplift.

### 8.2 Nebius: Soperator, preemption, shared root filesystem, GB300 recovery

- **[observed — vendor mechanism]** Nebius Soperator runs Slurm components as Kubernetes resources, reconciled from a SlurmCluster custom resource. Its docs describe a shared root filesystem implemented as a Kubernetes PersistentVolume and say it preserves data when nodes restart; node-local SSD is ephemeral and recommended for scratch/cache, not durable shared data ([Soperator architecture](https://docs.nebius.com/slurm-soperator/overview/architecture)). This is a persistence statement, not a published durability/availability percentage, backup/restore guarantee, corruption rate, or multi-week endurance result.
- **[observed — vendor policy]** Nebius preemptible VMs can be stopped at any time for capacity or price reasons, with SIGTERM 60 seconds before SIGKILL. Attached-volume data is preserved; dynamic public IPs are not, and local SSD data is lost on stop. Preemptible VMs have no guaranteed availability; only `FAIL` recovery policy is supported (not VM auto-`RECOVER`), and preemption action is `STOP` ([Nebius preemptible VM docs](https://docs.nebius.com/compute/virtual-machines/preemptible)). This is an explicit, verified policy: tenant software must checkpoint on signal and relaunch/recover the VM/job; the provider does not promise transparent VM recovery.
- **[observed — independent ClusterMAX observation]** ClusterMAX 3.0 reports that Nebius automatically returned a node to service after synthetic error injection on the tested GB300 rack, with immediate detection but **8h40m end-to-end** recovery. SemiAnalysis notes other tested GB300 racks did not automatically reboot/return injected failed nodes ([ClusterMAX 3.0](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)). This is an observed test event on a particular allocation, not a general Nebius MTTR or a commitment; it directly qualifies broad “autohealing” language.
- **[inference]** The Soperator design’s shared-root persistence and a node-recovery controller address separate failure layers. A node returning after 8h40m does not establish whether a distributed training job resumes correctly, nor whether its checkpoint filesystem remains available throughout the incident.

### 8.3 Lambda: 1-Click Clusters and filesystem boundary

- **[observed — vendor mechanism/product]** Lambda 1-Click Clusters are reserved multi-node H100/B200 clusters (16–512 GPUs in current docs), with 3 CPU management nodes, Slurm-style admin/job-scheduling use, and Lambda filesystems automatically attached to nodes; reservation duration is specified in weeks ([Lambda 1CC docs](https://docs.lambda.ai/public-cloud/1-click-clusters)). The docs establish a long-reservation product and shared filesystem integration, not an uptime SLA or job-level recovery guarantee.
- **[observed — vendor caveat]** Local NVMe is ephemeral and data is deleted/unrecoverable when the reservation ends; users are responsible for backing up data, e.g. to a Lambda filesystem. Filesystem S3 Adapter availability is region-limited ([Lambda 1CC docs](https://docs.lambda.ai/public-cloud/1-click-clusters)). The cited documentation does not state a shared-filesystem durability SLA, snapshot cadence, replication factor, or recovery-time objective.
- **[observed — independent ClusterMAX observation]** ClusterMAX 3.0’s Lambda testing reported active health checks autoremediating two synthetic XIDs in under 15 minutes, while a genuine XID 79 path lacked visible K8s GPU-XID/cordon/monitoring signals and returned after two hours. The review also notes Slurm CPU allocation defaults, absent compute-node SSH outside allocations, and stale CUDA/driver versions in that tested environment ([ClusterMAX 3.0](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)). These are bounded outcomes from one test engagement, not present-day policy or fleet rates.

### 8.4 Together: documented storage/health checks versus observed drain behavior

- **[observed — vendor mechanism]** Together’s GPU-cluster overview describes persistent shared volumes as surviving pod restarts, node reboots, and cluster deletion; on Slurm `/home` is NFS-backed/persistent, while Kubernetes `/home` and local NVMe are ephemeral ([Together GPU clusters overview](https://docs.together.ai/docs/gpu-clusters-overview)). This does not specify backup, replication, filesystem failure-domain, durability percentage, or tested checkpoint recovery.
- **[observed — vendor mechanism]** Together documents active checks that fully utilize the GPU and can interfere with running jobs, and recommends maintenance/idle windows; passive health checks monitor production workloads without impact ([Together health checks](https://docs.together.ai/docs/health-checks)). The documentation describes checks and repair recommendations, not a no-disruption guarantee.
- **[observed — independent ClusterMAX observation]** ClusterMAX 3.0 reports Together’s Slurm `HealthCheckProgram` ran `dcgmi diag -r 1` on already-scheduled nodes under a 45-second timeout; the diagnostic timed out and was misclassified as failure, draining active nodes mid-run. Together fixed the issue after feedback. In a separate PCIe reset test, Slurm drained the node in 67 seconds and automatic replacement completed in 35m7s. The report also describes two nodes failing during compute testing, one sent for RMA without notice, and a storage-NIC provisioning race that required manual reprovisioning ([ClusterMAX 3.0](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)). This is valuable direct counterevidence to treating “health checks” as uniformly safe: health-check scheduling and timeout policy can themselves interrupt work. It is one tested environment/time, not fleet statistics.
- **[inference]** The verified Together docs and ClusterMAX observations are not contradictory: passive monitoring can be non-invasive while active checks consume GPUs; scheduler-integrated checks can still cause interruption if run against allocated nodes or use unsuitable timeouts. Ask for policy by check type and state, not a generic health-check feature list.

## 9. Stronger conclusions after source review

Source basis: the product URLs in §8 and
[ClusterMAX 3.0](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard).
This section compares those bounded disclosures.

- **[observed]** Specific interruption handling is materially different by product. Nebius preemptible VMs explicitly stop rather than recover automatically; CoreWeave SUNK provides a user-code checkpoint-on-SIGTERM recipe; Crusoe advertises AutoClusters; Lambda 1CC docs describe reserved cluster/filesystem workflow but no job recovery contract; Together documents health-check and storage behavior, with ClusterMAX reporting a health-check timeout that drained active work.
- **[observed]** The best public quantitative counterevidence is test-event data, not multi-week run populations: Nebius GB300 synthetic-error recovery 8h40m; Together injected PCIe reset to replacement 35m7s plus a separate misconfigured health check draining active jobs; Lambda two synthetic errors under 15 minutes but genuine XID 79 return in two hours. Do not compare these as provider MTTR rankings: event types, cluster state, and measured endpoints differ.
- **[inference]** Bench should test health-policy semantics safely: identify active versus passive checks, determine whether checks can run on allocated jobs, inject only a controlled software-level test event with operator approval, timestamp detection/drain/requeue/replacement, and execute checkpoint resume. For NVL72, test the rack-specific degradation/recovery contract rather than assuming a four-GPU tray can be hot-swapped.


## Gaps

- No verified public source here provides comparable multi-week job counts, interruption rates per GPU-hour, completion denominators, p50/p95 recovery, checkpoint replay loss, or paid-versus-useful GPU-hour goodput for CoreWeave, Nebius, Crusoe, Lambda, or Together ([ClusterMAX 3.0](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)).
- CoreWeave docs establish SUNK straggler telemetry and a user-code SIGTERM checkpoint example, but not production recovery guarantees, false-positive rates, or complete optimizer/RNG/dataloader restoration. Tensorizer sources describe serialization/model loading, not distributed training restart orchestration ([SUNK](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/sunk/discover_sunk/straggler-detection); [signal guide](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/sunk/run_workloads/handle-slurm-signals); [Tensorizer](https://github.com/coreweave/tensorizer)).
- Nebius Soperator documents shared-root PV persistence across node restarts, but not backing-storage durability SLA or checkpoint restore performance; preemptible policy is explicit, but SKU-specific reclaim frequency and price history remain unverified ([Soperator architecture](https://docs.nebius.com/slurm-soperator/overview/architecture); [preemptible policy](https://docs.nebius.com/compute/virtual-machines/preemptible)).
- Lambda 1CC docs describe attached filesystems and warn about ephemeral-local-data deletion, but do not provide shared-filesystem durability/backup guarantees or recovery distributions ([Lambda 1CC docs](https://docs.lambda.ai/public-cloud/1-click-clusters)). Together docs describe persistence and check types but not complete filesystem failure domains, backup terms, or current health-check scheduling/timeout policy; verify ClusterMAX’s reported correction on the offered site/SKU ([Together overview](https://docs.together.ai/docs/gpu-clusters-overview); [health checks](https://docs.together.ai/docs/health-checks); [ClusterMAX 3.0](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard)).
- Comparable current spot/preemption policies for CoreWeave, Lambda, and Together were not verified; do not generalize Nebius’ documented policy to them.
- No source here quantifies Chennai-specific upstream power/connectivity event correlation or long-run failure rates for this exact GB300 NVL72 18-tray rack. Before lease, request binding site/SKU SLA, maintenance and preemption terms, filesystem service schedule, checkpoint/recovery runbook, and historical events with denominators ([CoreWeave SLA terms](https://docs.coreweave.com/policies/terms-of-service); [Nebius SLA](https://docs.nebius.com/legal/sla)).

# N01 — Neocloud training promises

State: done.
Research date: 2026-10-11.
Child: neoclouds.
