# N08 — *Designing Deep Learning Systems*

Research date: 2026-10-11. All claims below carry a source URL.

Bench safety: operator approval is necessary before process interruption.
Default checks exclude power removal, PCIe reset, and hardware-error injection.
Report expected checkpoint rollback and replay separately from silent duplicate or skipped progress.

Scope: independent supplement for a GB300-class, NVL72-class rack (18 trays) in Chennai; measured named workload only. A two-hour measurement window informs a 30–90-day lease decision and a 54-day Llama-class run. PASS means measured evidence, not specifications. Meta inventory: 466 total interruptions = 47 planned + 419 unexpected; unexpected denominator is 419. [Llama 3, §3.3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783v3)

Labels: [observed] source explicitly states it; [calculated] arithmetic; [inference] application to this rack. No book claim is treated as a rack test result.

## 1. Verified edition, chapters, access

[Observed] Manning identifies the authors as Chi Wang and Donald Szeto, and describes *Designing Deep Learning Systems: A software engineer’s guide* as a production-platform engineering book. Its stated scope includes dataset management, model training/serving, hyperparameter tuning, and automated training in TensorFlow and PyTorch. [Manning book page](https://www.manning.com/books/designing-deep-learning-systems)

[Observed] The O’Reilly catalog URL supplied for this research is `https://learning.oreilly.com/library/view/-/9781633439863/?orm_source=mcp`; direct fetch was denied. Search results confirmed the matching title at O’Reilly’s public catalog route [O’Reilly catalog](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/designing-deep-learning/9781633439863), but the retrieved primary full text for chapter verification came from Manning’s public LiveBook, not O’Reilly.

[Observed] Manning LiveBook chapter pages verify the relevant chapter names and contents: Chapter 3, “Model training service,” covers service design, workflow, training code patterns, and job status; Chapter 4, “Distributed training,” covers data/model/pipeline parallelism and a sample data-parallel training service; Chapter 5, “Hyperparameter optimization service,” covers HPO approaches and service design. [Ch. 3](https://livebook.manning.com/book/designing-deep-learning-systems/chapter-3) [Ch. 4](https://livebook.manning.com/book/designing-deep-learning-systems/chapter-4) [Ch. 5](https://livebook.manning.com/book/designing-deep-learning-systems/chapter-5)

[Observed] Chapter 4’s stated focus is supporting distributed training from a software-engineering perspective, including executing researchers’ code across machines. Chapter 5 concerns automated hyperparameter selection. These are not evidence of fault-tolerance procedures, optimizer/RNG/data-cursor checkpoint completeness, node-failure recovery, loss-spike triage, or validating hardware. [Ch. 4](https://livebook.manning.com/book/designing-deep-learning-systems/chapter-4) [Ch. 5](https://livebook.manning.com/book/designing-deep-learning-systems/chapter-5)

## 2. Training-run validation and reliability evidence

[Observed] The verified book material is about building training services and automating training/optimization. Chapter 3 calls the service responsible for managing compute resources and executing training code; Chapter 4 addresses parallelism and multiworker training challenges. Manning describes model training, dataset management, and HPO as platform capabilities. [Ch. 3](https://livebook.manning.com/book/designing-deep-learning-systems/chapter-3) [Ch. 4](https://livebook.manning.com/book/designing-deep-learning-systems/chapter-4) [Manning overview](https://www.manning.com/books/designing-deep-learning-systems)

[Inference] These topics can inform how a rack workload is launched, observed as a managed job, and connected to its data/training components. They do not establish a measured MFU method or threshold, hardware qualification, interruption/recovery statistics, or a correctness guarantee for resuming a real distributed run. Do not turn “multiworker training challenges” into a claim that the book supplies a fault-tolerance or checkpoint-validation protocol.

[Inference] There is no verified book evidence here about accounting for MFU, measuring interruption frequency, classifying flaky nodes, loader stalls, or diagnosing a loss spike. A clean two-hour trace cannot establish a 54-day reliability claim. Report only observations under the exact named workload and interval; state untested duration and failure modes explicitly.

[Inference] Automated hyperparameter optimization and training optimization are different from fault tolerance and physical hardware validation. HPO explores model/training choices; a training service orchestrates jobs and resources. Neither, by itself, demonstrates that saving and restoring model weights, optimizer state, RNG streams, scheduler state, sampler/data position, and distributed metadata is complete or correct. The chapter abstracts and Manning overview support the first distinction, not a claim that the book teaches the second. [Ch. 3](https://livebook.manning.com/book/designing-deep-learning-systems/chapter-3) [Ch. 5](https://livebook.manning.com/book/designing-deep-learning-systems/chapter-5)

## 3. Portable techniques and measured checks

These are [inference] proposals for applying the book’s service-oriented framing. They are not quoted book procedures or universal GB300 gates.

1. **Name and freeze the workload.** Record model/code and data versions, precision, sequence length, batch, parallelism, optimizer, framework, and launch configuration. [Manning](https://www.manning.com/books/designing-deep-learning-systems) [Measured check] Run that exact job across the intended 18 trays; report interval, warm-up exclusion, tokens/s, step-time distribution, and the declared MFU formula. Compare only with a tenant-approved target or baseline, not a vendor peak.
2. **Measure the whole training service path.** Chapter 3 frames training as managed compute plus execution; Chapter 4 treats distributed execution. [Ch. 3](https://livebook.manning.com/book/designing-deep-learning-systems/chapter-3) [Ch. 4](https://livebook.manning.com/book/designing-deep-learning-systems/chapter-4) [Measured check] Capture per-rank step times, collectives, GPU telemetry, dataloader wait, and storage-read stalls during the named workload; identify observed slow ranks and stall intervals rather than labeling a node faulty from one symptom.
3. **Exercise a real interruption and restore.** The verified chapter contents do not specify checkpoint semantics; this is an acceptance-test proposal, not book-derived functionality. [Ch. 3](https://livebook.manning.com/book/designing-deep-learning-systems/chapter-3) [Measured check] Save, terminate and resume the tenant’s representative job; verify expected step and data position, model/optimizer/scheduler state, and relevant RNG/sampler state against the declared contract. Record save/load time, lost work, replay/skip behavior, and integrity result. Do not claim complete correctness if the production state contract was not exercised.
4. **Triage anomalies with multiple signals.** HPO is not fault diagnosis. [Ch. 5](https://livebook.manning.com/book/designing-deep-learning-systems/chapter-5) [Measured check] Preserve step-level loss and gradient summaries alongside rank timing, device/error telemetry, input wait, and checkpoint events; investigate a spike or stall by correlating signals. A normal short loss trace does not rule out silent corruption or later failures.
5. **Report interruption evidence as sampled exposure.** [Measured check] Count observed job interruptions, restart outcomes, and affected ranks during the actual measurement interval; distinguish observed events from injected drills. Zero events in two hours means “none observed in this interval,” not a long-run failure-rate estimate or assurance for 54 days.

[Calculated] 54 days = 1,296 hours, 648 two-hour windows. The ratio is exposure arithmetic, not a reliability estimate.

## 4. Canon relation and candidate

[Observed] Canon N07 already treats books as systems-framing sources and ranks current operational documentation and reliability evidence above books for distributed training failure engineering. It identifies *Designing Machine Learning Systems* (DMLS), *Reliable Machine Learning*, and *AI Engineering* as separate titles; N08 is *Designing Deep Learning Systems*, by Chi Wang and Donald Szeto. [Canon: N07](../books.md)

[Inference] Add N08 as a distinct, lower-priority platform-engineering supplement, not as another reliability handbook or as the previously listed DMLS by Chip Huyen. Its verified service/parallelism/HPO topics complement broad systems framing, while it does not fill N07’s gaps on hardware screening, checkpoint/restart correctness, flaky-node evidence, MFU accounting, or multiweek reliability.

[Observed] The Manning public page links “Look inside” to the LiveBook; O’Reilly’s supplied access URL denied fetch, and no chapter-level O’Reilly text was verified in this pass. [Manning LiveBook](https://livebook.manning.com/book/designing-deep-learning-systems) [O’Reilly supplied URL](https://learning.oreilly.com/library/view/-/9781633439863/?orm_source=mcp)

## Gaps

- The supplied O’Reilly learning URL was inaccessible to fetch. Edition/author/title are corroborated by public Manning and O’Reilly catalog results, and chapter details by Manning LiveBook; exact O’Reilly edition metadata and full text were not independently inspected.
- Verified public chapter material does not establish checkpoint/resume correctness, optimizer/RNG/data-state completeness, interruption statistics, loss-spike diagnosis, flaky-node screening, or loader-stall measurement.
- No two-hour measurement establishes 30–90-day or 54-day reliability. Rack/workload-specific thresholds and confidence claims require tenant targets, measured evidence, and appropriately long exposure.
- No source reviewed validates a universal GB300/NVL72 acceptance gate. Use workload-specific measured checks, not specifications or book descriptions.

## 3. Portable techniques (proposals; primary-source basis and measurable evidence)

[NVIDIA Megatron-LM](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM)
2. **Exercise checkpoint and resume state safely.** Save a checkpoint during a representative run, validate it, then conduct a scheduled process/job restart in an isolated acceptance window. Record save/load time, restored step, optimizer/model state, consumed-data position, sampler/RNG state where applicable, lost work, and silent duplicate/skipped-step check. Report expected checkpoint rollback and replay separately. Evidence: successful resumed steps and checkpoint integrity under the tenant’s trainer. 3. **Make interruption statistics explicit.** Report planned and unexpected counts separately; use 419 as denominator for attribution of unexpected interruptions in the supplied history, and state missing/unknown attribution rather than silently dropping cases. For new observations, record exposure hours, event timestamps, cause confidence, and censored/unknown events. Evidence: auditable event ledger and denominator. This is accounting discipline, not a reliability forecast.
4. **Triage loss spikes with corroborating signals.** Preserve loss, gradient/parameter norms, rank identity, step/data position, hardware/error telemetry, and nearby collective/loader timing; compare to run-specific baseline and investigate before resuming. Loss alone is not proof of hardware fault or health. Evidence: timestamp-correlated traces and a documented disposition. [SDC study](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.00726v1) · [NVIDIA Megatron Bridge resiliency](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/training/resiliency.html)
5. **Screen stragglers and loader stalls under the actual workload.** Collect per-rank step latency/tokens per second, input wait time, storage read latency/throughput, and CPU utilization; inspect persistent outliers and correlate with node telemetry. Evidence: rank-level distributions and stall attribution in the measured interval, not a generic hardware threshold. [NVIDIA Megatron Bridge resiliency](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/training/resiliency.html) · [PyTorch profiler recipe](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/recipes/recipes/profiler_recipe.html)

[Course contents](https://www.oreilly.com/videos/designing-machine-learning/0636920953234) **Evidence:** retain per-step/per-rank measurements and calculate observed throughput and dispersion for the two-hour run; do not claim a universal GB300 pass threshold.
2. **Expose input-pipeline waits separately.** Instrument data-wait time and step time so a slow step is distinguishable from loader starvation; capture the actual data path used. Source basis: training-data and data-engineering lessons. [Course contents](https://www.oreilly.com/videos/designing-machine-learning/0636920953234) **Evidence:** quantify waiting/step-time fractions during the measured workload; a short run cannot establish behavior under later storage contention.
3. **Test resume as an explicit interruption drill.** Save a checkpoint, interrupt the process/job in a controlled way, resume, and verify expected step and consumed-data position; measure save, restore, and lost-work time. This is a proposed rack test, not a technique verified in the video. The catalog only names automated training and experiment tracking. [Course contents](https://www.oreilly.com/videos/designing-machine-learning/0636920953234) **Evidence:** preserve checkpoint identity, before/after step and sampler position, restore outcome, and timings. Do not imply the catalog teaches checkpoint semantics.
4. **Triage loss with context, not loss alone.** Log loss alongside step time, rank identity, data position, and available device/job telemetry; flag excursions for investigation rather than declaring a fault from loss alone. The course listing supports observability/metrics as broad topics, not this specific diagnostic method. [Course contents](https://www.oreilly.com/videos/designing-machine-learning/0636920953234) **Evidence:** show the aligned trace and disposition of any anomaly observed in the window. A clean two-hour trace does not exclude rare or silent faults.
5. **Report interruptions and stragglers as observed events.** Preserve per-rank progress and job interruptions during the exact workload; distinguish measured outliers from inferred hardware causes. The catalog supports observability and experiment management at a general level only. [Course contents](https://www.oreilly.com/videos/designing-machine-learning/0636920953234) **Evidence:** report counts, durations, affected ranks, and whether recovery succeeded; do not label a node defective without corroborating diagnosis.

[Observed] Context for interpreting incident counts: the Llama 3 paper reports Meta’s 466 total interruptions as **47 planned and 419 unexpected**. Hardware-related attribution uses the 419 unexpected events, not all 466. These are not course findings. [Llama 3, §3.3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783v3)

[Inference] A two-hour workload can show measured behavior and recovery for the named test, not a 30–90-day lease guarantee or 54-day Llama training warranty. Two hours is a sample, not a long-run reliability demonstration. Do not turn this course’s cloud-systems framing into universal GB300 acceptance gates or destructive default tests.

## 4. Canon relation / candidate

[Observed] The canon already ranks Chip Huyen’s *Designing Machine Learning Systems* (DMLS book) as a systems-framing source, with verified chapters on distributed training, debugging, monitoring, and infrastructure. [Canon, N07](../books.md)

[Inference] Treat this video as an adjacent, lower-evidence companion rather than a new reliability authority: its public outline adds explicit production-system, training-data, experiment-management, and observability topics, but the accessible sources do not establish material depth on distributed pretraining reliability beyond the book’s canon entry. Candidate canon note: “O’Reilly video by Kyle Gallatin; catalog topics include training data, experiment management, automation and observability; playback inaccessible; runtime/year unverified; not a checkpoint/fault-engineering reference.”

## Gaps

- O’Reilly Learning playback was blocked with HTTP 403; no transcript or lesson-level content was verified.
- The official catalog evidence available here did not verify the stated 2024 date or 75-minute runtime.
- No public evidence reviewed establishes course coverage of MFU accounting, interruptions/recovery, checkpoint state semantics, loss triage, flaky-node detection, or loader-stall diagnosis.
- No two-hour test can establish a 54-day run guarantee; use the exact tenant workload and report measurements, interruptions, and recovery outcomes without extrapolating to long-term uptime.

# N06 — Train Large Language Models Faster: Parallelism Deep Dive

Research date: 2026-10-11. All claims below carry a source URL.

Bench safety: operator approval is necessary before process interruption.
Default checks exclude power removal, PCIe reset, and hardware-error injection.
Report expected checkpoint rollback and replay separately from silent duplicate or skipped progress.

Claims are labelled [observed] (source states it), [calculated] (arithmetic from source data), or [inference] (application/proposal). Context: measured training acceptance for one GB300-class NVL72-class 18-tray rack in Chennai, about two hours before a 30–90-day lease / 54-day Llama run. PASS means a measurement on a named workload, not a vendor specification. This note assesses course coverage; it does not certify hardware or forecast survival/convergence.

## 1. Verified edition and chapters

[Observed] O’Reilly’s fetched catalog page identifies **Train Large Language Models Faster - Parallelism Deep Dive**, Paulo Dichone, Packt Publishing, ISBN 9781806110896, published June 2025, intermediate-to-advanced, English, total runtime **8h 50m**. The course is an on-demand video; full viewing is behind membership access. [O’Reilly course and outline](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781806110896/?orm_source=mcp)

[Observed] The accessible catalog provides a 16-chapter outline. Relevant chapters are 8 (data/model/hybrid parallelism, 49m); 9 (pipeline parallelism, bubbles/schedules, activation recomputation, frameworks, 55m); 10 (tensor parallelism, communication patterns/device mesh, 39m); 11–13 (hands-on data-parallel exercises and Runpod multi-GPU demonstration, 59m, 36m, 37m); and 14 (fault tolerance and checkpoint strategies, 49m). Chapter 14 titles explicitly include failure types/strategies; basic, incremental, asynchronous and multi-level checkpointing; storage; and a hybrid approach. [O’Reilly course and outline](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781806110896/?orm_source=mcp)

[Observed] Course outline names PyTorch, Transformers, TorchDistributed, DeepSpeed and Megatron-LM in Chapter 11; Chapter 12 names DeepSpeed. It also names MNIST, WikiText-2, IMDB and Runpod.io demonstrations. The retrieved syllabus does **not** establish pinned framework/library versions. “GPT-3 training” appears as a section title, but that alone does not show the instructor conducted or reproduced a GPT-3 benchmark. [O’Reilly course and outline](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781806110896/?orm_source=mcp)

[Observed] Packt’s official product search result describes an in-depth course on parallelism, but fetching the product page hit bot verification. An official Packt section result matches the ISBN and course title. Packt subscription chapter pages returned 403 on direct fetch. Therefore the O’Reilly catalog is the available detailed primary syllabus, not a viewing of the full video or lesson materials. [Packt product search result](https://www.packtpub.com/en-us/product/train-large-language-models-faster-parallelism-deep-dive-9781806110896) [Packt section](https://www.packtpub.com/en-sg/product/train-large-language-models-faster-parallelism-deep-dive-video-9781806110896/chapter/types-of-parallelism-in-llm-training-data-model-and-hybrid-parallelism-p8/section/real-world-example-data-parallelism-in-gpt-3-training-video8_4) [Packt subscription lesson](https://subscription.packtpub.com/video/data/9781806110896/p14/video14_4/basic-checkpointing-in-llm-training)

## 2. Training validation and reliability covered

[Observed] This is broader than a parallelism-only lecture: the syllabus includes pipeline bubbles, tensor communication, hands-on small-dataset distributed exercises, fault-tolerance concepts and multiple checkpoint strategies. Its strongest rack-relevant material is conceptual coverage of parallel layout/performance trade-offs and checkpoint design. [O’Reilly outline](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781806110896/?orm_source=mcp)

[Observed] Hands-on examples are explicitly described as small-model MNIST, WikiText-2, IMDB on Runpod, plus a “simulated parallelism on GPU” takeaway. The catalog does not state that these exercises measure rack-scale MFU, establish a repeatable numerical baseline, inject failures, restore optimizer/RNG/data-loader state, or verify exact-once data progress. They are tutorial/demo evidence, not evidence of production-scale benchmarking or successful fault recovery. [O’Reilly outline](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781806110896/?orm_source=mcp)

[Observed] The catalog advertises understanding and implementation of fault tolerance/checkpointing; the syllabus lists checkpoint types and storage considerations. It does not expose checkpoint schema, consistency guarantees, optimizer-state handling, RNG/sampler/data cursor handling, corruption validation, restart test results, recovery-time measurements, interruption-frequency statistics, or loss-triage procedures. A fault-tolerance title is not proof of tested recovery. [O’Reilly outline](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781806110896/?orm_source=mcp)

[Inference] The course helps an engineer ask which parallelism layout and checkpoint architecture to try. It cannot, from catalog evidence, supply a measured PASS/FAIL criterion for an NVL72-class rack, universal MFU threshold, flaky-node screening method, loader-stall diagnosis, or rare-failure rate. No recovery conclusion follows merely from parallelism coverage.

For interruption accounting, keep denominator semantics explicit: the cited Meta figure is **466 total = 47 planned + 419 unexpected** [calculated]; attribute unexpected interruptions against **419**, not 466. The course catalog offers no interruption statistics and does not support a rack survival/convergence forecast. [Llama 3, §3.3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783v3)

## 3. Portable bench checks [inference/proposal]

These are proposed measurements, not procedures demonstrated or validated by the course. Use a tenant-approved representative job and preserve logs/config hashes.

1. **Parallelism/MFU accounting:** Fix model, precision, sequence length, global batch, parallel degrees, optimizer and software versions. After declared warm-up, measure tokens/s, step-time distribution and rank spread; report the exact MFU FLOP convention and inputs. Compare only with a stated workload target/baseline, never a universal threshold. The course syllabus covers parallelism, pipeline bubbles and communication patterns, not rack MFU results. [Course outline](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781806110896/?orm_source=mcp) [Megatron-LM performance guidance](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM)
2. **Checkpoint/resume correctness:** Save at a known step; verify model and optimizer state, scheduler/step, RNG and sampler/data cursor as applicable; restart the same job and check continuity, loss/gradients and consumed sample/token position. Record save/load duration, lost work and replay/skip behavior. Course covers checkpoint strategies, but the specific state contract and successful restore are not established by the syllabus. [Course outline](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781806110896/?orm_source=mcp) [PyTorch Distributed Checkpoint](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.checkpoint.html)
3. **Interruption/recovery evidence:** In an isolated, approved test, cause a controlled worker/job interruption and record detection, restart outcome, checkpoint age, recovery time, lost/replayed steps and any rank failures. Distinguish planned from unexpected events; if referencing Meta’s 466/47/419 split, use 419 as the unexpected-event attribution denominator. This measures one exercised mode; do not generalize to all failures. [Course outline](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781806110896/?orm_source=mcp) [PyTorch torchrun fault-tolerance tutorial](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/ddp_series_fault_tolerance.html)
4. **Loss/numerical triage and flaky-rank screening:** Log loss, gradient norms, step latency and per-rank telemetry together. Flag outliers for investigation; a loss spike alone is neither proof of hardware fault nor proof of healthy training when absent. A two-hour observation can surface immediate repeatable issues, not bound rare SDC/failure probability. The syllabus does not establish an SDC detector or node-screening benchmark. [Course outline](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781806110896/?orm_source=mcp) [SDC in LLM training study](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.00726v1) [AEGIS OSDI ’26](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi26/presentation/lei)
5. **Loader/collective stall accounting:** Instrument data-wait time, step duration, collective timing and per-rank progress under the same named workload; preserve a trace to distinguish input starvation from communication/compute imbalance. The course lists storage/network fundamentals and distributed communication, but the catalog does not show a loader-stall measurement procedure. [Course outline](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781806110896/?orm_source=mcp) [PyTorch profiler recipe](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/recipes/recipes/profiler_recipe.html)

## 4. Canon relation and new-candidate judgment

[Observed] The initial canon, before this supplement, at [.lavish/training-research/books.md](../books.md) ranks current Megatron Bridge resiliency guidance and PyTorch DCP/torchrun documentation above books for operational recovery; it treats DMLS and *Reliable Machine Learning* as broad framing and did not list this course. The course’s distinct addition is one structured, video-based treatment spanning parallelism concepts through checkpoint strategy, with small hands-on examples. [Existing canon](../books.md) [O’Reilly course](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781806110896/?orm_source=mcp)

[Inference] **New candidate: useful supporting tutorial, not a canon replacement or rack-validation authority.** Add it as an optional conceptual primer for parallelism and checkpoint vocabulary, not as evidence for measured MFU, correctness, reliability or 54-day fitness. Operational docs remain the better source for version-specific APIs and executable recovery drills.

## Gaps

- Full Packt product/lesson fetch was blocked (bot verification / HTTP 403). O’Reilly supplied the identity and detailed catalog outline; the course video itself was not inspected. [Packt product](https://www.packtpub.com/en-us/product/train-large-language-models-faster-parallelism-deep-dive-9781806110896) [Packt lesson](https://subscription.packtpub.com/video/data/9781806110896/p14/video14_4/basic-checkpointing-in-llm-training)
- The public syllabus does not provide version-pinned PyTorch, DeepSpeed, Transformers or Megatron-LM; check the actual lessons/materials before treating any command or API as current.
- It does not provide measured NVL72/GB300 rack benchmarks, reproducible MFU accounting, interruption/recovery stats, complete optimizer/RNG/data restore validation, loader-stall data, or flaky-node/SDC results.
- A two-hour pass is only measured health under a named workload and interval; it cannot establish 30–90-day survival or convergence.

This supports monitoring design and observable application behavior, but the visible chapter does not document MFU accounting, rank-level stragglers, GPU fault screening, training-loss triage, or restart drills. [Manning LiveBook Ch. 11](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-platform-engineering/chapter-11)

**Meaning for this run.** [Inference] These chapters can help shape a workload’s metrics/artifact pipeline and data-quality/lineage records. They do not provide decisive evidence to certify a 54-day distributed Llama training run, and it would overstate the book to say otherwise. No claim of checkpoint/MFU/recovery coverage is made from title-page language such as “reliable ML system.”

## 3. Portable bench techniques (proposals, not book-prescribed rack gates)

1. **Make throughput accounting auditable.** [Inference] Run the tenant-approved training harness, identify warm-up separately, and retain step time and tokens/s over the measured interval; report model/config/software identifiers, batch, sequence length, precision, parallelism, and the exact FLOP convention if calculating MFU. Compare only to an agreed baseline for that same workload. A metrics/artifact pipeline is consistent with Ch. 8–9’s tracking coverage, but this accounting procedure is a bench proposal, not a quoted book recipe. [Ch. 8](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-platform-engineering/chapter-8) [Ch. 9](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-platform-engineering/chapter-9)

2. **Measure interruption and resume, rather than assume it.** [Inference] If the tenant-approved harness supports it, trigger a controlled process/job interruption, then record checkpoint age, save/restore durations, restart outcome, resumed step and any lost/replayed work. Verify the actual trainer’s required state (not merely model weights) against its own contract. Do not imply this book specifies full checkpoint state or teaches restart semantics: those topics are not evidenced in its accessible training chapter. Preserve artifacts and use a non-destructive, explicitly authorized test. [Ch. 8](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-platform-engineering/chapter-8) [Ch. 9](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-platform-engineering/chapter-9)

3. **Record loss with context; do not use loss alone as a health oracle.** [Inference] Keep step-indexed loss and relevant training metrics/artifacts alongside rank/step timing, interruption events, and data-quality provenance. If a trace is abnormal, triage against the named workload and its logged context; a short normal-looking loss curve cannot prove numeric correctness or rule out silent corruption. Ch. 8–9 establish metric tracking/validation as topics, not specialized loss-spike or SDC diagnosis. [Ch. 8](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-platform-engineering/chapter-8) [Ch. 9](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-platform-engineering/chapter-9)

4. **Separate input/data and compute symptoms.** [Inference] Retain data source/version and quality checks, and instrument loader wait/step timing in the chosen training harness. Report observed stall intervals and whether they co-occur with data access or compute/communication slowdowns; do not relabel generic pipeline monitoring as GPU data-loader diagnosis. The book’s Ch. 9 supports dataset management and quality assurance, while its visible material does not establish low-level loader-stall methods. [Ch. 9](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-platform-engineering/chapter-9)

[Inference] For all four proposals, the two-hour result is only “measured under named workload for stated interval.” It is not a forecast of a 30–90-day lease or a 54-day run. [Calculated] 54 days equals 1,296 hours, 648 two-hour windows; simple exposure multiplication is not a failure-rate estimate and establishes no forecast.

## 4. Canon relation and evidence-supported supersession limits

[Observed] The existing research canon ranks *MLOps Engineering at Scale* below docs/papers and below *Designing Machine Learning Systems* (DMLS) and *Reliable Machine Learning* for this rack-training purpose. Its Manning catalog evidence supports pipeline lifecycle, cloud-oriented workflow and monitoring, but not rack-level distributed pretraining claims. [Existing canon](../books.md) [Manning _MLOps Engineering at Scale_](https://www.manning.com/books/mlops-engineering-at-scale)

[Inference] This 2026 title is a useful **new MLOps/platform candidate**, not an evidenced replacement for distributed training reliability documentation or papers. Its stronger verified points relative to a generic pipeline-only reading are concrete chapters for training/evaluation components, metrics/artifacts, data handling/lineage, and monitoring. It could supersede *MLOps Engineering at Scale* for selected platform-engineering reading where the question is specifically orchestration, training pipeline structure, experiment tracking, data management or ML application monitoring—subject to direct comparison of relevant full chapters. The Manning catalog describes the earlier book as AWS/serverless-oriented; this new book’s accessible contents show Kubernetes/Kubeflow and broader platform tooling. That is a scope distinction, not proof of greater operational depth for every use. [New book contents](https://learning.oreilly.com/library/view/machine-learning-platform/9781633437333/) [MLOps Engineering at Scale catalog](https://www.manning.com/books/mlops-engineering-at-scale)

[Inference] Do **not** promote it above DMLS or *Reliable Machine Learning* as a whole without a comparative chapter-level review. The accessible contents establish the new book’s practical implementation focus, but not that it supersedes DMLS’s wider ML-systems framing or *Reliable Machine Learning*’s reliability/monitoring treatment. Above all, no inspected passage establishes it as a source for MFU formulae, full distributed checkpoint/resume state, interruption/recovery statistics, flaky-node detection, loss-spike/SDC triage, or GPU dataloader-stall diagnosis. Use workload-specific measured checks and current framework/vendor operational documentation for those decisions; set no universal GB300 gate from this book.

## Gaps

- No verified passage in the accessible chapters documents MFU accounting or GPU-flop conventions.
- No verified passage specifies complete distributed training checkpoint state, interruption/recovery statistics, or a checkpoint-resume validation procedure.
- No verified passage addresses flaky GPU/node screening, rank-level stragglers, loss-spike/SDC diagnosis, or device-level loader stalls.
- O’Reilly lists 504 pages and February 2026; Manning confirms ISBN and ©2026, and its catalog dates print availability February 23, 2026. Exact differences in MEAP versus final pagination, and format-specific page counts, could not be verified from the accessible primary pages.
- The public chapter evidence concerns practical platform examples; it cannot validate this rack’s performance or forecast 30–90-day reliability. Run and report measured named-workload checks; obtain the tenant’s exact training and recovery contract for an acceptance test.

# N03 — *Machine Learning System Design*

Research date: 2026-10-11. All claims below carry a source URL.

PASS means measured evidence for the named workload, not a specification claim. The acceptance window is about two hours before a 30–90-day lease and a possible 54-day Llama-class training run.

## 1. Verified edition and chapters

[Observed] Manning identifies the authors as **Valerii Babushkin and Arseny Kravchenko** (not “Dmitry Babushkin”), title *Machine Learning System Design: With end-to-end examples*, January 2025, ISBN 9781633438750, 376 pages. [O’Reilly book record](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/machine-learning-system/9781633438750)

[Observed] Directly readable Manning LiveBook samples verify Chapter 6 “Gathering datasets” (data sources, ETL, metadata, healthy data pipelines); Chapter 10 “Training pipelines” (tools/platforms, scalability, configurability, testing, property-based testing); Chapter 12 “Measuring and reporting results” (model performance, experiments, reporting); Chapter 13 “Integration” (release cycle, operation, overrides/fallbacks); and Chapter 14 “Monitoring and reliability” (software health, data quality/integrity, model quality/relevance, monitoring and response). [Ch. 6](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-system-design/chapter-6) [Ch. 10](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-system-design/chapter-10) [Ch. 12](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-system-design/chapter-12) [Ch. 13](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-system-design/chapter-13) [Ch. 14](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-system-design/chapter-14)

[Observed] Public samples expose outlines and selected introductory text, not necessarily full chapters. These topics are verified; coverage of MFU accounting, complete distributed checkpoint/resume state, interruption recovery, flaky-node detection, or loader-stall instrumentation is not established. Manning confirms the authors are Valerii Babushkin and Arseny Kravchenko.

## 2. Training-run validation and reliability evidence

[Observed] Chapters 6, 10, 12, 13, and 14 provide verified dataset/pipeline, pipeline testing, measurement/reporting, operational, and monitoring/reliability framing. The public evidence does not demonstrate a distributed-pretraining procedure. [Ch. 6](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-system-design/chapter-6) [Ch. 10](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-system-design/chapter-10) [Ch. 12](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-system-design/chapter-12) [Ch. 13](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-system-design/chapter-13) [Ch. 14](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-system-design/chapter-14)

[Inference] The verified chapters support requirements, data-pipeline health, testing, measurement/reporting, operational monitoring, and data/model-quality framing. Useful for acceptance criteria and observability, but not evidence of runtime training reliability. MFU accounting, interruption/restart drills, complete checkpoint/resume state, loss-spike diagnosis, flaky-node detection, and loader-stall instrumentation remain unverified, not proven absent.

[Observed] The Llama 3 paper reports 466 total interruptions = 47 planned + 419 unexpected. Unexpected-event attribution uses 419; these are context inputs, not claims from this book. [Llama 3, §3.3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783v3)

[Inference] A two-hour measurement window is not a 54-day guarantee. [Inference] Report measured named-workload throughput/MFU with declared formula and configuration, per-rank timing, loader wait, interruption counts/classification, checkpoint save/restore and resumed-state correctness, and observed loss behavior. A short normal loss trace or absence of a node failure cannot establish multiweek reliability.

[Inference] Runtime evidence is better sourced from executable framework/vendor documentation and workload-specific measurement than from this book’s public catalog description. The existing canon’s operational sources include [Megatron Bridge resiliency](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/training/resiliency.html), [PyTorch Distributed Checkpoint](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.checkpoint.html), and [PyTorch torchrun fault-tolerance tutorial](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/ddp_series_fault_tolerance.html). These are not evidence of what this book contains; they illustrate the gap between system-design framing and runtime recovery contracts.

## 3. Portable bench techniques

1. [Inference/proposal] **Freeze a workload card before timing.** Record model/workload identity, software/config hashes, precision, sequence/batch, parallelism, data source, warm-up exclusion, interval, and MFU convention. Compare only results for the same declared workload; do not make a universal GB300 threshold. [Manning Chapter 12 measuring/reporting](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-system-design/chapter-12); [Megatron-LM workload-specific performance context](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM). Measured evidence: tokens/s, step-time distribution and MFU under the recorded settings.
2. [Inference/proposal] **Measure input-path wait separately from compute.** Capture loader wait and per-rank step timing during the named run, so a slow input pipeline is not mislabeled as low hardware capability. [Manning Chapter 6 data-pipeline health](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-system-design/chapter-6); [Chapter 10 pipeline testing](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-system-design/chapter-10); [PyTorch profiler recipe](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/recipes/recipes/profiler_recipe.html). Measured evidence: loader-wait distribution and rank-level timing for the test interval.
3. [Inference/proposal] **Make recovery an explicit, non-destructive drill.** Use a disposable test job/checkpoint; record which state is saved, stop/restart the process or job, and verify resumed step/data position and training-state continuity. Do not imply that model weights alone constitute complete resume state. [PyTorch DCP](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.checkpoint.html); [torchrun fault-tolerance tutorial](https://docs.pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/ddp_series_fault_tolerance.html). Measured evidence: checkpoint write/read time, verified resume point, and lost-work interval.
4. [Inference/proposal] **Classify interruptions and node outliers rather than hiding them in averages.** Separate planned maintenance from unexpected interruptions, retain per-rank timings, and record recovery outcomes; the supplied meta-count makes the hardware denominator 419 unexpected interruptions, not all 466. [Llama 3 interruption anchor](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783v3); [Megatron Bridge resiliency](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/megatron-bridge/latest/training/resiliency.html). Measured evidence: counts by class, restart result, and rank timing distribution. This is an observation protocol, not a claim that two hours validates a rare-event rate.
5. [Inference/proposal] **Treat loss spikes as investigation triggers, not standalone verdicts.** Correlate loss with step/rank timing, input position and available health telemetry; report the observed trace and exceptions without claiming that no spike proves correctness. [Manning Chapter 12 measurement/reporting](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-system-design/chapter-12); [Chapter 14 monitoring/reliability](https://livebook.manning.com/book/machine-learning-system-design/chapter-14); [SDC study cited in canon](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.00726v1). Measured evidence: loss and relevant telemetry over the stated interval; no multiweek guarantee.

## 4. Canon relation and candidate status

[Inference] Add this as a **new candidate / complementary system-design source**, below operational distributed-training references for rack acceptance. Verified Chapters 6, 10, 12, 13, and 14 add pipeline design/testing, measurement/reporting, operational, and monitoring framing. They do not establish implementation-level distributed-training reliability coverage. It is not a replacement for the existing canon’s Megatron/PyTorch recovery material or its current reliability evidence.

[Observed] The existing canon already distinguishes book-level system framing from runtime training reliability and includes *Designing Machine Learning Systems*, *Reliable Machine Learning*, operational framework documentation, and reliability papers. [Canon](../books.md) This is a complementary candidate for pipeline design, measurement, and monitoring; the public samples enable chapter-level comparison, while runtime training reliability remains unverified.

## Gaps

- O’Reilly supplied learning URL returned HTTP 403. Manning LiveBook supplied readable samples for Chapters 6, 10, 12, 13, and 14, but not full-book text; claims are bounded to visible outlines and excerpts.
- The samples verify the cited chapter titles and headings, but do not resolve whether full-book text covers MFU, complete checkpoint/resume state, interruption recovery, loss-spike diagnosis, flaky-node detection, or loader-stall instrumentation.
- Public catalog evidence cannot establish a GB300/NVL72 threshold or a 54-day reliability guarantee. PASS must remain a measured assertion for a named workload and stated interval.

## 2. Training-run validation and reliability evidence

[Observed] The verified material supports broad reliability framing, data management, production monitoring/observability, and organizational practice. Chapter 4’s surfaced description says it covers infrastructure that accepts and prepares data for the training system. Chapter 9 is explicitly production-model monitoring and observability. [Chapter 4](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/reliable-machine-learning/9781098106218/ch04.html) · [Chapter 9](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/reliable-machine-learning/9781098106218/ch09.html)

[Observed] The accessible catalog headings and chapter abstract do not establish book guidance for MFU accounting; distributed GPU training telemetry; checkpoint save/load/resume; optimizer, RNG, sampler/data-position recovery; restart correctness; loss-spike triage during pretraining; flaky GPU screening; or GPU-side dataloader stalls. The book’s verified “training data” topic is not proof of device-level data-stall diagnosis. No specific procedure, threshold, or executable rack test was verified.

[Inference] Therefore the book is relevant to the acceptance case’s system-level monitoring and data-management concepts, but its available evidence does not make it an operational guide for certifying a multi-node LLM training rack. Do not claim the book prescribes a checkpoint drill, an MFU method, or a GB300/NVL72 reliability gate.

## 3. Portable bench techniques (inferences/proposals, not book procedures)

These are proposed ways to translate the verified high-level themes into measurable evidence. They are not attributed to the book and do not define universal pass thresholds.

1. **Name the workload and report its measured performance.** [Inference] For an agreed training configuration, record model/workload identity, software and config versions, measurement interval, warm-up treatment, tokens or steps per second, step-time distribution, and the declared MFU convention if MFU is reported. **Check:** report actual measurements and per-rank spread against a tenant-approved reference/envelope; do not treat vendor peak as PASS.
2. **Measure input-path waiting separately.** [Inference] Add instrumentation that distinguishes training compute/collective time from input wait or data-loading time. **Check:** report observed wait-time distribution and throughput during the named workload, with instrumentation and interval stated; a short sample does not establish long-run storage behavior.
3. **Test the actual recovery contract, if the tenant harness is available.** [Inference] Define what state and data position must survive; execute a controlled save/restore/restart on the representative job and compare resumed step, optimizer/training state, RNG and consumed-data position according to that contract. **Check:** record checkpoint integrity, save/load/resume duration, lost work, and any duplicate/skipped data. Do not substitute a weights-only load for a training-resume test.
4. **Correlate anomalies instead of using loss as a sole health verdict.** [Inference] If the workload exhibits a loss spike, preserve aligned loss/step, gradient or training telemetry, rank/node health, and input/collective timings for triage. **Check:** report whether an anomaly occurred and the evidence examined; a normal short loss trace does not prove absence of silent corruption or future faults.
5. **Screen for immediate weak nodes under exercised load.** [Inference] Preserve node/rank-level throughput and available health/error telemetry during the named run; flag persistent outliers for investigation. **Check:** state the observed interval, signals, and follow-up disposition. Do not call a two-hour clean sample a multi-week failure-rate estimate, or run destructive fault injection by default.

[Calculated] A two-hour sample is 1/648 of 54 days (54×24÷2). The exposure ratio is arithmetic, not a reliability forecast. It provides no defensible 30–90-day failure probability without representative longer exposure and an explicit statistical model.

## 4. Canon relation and headline decision

[Observed] The existing canon notes place *Reliable Machine Learning* tied with *Designing Machine Learning Systems* as a broad systems/monitoring book, while explicitly limiting claims to visible contents because the catalog was access-denied. This pass independently confirms the access barrier and strengthens the evidence for its data-management, monitoring/observability, and whole-system framing through official chapter/index search results, a Google Research chapter abstract, and author Q&A. It does not uncover full text or rack-scale pretraining reliability methods. [Canon](../books.md) · [Google Research chapter abstract](https://research.google/pubs/chapter-1b-data-management-principles-_reliable-machine-learning-applying-sre-principles-to-ml-in-production) · [Author Q&A](https://datatalks.club/books/20221121-reliable-machine-learning.html)

[Inference] Keep the book tied with DMLS as a broad conceptual canon, with this book stronger for SRE/monitoring and organization-level reliability framing. Do not promote it as the headline operational source for this bench: verified evidence does not cover the decisive training-run checks (MFU accounting, checkpoint/resume correctness, loss triage, flaky-node screening, or datastalls). It is useful context, not a measured pass standard.

## Gaps

- O’Reilly blocked direct access to the supplied Learning URL, catalog, and chapter pages (HTTP 403); full text and detailed passages could not be verified.
- Contents headings and an abstract do not show the depth, examples, or actual prescriptions in the relevant chapters.
- No verified passage establishes training-scale MFU, optimizer/RNG/data-position recovery correctness, pretraining loss-spike diagnosis, GPU flaky-node screening, or device-level datastall measurement.
- Pagination/date remain discrepant: supplied catalog says 408 pages; search-indexed O’Reilly metadata says 466 pages; Google Books says 410 pages and 2021, while O’Reilly indexed metadata identifies 2022. Direct publisher access was blocked, so 466 pages and the edition/date reconciliation are unverified. A differing-format/edition explanation is [inference], not an established fact.
- No source here supplies a universal two-hour pass threshold or a 30–90-day reliability forecast for this rack and workload.

# Machine Learning System Design, Video Edition

Research date: 2026-10-11. All claims below carry a source URL.

Bench safety: operator approval is necessary before process interruption.
Default checks exclude power removal, PCIe reset, and hardware-error injection.
Report expected checkpoint rollback and replay separately from silent duplicate or skipped progress.

Claims are marked [observed] (explicitly present in source), [calculated] (arithmetic), or [inference] (application to rack certification). Scope: GB300-class NVL72-class rack, 18 trays, Chennai; roughly two-hour measured acceptance before a 30–90-day lease / 54-day Llama-class run. PASS means measured under a named workload, never a specification claim.

## 1. Verified edition, chapters, and access

[Observed] The supplied O’Reilly URL resolves to **Machine Learning System Design, Video Edition**, by Arseny Kravchenko and Valerii Babushkin, published by Manning. O’Reilly lists February 2025, intermediate level, English, and **13h 29m**. The page says video editions show the book’s content, figures, code, diagrams, and text while a narrator reads it—“Like an audiobook that you can also watch as a video.” [O’Reilly video product and contents](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781633438750VE/?orm_source=mcp)

[Observed] The publicly visible contents include Parts 1–4 and chapters 1–16. Relevant named lessons include Chapter 6 “Properties of a healthy data pipeline”; Chapter 10 “Training pipelines,” “Scalability,” “Testing”; Chapter 12 “Measuring and reporting results”; Chapter 13 “Operating the system”; and Chapter 14 “Monitoring and reliability,” including “Software system health,” “Data quality and integrity,” and “Model quality and relevance.” The full visible list also includes dataset gathering, validation schemas, loss functions/metrics, baselines, error analysis, and serving/inference optimization. These are lesson titles, not a transcript or proof of technical depth. [O’Reilly contents](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781633438750VE/?orm_source=mcp)

[Observed] The catalog page is accessible for metadata and contents, but viewing is gated by membership/trial (“Watch now / Unlock full access”). I did not access video lessons or transcripts. [O’Reilly access page](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781633438750VE/?orm_source=mcp)

[Observed] Manning’s official page for the distinct title *Machine Learning Platform Engineering* describes building an internal ML platform, orchestration, resource allocation for training/inference/serving, and tools including Kubeflow, MLflow, BentoML, Evidently, and Feast. The O’Reilly URL supplied here identifies **Machine Learning System Design** only; it does not identify that second title or a video edition of it. The second catalog title is therefore **unverified as a video edition; a corresponding video URL is missing**. Do not merge the titles or guess a URL. [Manning: Machine Learning Platform Engineering](https://www.manning.com/books/machine-learning-platform-engineering) [Supplied O’Reilly item](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781633438750VE/?orm_source=mcp)

## 2. Training-validation and reliability coverage

[Observed] The titles directly support broad training-pipeline, testing, measurement/reporting, system operation, monitoring, data-integrity, and healthy-data-pipeline themes. They do not name MFU accounting, interruption/recovery drills, complete checkpoint/resume state, flaky-node detection, or GPU-cluster acceptance. The contents page alone cannot establish whether these topics are discussed inside a lesson. [O’Reilly contents](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781633438750VE/?orm_source=mcp)

[Inference] This is useful systems-design context, not a verified rack-scale distributed-training reliability procedure. In particular, a lesson titled “Training pipelines” or “Monitoring and reliability” is not evidence of checkpoint completeness, resume equivalence, node fault tolerance, or a multiweek warranty.

[Inference] For a two-hour acceptance, attach evidence to the exact representative workload: declared model/config/software, warm-up exclusions, tokens/s and step-time distribution, MFU convention, rank-level variation, loader-wait measurements, interruptions and recovery result, and checkpoint contents plus restore validation. No universal GB300/NVL72 pass threshold follows from this video catalog. Report “measured healthy under named workload for stated interval,” not “will survive 54 days.”

## 3. Portable techniques (inference/proposal)

1. [Inference/proposal] Turn the design-document framing into a workload acceptance record: goals, explicit non-goals, workload/config identity, measurement window, and tenant-approved thresholds. Measure throughput/MFU under that named configuration; do not compare unqualified peak specifications. Relevant listed lessons: “Design document,” “Measuring and reporting results.” [O’Reilly contents](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781633438750VE/?orm_source=mcp)
2. [Inference/proposal] Instrument the input path separately: record loader wait/timeouts, data-read latency, and step-time gaps alongside data-quality/integrity checks. Use these as measured signals to distinguish a loader stall from compute/collective delay; the catalog supports only general pipeline/data-integrity framing, not a specific stall detector. [O’Reilly contents](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781633438750VE/?orm_source=mcp)
3. [Inference/proposal] Make interruption recovery an explicit acceptance experiment: save the complete trainer state required by the actual job, stop/restart it, and verify resumed step and consumed-data position. Record checkpoint write/read times and lost work. The contents list testing and operations, but does not establish this particular procedure or guarantee that all state is saved. [O’Reilly contents](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781633438750VE/?orm_source=mcp)
4. [Inference/proposal] Triage loss anomalies with correlated evidence—step timing, data identity/quality, gradients or other trainer telemetry, and hardware/node health—rather than treating loss alone as a diagnosis. The lesson list includes loss/metrics and monitoring, but no specific SDC or flaky-node method is verified. [O’Reilly contents](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781633438750VE/?orm_source=mcp)
5. [Inference/proposal] Track every interruption and recovery event distinctly from steady-state performance, including reason, affected ranks, restart outcome, and remaining unknowns. Such a short test may reveal immediate faults; it cannot establish long-run reliability. [O’Reilly contents](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781633438750VE/?orm_source=mcp)

[Calculated] A 54-day run is 1,296 hours, or 648 two-hour windows. This ratio is exposure arithmetic, not a reliability estimate. [Inference] No two-hour longrun warranty can be derived from the video or a short test.

## 4. Canon relation and format duplication

[Observed] The initial canon, before this supplement, in [books.md](../books.md) lists Chip Huyen’s *Designing Machine Learning Systems* (DMLS), but did not list *Machine Learning System Design*. These are distinct works. Treat *Machine Learning System Design* as a new title/new candidate for the canon; this video is an alternate format of the separately researched Manning book by Babushkin and Kravchenko, not a related edition of DMLS. [Canon](../books.md) [Video item](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781633438750VE/?orm_source=mcp) [Related Manning book format](https://learning.oreilly.com/library/view/-/9781633438750/)

[Observed] O’Reilly describes Video Editions as rendering the book’s text and figures while narrated. The matching title is also linked from the video page as a book-format item. This makes the video an alternate format of *Machine Learning System Design*, not independent technical corroboration. Public metadata does not establish whether the lesson sequence or full content differs from the book; duplication is likely at least in the underlying text, but exact completeness/equivalence is unverified. [O’Reilly video product](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781633438750VE/?orm_source=mcp) [Related book link](https://learning.oreilly.com/library/view/-/9781633438750/)

[Inference] Add this as a format-specific catalog entry and a supplementary systems-design resource, not as a new independent reliability evidence source. Its broad framing can complement the canon’s operational docs, but it does not replace measured workload results or the canon’s specialized checkpoint/restart and resiliency references.

## Gaps

- [Observed] The supplied URL verifies *Machine Learning System Design, Video Edition* only. The catalog entry’s second title, **Machine Learning Platform Engineering Video Edition**, remains unverified, and its URL is missing. Manning’s book page is not proof that a video edition exists. [O’Reilly item](https://learning.oreilly.com/videos/-/9781633438750VE/?orm_source=mcp) [Manning book page](https://www.manning.com/books/machine-learning-platform-engineering)
- [Observed] Subscription-gated lessons were not inspected; no transcript, runtime-by-lesson breakdown, or evidence beyond visible metadata and contents is claimed.
- [Observed] The accessible catalog contents do not verify MFU accounting, interruption/recovery, complete checkpoint state, loss triage methods, flaky-node detection, or loader-stall diagnostics.
- [Inference] Neither this video nor a two-hour acceptance provides evidence for a 54-day reliability guarantee. Use longer exposure, fleet history, and an explicit reliability model for that question.

[Observed] The supplied O’Reilly Learning URL, ISBN 9781617296192, was fetched but returned an access-denied page; no ebook text was available through it. [Supplied O’Reilly URL](https://learning.oreilly.com/library/view/-/9781617296192/?orm_source=mcp)

## 2. Relevance to training-validation topics

[Observed] The clearest operationally relevant chapter is Ch. 4, “Structuring DL projects and hyperparameter tuning.” The other chapter titles and publisher description focus on vision architectures and tasks, not distributed training operations. [Google Books TOC](https://books.google.com/books/about/Deep_Learning_for_Vision_Systems.html?id=sDszEAAAQBAJ) [Manning](https://www.manning.com/books/deep-learning-for-vision-systems)

[Inference] Ch. 4 is a useful source of experimental discipline and debugging habits, but the verified chapter listing does not establish guidance on MFU accounting, distributed checkpoint/restart correctness, interruption recovery, flaky accelerator nodes, data-loader stalls, or long-run reliability. Do not cite this book as evidence that an NVL72-class rack is reliable or that a 54-day Llama run will complete.

[Inference] For a two-hour category window, use the book only to inform a controlled, named-workload experiment: capture the configuration and baseline, vary one factor at a time where safe, and keep observed outcomes separate from diagnosis. Measure tokens/s and step-time distribution, declared MFU convention, rank skew, loader wait, loss/gradient signals, and checkpoint save/restore under the actual tenant-representative training stack. These are proposed checks, not book-prescribed thresholds. No universal hardware gate follows from this book.

## 3. Portable techniques — proposals, not distributed-LLM claims

1. **Structure the experiment and hold a baseline.** [Observed] Ch. 4 explicitly concerns project structure and hyperparameter tuning. [TOC](https://books.google.com/books/about/Deep_Learning_for_Vision_Systems.html?id=sDszEAAAQBAJ) [Inference] For the rack, record model/workload identity, software and config, parallelism, precision, batch/sequence settings, warm-up exclusion, measurement interval and metric definitions before comparing runs. **Measured check:** repeat the same workload/config; report tokens/s, step-time percentiles, per-rank spread and MFU formula. The book’s vision context does not validate any particular LLM settings or MFU threshold.

2. **Debug with controlled changes rather than confounded tuning.** [Observed] Ch. 4 title explicitly pairs project structuring with hyperparameter tuning. [Inference] If throughput, loss or stability changes, preserve the baseline and change one workload or system variable at a time when feasible; log the exact change and rollback path. **Measured check:** compare matched intervals and record loss plus gradient-norm telemetry, but treat anomalies as signals to investigate—not proof of faulty hardware. No source claim here covers distributed fault attribution.

3. **Keep data preparation and model behavior observable separately.** [Observed] The book is about end-to-end vision systems and includes classification, detection, transfer learning and embeddings; publisher materials describe real-world vision applications. [Manning](https://www.manning.com/books/deep-learning-for-vision-systems) [Inference] For a training bench, instrument input wait separately from accelerator compute/collectives so a slow step is not automatically called a GPU problem. **Measured check:** collect loader wait/throughput alongside step time and rank timings during the named workload. This is an adaptation; no verified source text establishes distributed LLM loader-stall diagnostics.

4. **Treat loss behavior as task- and data-dependent, not a stand-alone health verdict.** [Observed] The verified contents cover model development topics in a vision-learning context, but the accessible sources do not reveal detailed loss-spike or gradient-debugging prescriptions. [Inference] Track loss and gradient norms against the same workload’s baseline; on an anomaly, preserve logs/checkpoint and correlate with rank, input, and system telemetry before deciding whether to resume or reject. **Measured check:** report anomaly count/timing and the evidence used for disposition; do not claim “no spike” proves correctness.

5. **Make recovery a separate, explicit experiment.** [Observed] The verified TOC and Manning description do not claim checkpointing, restart semantics, or interruption recovery. [Inference] Since those are critical to the rack decision but outside established book coverage, run a non-destructive checkpoint/restore drill using the actual tenant stack: save, validate, restart from that artifact, and verify expected step and data position. **Measured check:** record checkpoint integrity, save/load time, restored step/state and lost-work interval. Do not treat ordinary vision examples or this book as proof of distributed recovery correctness.

## 4. Canon relation and candidate

[Observed] The canonical `.lavish/training-research/books.md` already prioritizes operationally specific Megatron Bridge resiliency and PyTorch distributed-checkpoint/torchrun documentation, and explicitly distinguishes measured two-hour evidence from multi-week reliability claims. It also ranks DMLS and *Reliable Machine Learning* for broad systems/monitoring context. This book was not in its ranked canon. [Canon](../books.md)

[Inference] Add this as a low-priority, narrowly scoped candidate only: its strongest verified fit is Ch. 4’s project structuring and hyperparameter-tuning framing; it is not a reliability reference for distributed pretraining. It does not displace the canonical operational docs, nor add a book-based acceptance threshold. The Llama 3 accounting context remains 466 total = 47 planned + 419 unexpected, with 419 as the hardware-attribution denominator; this book supplies no evidence to revise that accounting. [Llama 3, §3.3.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783v3) A two-hour measurement cannot forecast the 54-day run.

## Gaps

- The supplied O’Reilly URL was inaccessible. No full text or sample chapter was retrieved; Manning’s public title page and Google Books’ TOC are the basis for chapter claims.
- The 2020 publication year and catalog 480-page count were supplied in the task but not independently confirmed from accessible primary page text.
- The visible TOC/catalog cannot establish the detailed methods or numerical recommendations inside Ch. 4. No numerical loss, gradient, throughput or reliability thresholds are attributed to the book.
- Verified sources do not cover distributed LLM MFU conventions, interruptions/recovery, checkpoint/resume correctness, flaky nodes, loader stalls, or 30–90-day/54-day reliability. Validate those with the named workload and current framework/vendor operational documentation; do not infer a long-run forecast from a two-hour pass.

# Training-run health research

Question: What can a two-hour rack test measure before a tenant starts a 30–90-day training run?

Research date: 2026-10-11.

Audience: rack-bench maintainers, operators, and training tenants.
Scope: one GB300-class NVL72-class rack, 18 trays, Chennai, India.
Expected answer: seven sourced briefs and a proposed measured training suite.
Exclusions: vendor-only PASS claims, unsafe default fault injection, and multi-week reliability guarantees.
This report contains research, not rack measurements.
The [catalog supplement](oreilly.md) adds ten source notes without changing the seven category nodes.
Its [separate report](oreilly/research.md) contains the supplement map and lessons.

## Node map

Each node uses an independent category search.
No lesson requires another category's result.
The proposed suite uses all seven results.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
N01["Neocloud training promises"]
N02["Hyperscaler pre-flight and recovery"]
N03["AI-lab training failures and accounting"]
N04["Company reliability practice"]
N05["ClusterMAX training coverage"]
N06["Academic methods and benchmark limits"]
N07["Books and canonical guides"]
```

## Node table

| Node | Question | Dependencies | Acceptance condition | Child | State |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| N01 | What do neoclouds promise for long training runs? | None | Separate claims, measured interruptions, recovery tools, and gaps. | neoclouds | done |
| N02 | What must hyperscaler tenants check before long runs? | None | Source AWS, Azure, and GCP recipes, recovery limits, and test needs. | hyperscalers | done |
| N03 | What do public AI-lab runs show about training health? | None | Check interruption denominators, MFU, resume state, and loss triage. | ai-labs | done |
| N04 | What company practices detect and contain training failures? | None | Explain telemetry, straggler screening, restart, and GB300 transfer limits. | large-companies | done |
| N05 | What training health does ClusterMAX measure or omit? | None | Check current methodology, reliability criteria, public tooling, and bounded gaps. | clustermax | done |
| N06 | What academic methods support training validation? | None | Check recovery papers, failure traces, stability, and MLPerf boundaries. | academia | done |
| N07 | Which books and guides support this bench? | None | Rank relevant chapters and docs; distinguish coverage from evidence. | books | done |

## N01: Availability is not training progress

The question separates provider promises from measured job behavior.
An availability SLA defines service downtime and remedies.
Goodput measures useful training progress over time or paid capacity.
These quantities differ because checkpoint rollback and restart consume time.

CoreWeave documents checkpoint signal handling and straggler detection.
Nebius documents Soperator persistence and separate preemptible-VM limits.
Lambda documents reserved clusters and ephemeral-storage limits.
Together documents active and passive health checks.
These descriptions establish mechanisms, not multi-week outcomes.

ClusterMAX reports a Together health-check timeout that drains active jobs.
It reports one Nebius GB300 recovery that takes 8h40m.
Neither event establishes a provider-wide recovery-time distribution.
Test the actual job recovery path before the lease.
Keep maintenance, storage, and replacement terms separate from rack health.
See the [brief](neoclouds.md), [record](nodes/N01.md), and
[ClusterMAX source](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard).

## N02: Check the actual launcher and transport

The question identifies tenant checks before a long run.
A replacement node does not necessarily restore training state.
AWS documents configurations that requeue a job from the beginning.
The tenant must verify supported auto-resume and checkpoint behavior.

AWS's EFA recipe checks the selected NCCL transport in logs.
Azure documents health agents, topology, and drain state.
Google A3 guides describe NCCL plugin and launcher constraints.
These recipes do not describe interchangeable GB300 settings.
Record the installed versions, rank map, and actual transport.

A termination notice helps only when the trainer handles it.
Measure signal-to-checkpoint time against the applicable notice window.
Lease expiry and replacement capacity remain separate questions.
Two hours cannot establish future capacity or notice delivery.
See the [brief](hyperscalers.md), [record](nodes/N02.md),
[AWS EFA recipe](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/efa-start-nccl.html), and
[AWS recovery guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-hyperpod-resiliency-slurm-auto-resume.html).

## N03: Count useful work and correct recovery

The question uses public training runs to define health evidence.
Meta reports 466 interruptions during a 54-day Llama 405B snapshot.
The total contains 47 planned and 419 unexpected interruptions.
The hardware percentages refer to unexpected interruptions.
Some table percentages do not reconcile with the printed counts.
Do not convert this fleet record into a rack survival forecast.

MFU compares declared model FLOPs with a precision-specific peak.
Its meaning depends on the model, token count, and measured interval.
Report useful tokens/s and full-window goodput beside MFU.

BLOOM records optimizer, tensor-parallel, and RNG synchronization defects.
A restart can run while its state remains incorrect.
Compare resumed state with an uninterrupted control on the same remaining batches.
Record optimizer, scheduler, RNG, data position, and step counters.
See the [brief](ai-labs.md), [record](nodes/N03.md),
[Meta paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.21783v3), and
[BLOOM chronicles](https://github.com/bigscience-workshop/bigscience/blob/master/train/tr11-176B-ml/chronicles.md).

## N04: Diagnose the first stalled rank

The question examines detection, diagnosis, exclusion, and recovery.
Synchronous training waits for every required rank.
One slow rank can reduce throughput across the allocation.
A collective timeout does not identify the original fault.
A rank can stall in its loader before it enters the collective.

MegaScale uses heartbeats, rank timing, traffic metrics, and diagnostic tests.
Meta uses repeated health checks and historical suspect-node evidence.
These methods connect training symptoms with resource identity.
Collect per-rank compute, communication, input wait, and checkpoint spans.
Join these spans with device and fabric events.

Silent corruption can leave values within numeric limits.
A normal loss curve does not prove correct computation.
Known-answer steps provide limited checks, not complete silent-error coverage.
Two hours cannot reproduce historical screening or delayed numerical effects.
See the [brief](large-companies.md), [record](nodes/N04.md),
[MegaScale](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi24-jiang-ziheng.pdf), and
[Meta hardware methods](https://engineering.fb.com/2025/07/22/data-infrastructure/how-meta-keeps-its-ai-hardware-reliable/).

## N05: Keep ClusterMAX evidence types separate

The question checks current coverage instead of an inherited market claim.
ClusterMAX 3.0 describes Llama 3.1 8B and GPT-OSS MoE training.
It also describes an eight-hour combined compute/network burn-in.
Its public cmax tool remains a configuration audit.
Thus, a synthetic-only description of ClusterMAX is incorrect.

The inspected public methodology does not establish numerical resume equivalence.
It does not publish a standardized loss acceptance procedure for the named pretraining runs.
Its fault drills time detection, drain, and return to service.
These endpoints differ from restored training progress.

Keep audit, workload performance, burn-in, recovery, and convergence results separate.
The proposed bench adds explicit state comparison and progress accounting.
This describes a public-method gap, not unknown private procedures.
A two-hour suite cannot reproduce the eight-hour burn-in.
See the [brief](clustermax.md), [record](nodes/N05.md),
[methodology](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/clustermax-30-the-industry-standard), and
[public cmax](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/clustermax).

## N06: Test the checkpoint transaction

The question checks recovery mechanisms and benchmark boundaries.
Checkpoint staging, persistence, and publication are different operations.
CheckFreq preserves data position and separates snapshot from persistence.
MegaScale also separates host staging from remote writes.
A staged snapshot does not establish a durable checkpoint.
Reject incomplete generations and load the previous complete generation.

Oobleck reconstructs state through replicas.
Varuna uses elastic configurations and checkpoint-based recovery with background copying.
Do not label these mechanisms as one generic recovery method.

MLPerf Closed measures time to its defined quality target.
Open permits arbitrary stopping criteria with reported quality.
General checkpoint optionality has a Qwen3.5 post-training exception.
That scoring exception does not test crash-recovery correctness.
